<webpage_content>
[Skip to content](#content)


[![Parkinson's News Today logo](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Parkinsons-News-Today.svg)](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com) 

[Newsletter](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/newsletter)

# Parkinson’s disease symptoms

Last updated Aug. 23, 2023, by [Marisa Wexler](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/author/marisa-wexler/), MS  
 ![✅](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/14.0.0/svg/2705.svg) *Fact-checked by [Ana de Barros](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/author/ana-de-barros/), PhD*

[Motor symptoms](#Motor)

[Nonmotor symptoms](#Nonmotor)

[Early signs](#Early)

[Related conditions](#Related)

[FAQs](#faqs)

[Parkinson’s disease](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/what-is-parkinsons-disease/) can cause a wide array of symptoms. The disease is perhaps best known for how it affects movement and balance, creating problems with tremor, rigidity, and slowed movement. People with Parkinson’s can also experience nonmotor symptoms that may lead to problems with cognition, mental health, and sleeping.

Parkinson’s is a progressive disorder where symptoms usually start off very subtly, then gradually worsen with time. The disease affects every person differently, and not everyone will experience all the possible symptoms or progress at the same rate. With advances in treatment, most people with Parkinson’s, estimated at [more than 10 million worldwide](https://www.parkinson.org/understanding-parkinsons/statistics#:~:text=Nearly%2090%2C000%20people%20in%20the,are%20diagnosed%20before%20age%2050.), are expected to have a normal or near-normal life expectancy.

[Parkinson’s is caused by](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/what-causes-parkinsons-disease/) the loss of brain cells responsible for making a chemical messenger called dopamine. The lack of dopamine signaling is ultimately what gives rise to most symptoms of Parkinson’s disease.

## Motor symptoms

Parkinson’s disease is characterized by changes in movement. The presence of these [motor symptoms](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/parkinsons-disease-symptoms/motor/) is critical for confirming a [diagnosis of Parkinson’s](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/parkinsons-disease-tests-diagnosis/).

Motor symptoms in Parkinson’s [are commonly divided](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0149763415300919?via%3Dihub) into four main categories:

* bradykinesia (slowed movements)
* tremor
* rigidity
* postural instability (problems with balance and walking difficulties).

### Slowed movements

[Bradykinesia](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/parkinsons-disease-symptoms/motor/bradykinesia/), or abnormally slowed movements, is one of the disease’s core symptoms. In fact, based on current diagnostic criteria, a person can only be [formally diagnosed with Parkinson’s if this symptom is present](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7385761/#:~:text=The%20diagnosis%20of%20PD%20is,or%20pronation%E2%80%93supination%20hand%20movements.&text=In%20addition%2C%20rest%20tremor%20or,to%20confirm%20a%20parkinsonian%20syndrome.), alongside other motor symptoms such as tremor and rigidity.

Bradykinesia may manifest with changes in walking that cause a slow, shuffling gait or less swinging of the arms while walking. Patients may also experience more difficulty in starting movements, such as rising from a chair.

Parkinson’s bradykinesia can affect the hands, making it more difficult to perform activities that require a lot of dexterity and precise control of the fingers, such as buttoning a shirt, brushing teeth, cutting food, or opening packages. The face may be affected, leading to slowed blinking and less active facial expressions.

People who are experiencing bradykinesia often describe it as feeling similar to profound tiredness or abnormal muscle weakness.

### Tremor

[Tremor](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/parkinsons-disease-symptoms/motor/parkinsonian-tremor/), or involuntary shaking, is one of the most well-known symptoms of Parkinson’s. Tremors make it harder to perform many activities that require fine motor coordination, such as shaving, writing, and getting dressed.

As one of the first early symptoms of Parkinson’s disease, tremor usually affects only one side of the body first, then spreads to affect both sides as the disease progresses.

The main type of tremor seen in people with Parkinson’s is known as a resting tremor. In this type of tremor, the shaking becomes most apparent when the person is not consciously moving their body, but during conscious movement, the tremor gets less intense or may seem to disappear entirely. For example, the hands may shake when the person is standing without moving their hands, then the shaking lessens when the person goes to pick something up.

Patients often experience a so-called [“pill-rolling” tremor](https://www.parkinson.org/understanding-parkinsons/movement-symptoms/tremor), which is characterized by hand movements that look as if the person is continually rolling a small object between the thumb and forefinger. They may also experience a supination and pronation tremor, where the palm flips up and down.

Tremor can also affect other body parts, including the mouth or legs. Some patients even report feeling an internal tremor, or an invisible shaking sensation in the abdomen or chest.

Although tremor is a well-known symptom of Parkinson’s and is present in most patients, as many as 1 in 5 people with the disease will not experience tremor. This symptom appears to be slightly less common in younger people with Parkinson’s.

### Rigidity

[Rigidity](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/rigidity/) refers to muscles that are abnormally stiff and tight, limiting normal range of motion. This can make movements such as standing up more challenging, and contribute to reduced swinging of the arms while walking, reduced facial expressions, and balance problems.

Due to the combination of rigidity and bradykinesia, many people with Parkinson’s have [abnormally small handwriting](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470193/), referred to as micrographia. These motor symptoms can also cause [vocal issues and problems with speech](https://www.parkinson.org/library/fact-sheets/speech-therapy#:~:text=Speech%20and%20Voice%20Disorders%20in,slowness%20of%20movement%20and%20tremor.). Many people with Parkinson’s have an unusually soft and quiet speaking voice, referred to as hypophonia.

Rigidity can lead to pain and discomfort in affected muscles and make it harder to roll over in bed, hampering efforts to get comfortable and fall asleep.

When force is applied to help bend the rigid limb of someone with Parkinson’s, the muscles will often respond with short, jerky movements and pauses in between. This is often called “cogwheel” rigidity, as the movement resembles the way a gear moves.

Rigidity usually isn’t a prominent symptom in the earliest stages of Parkinson’s. However, virtually all patients will experience some rigidity as the disease progresses. Rigidity typically affects just one side of the body at first, then it can spread to other areas over time.

### Problems with balance and walking

[Difficulties with balance and walking](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/gait-and-balance-problems/) affect most people with Parkinson’s, though these symptoms usually don’t develop until relatively late in the course of the disease.

Balance problems, also called [postural instability](https://www.parkinson.org/understanding-parkinsons/movement-symptoms/postural-instability), can increase the risk of falls, which can cause serious injury. Therefore, an important part of disease management for most patients is taking precautions to mitigate the risk of falls, including doing exercises to improve balance as well as removing tripping hazards from the environment.

People with Parkinson’s commonly experience [changes in how they walk](https://www.parkinson.org/understanding-parkinsons/movement-symptoms/trouble-moving), often taking many small steps at a slower pace than normal. They also tend to have difficulty turning around (usually needing to take many small steps to do so), and to shuffle while they walk, with less movement in the arms and torso.

Freezing, or [akinesia](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/parkinsons-disease-symptoms/motor/akinesia/), is when a person is momentarily unable to move their muscles or limbs, and commonly occurs in patients when they start walking, or when faced with a doorway or passerby. Freezing may increase the risk of falls.

### Medication side effects

Most people with Parkinson’s are treated with [levodopa and its derivatives](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/levodopa/), which are therapies that can help the brain to produce more dopamine. While these [treatments](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/approved-treatments-for-parkinsons-disease/) can be effective for managing Parkinson’s, their long-term use usually leads to [dyskinesia](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/dyskinesia/), or erratic, uncontrolled movements.

Dyskinesia is not a symptom of Parkinson’s itself, but since most patients are treated with levodopa and related therapies, many of them experience dyskinesia. This side effect usually develops after patients have been on these medications for several years.

### Other motor symptoms

In some patients, Parkinson’s causes other motor symptoms, including vision problems such as blurred vision or difficulty looking up, painful muscle cramps ([dystonia](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/parkinsons-disease-symptoms/motor/dystonia-and-pd/)), and difficulty maintaining an upright posture which can lead to stooping and abnormal curvature of the spine (scoliosis or kyphosis).

## Nonmotor symptoms

While these [nonmotor symptoms](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/parkinsons-disease-symptoms/non-motor/) are not used to define a Parkinson’s diagnosis, they can cause substantial problems in day-to-day life.

### Autonomic dysfunction

The autonomic nervous system is responsible for controlling involuntary bodily processes, such as regulating breathing, digestion, and blood pressure. People with Parkinson’s commonly experience autonomic dysfunction, where the autonomic nervous system is unable to properly regulate these involuntary processes. This can lead to symptoms including:

* difficulty swallowing (dysphagia)
* increased sweating ([hyperhidrosis](https://www.parkinsons.org.uk/information-and-support/skin-and-sweating-problems#:~:text=People%20with%20Parkinson's%20may%20have,also%20experience%20sweating%20at%20night.))
* excessive drooling ([sialorrhea](https://www.parkinson.org/understanding-parkinsons/movement-symptoms/drooling))
* orthostatic hypotension, where blood pressure suddenly drops when a person stands up, which can cause lightheadedness and, in severe instances, fainting
* gastrointestinal issues such as constipation or incontinence
* urinary issues such as needing to urinate frequently or feeling a strong sense of urgency to urinate
* problems with sexual performance and satisfaction such as erectile dysfunction or vaginal tightness.

### Mood and cognitive changes

Issues with mental health and cognition affect many people with Parkinson’s and may include:

* depression
* anxiety
* apathy (loss of motivation)
* psychosis, which can include hallucinations (seeing, hearing, or otherwise sensing something that isn’t there) and/or delusions (fixed beliefs with no basis in reality)
* problems with decision-making and multitasking
* memory issues
* bradyphrenia (slowed thinking) or abulia (temporary inability to think or act).

People with Parkinson’s have a six times higher chance of developing dementia, where cognitive problems become severe enough that they cause issues in day-to-day life.

### Sensory problems and skin issues

Many people with Parkinson’s experience changes in sensation such as:

* loss of smell (hyposmia)
* oily skin (seborrhea)
* tingling or burning sensations.

People with Parkinson’s are at increased risk of developing skin cancers such as melanoma.

### Sleep issues

People with Parkinson’s often have trouble getting good sleep, due to issues like [difficulty falling asleep](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/parkinsons-disease-and-sleep/) and waking up frequently in the night or very early in the morning. Patients also commonly report feeling sleepy during the daytime, and may experience sudden attacks of sleepiness.

Another common disease complication is [REM sleep behavior disorder](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/rem-sleep-behavior-disorder/symptoms-causes/syc-20352920), where a person will act out dreams by making noises and large, often violent, movements. (REM, or rapid eye movement, is the period of sleep where dreaming occurs).

Restless legs syndrome, where a person feels the need to move their legs due to uncontrolled discomfort, can affect people with Parkinson’s. This sensation typically is most problematic when a person is laying down or sitting, or trying to sleep.

## Early signs

Although when symptoms appear and how quickly they progress varies for every patient, certain symptoms and signs are [common in the early stages of Parkinson’s disease](https://www.parkinson.org/understanding-parkinsons/10-early-signs). These include:

* constipation
* REM sleep behavior disorder
* loss of smell
* depression
* fatigue
* tremor
* difficulty rising from a chair
* small, cramped handwriting
* weak voice
* reduced facial expression
* dizziness or fainting
* stooping or hunching over
* arms not swinging normally while walking.

## Related conditions that cause Parkinson’s-like symptoms

Most symptoms of Parkinson’s disease are not unique to Parkinson’s and are also found in other conditions. One of the main challenges in diagnosing Parkinson’s is ruling out other disorders that can cause similar symptoms.

Some of the [conditions that can cause Parkinson’s-like symptoms](https://www.parkinson.org/understanding-parkinsons/getting-diagnosed/conditions-that-mimic-parkinsons) include:

* Essential tremor, a type of uncontrolled shaking, can affect the hands, arms, and voice. These tremors usually affect both sides of the body and are worse when a person is moving, unlike the tremors seen in Parkinson’s disease that typically start on one side of the body and are usually worse when the patient is at rest.
* Normal pressure hydrocephalus occurs when the fluid around the brain and spinal cord does not drain properly, putting abnormal pressure on the nervous system. It can cause Parkinson’s-like symptoms such as trouble walking, issues with urination, and cognitive difficulties.
* Corticobasal syndrome is characterized by Parkinson’s-like symptoms like stiffness and tremor, but also other symptoms such as uncontrolled movements and difficulty with language.
* Multiple system atrophy can cause many symptoms similar to those seen in Parkinson’s, but it’s characterized by more widespread damage in the nervous system, particularly in the autonomic nervous system that controls unconscious bodily functions.
* Progressive supranuclear palsy is another disorder that can appear similar to Parkinson’s but is [marked by unique symptoms](https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/progressive-supranuclear-palsy-psp#:~:text=There%20are%20several%20key%20differences,bend%20forward%20rather%20than%20backward.), including abnormal eye movements and a tendency to lean backward (whereas people with Parkinson’s usually stoop forward).
* Dementia with Lewy bodies also causes many symptoms similar to Parkinson’s, but these symptoms usually appear in a different order. In Parkinson’s, motor symptoms develop early on, whereas in dementia with Lewy bodies, cognitive problems are the first symptoms to appear.

## FAQs about Parkinson's disease symptoms

[a

#### What are the most common symptoms of Parkinson’s disease?](#)

Category: [Symptoms](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/parkinsons-disease-symptoms/?include_category=symptoms)

Parkinson’s disease can cause a wide range of [motor](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/parkinsons-disease-symptoms/motor/) and [nonmotor](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/parkinsons-disease-symptoms/non-motor/) symptoms. Common motor symptoms include tremor, rigidity, slowed movements, and difficulty with balance and walking. Common nonmotor symptoms include constipation, sleep issues, loss of smell, and depression.

[a

#### What are the early signs of Parkinson’s disease?](#)

Category: [Symptoms](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/parkinsons-disease-symptoms/?include_category=symptoms)

Early warning signs of Parkinson’s disease may include [tremor](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/parkinsons-disease-symptoms/motor/parkinsonian-tremor/), difficulty rising from a chair, constipation, loss of smell, weak voice, small handwriting, trouble sleeping, reduced facial expression, arms not swinging normally while walking, and stooping or hunching over.

[a

#### What causes tremors in Parkinson’s disease?](#)

Category: [Symptoms](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/parkinsons-disease-symptoms/?include_category=symptoms)

Like many other symptoms of Parkinson’s, tremor is [caused](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/what-causes-parkinsons-disease/) by a lack of dopamine signaling. Dopamine is a chemical that nerves use to communicate with each other and the rest of the body. Parkinson’s is caused by the death and dysfunction of brain cells responsible for making dopamine.

[a

#### How quickly do Parkinson’s symptoms progress?](#)

Category: [Symptoms](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/parkinsons-disease-symptoms/?include_category=symptoms)

Although [Parkinson’s disease](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/what-is-parkinsons-disease/) symptoms tend to worsen over time, how quickly these symptoms progress varies from patient to patient, and it’s currently difficult to make accurate predictions about the speed of disease progression.

[a

#### Can Parkinson’s symptoms lessen?](#)

Category: [Symptoms](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/parkinsons-disease-symptoms/?include_category=symptoms)

While Parkinson’s symptoms tend to get progressively worse over time, symptom severity can vary from day to day and even from hour to hour. Symptoms that cause problems on one day may be less problematic the next. Medications to control symptoms may help to improve the experience of [living with Parkinson’s disease](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/living-with-parkinsons-disease-2/), but no [treatments](https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/approved-treatments-for-parkinsons-disease/) are currently available that can slow or stop the overall progression of the disease.

args.summary:
This webpage from Parkinson's News Today (last updated Aug. 23, 2023) provides a comprehensive overview of Parkinson's disease symptoms. Parkinson's disease affects an estimated 10 million people worldwide and is caused by the loss of dopamine-producing brain cells, leading to a wide range of motor and nonmotor symptoms that progressively worsen over time.

**Motor Symptoms:** The four main categories are: bradykinesia (slowed movements, which is required for formal diagnosis), tremor (most commonly "pill-rolling" resting tremor, but about 1 in 5 patients do not experience tremor), rigidity (abnormally stiff muscles, often with "cogwheel" rigidity), and postural instability (balance and walking difficulties, usually developing later in the disease). Long-term levodopa use can cause dyskinesia (erratic uncontrolled movements). Other motor symptoms include vision problems, dystonia, and spinal curvature.

**Nonmotor Symptoms:** These include autonomic dysfunction (difficulty swallowing, excessive sweating, drooling, orthostatic hypotension, gastrointestinal issues, urinary issues, sexual problems), mood and cognitive changes (depression, anxiety, apathy, psychosis, dementia risk is 6 times higher), sensory problems (loss of smell, oily skin, tingling), and sleep issues (difficulty falling/staying asleep, REM sleep behavior disorder, restless legs syndrome).

**Early Signs:** Constipation, REM sleep behavior disorder, loss of smell, depression, fatigue, tremor, difficulty rising from a chair, small handwriting, weak voice, reduced facial expression, dizziness, stooping, and reduced arm swing while walking.

**Related Conditions:** Essential tremor, normal pressure hydrocephalus, corticobasal syndrome, multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy, and dementia with Lewy bodies can all cause Parkinson's-like symptoms but have distinguishing features.

**FAQs:** Common symptoms include motor and nonmotor issues; early signs include tremor, constipation, and sleep problems; tremors are caused by dopamine deficiency; symptom progression varies by patient; and while symptoms can fluctuate day-to-day and medications help, no treatments currently slow disease progression.

# Slowness of movement (bradykinesia) and muscle rigidity in Parkinson’s

Slowness of movement (bradykinesia) and muscle stiffness (rigidity) are both typical motor [symptoms](https://www.fightparkinsons.org.au/understand-parkinsons/signs-symptoms) of Parkinson’s.

## Everybody with Parkinson’s bradykinesia

Bradykinesia, or slowness of movement, is one of the main [symptoms](https://www.fightparkinsons.org.au/understand-parkinsons/signs-symptoms) of Parkinson’s. This means it takes more time and effort for a person to complete daily tasks, which can result in fatigue.

When experiencing slowness of movement, a person with Parkinson’s may notice the following:

* Lack of spontaneous activity e.g. arm swing diminishes
* Fine motor coordination is reduced e.g. handwriting becomes smaller
* Changes in [walking](https://www.fightparkinsons.org.au/understand-parkinsons/signs-symptoms/walking-freezing-falling) such as short, shuffling steps
* Episodes of [freezing](https://www.fightparkinsons.org.au/understand-parkinsons/signs-symptoms/walking-freezing-falling) or periods of immobility
* Difficulty turning over in bed or rising from a chair
* It takes longer to do things.

#### Managing bradykinesia

Some people with Parkinson’s find physiotherapy helps to improve their symptoms. A [physiotherapist](https://www.fightparkinsons.org.au/living-with-parkinsons/build-your-team/) can recommend [exercises](https://www.fightparkinsons.org.au/living-with-parkinsons/management-lifestyle/exercise) and techniques to help with mobility.

[Medications for Parkinson’s](https://www.fightparkinsons.org.au/living-with-parkinsons/medication-side-effects) can also help improve movement and reduce slowness.

## Parkinson’s and rigidity

Rigidity or stiff or inflexible muscles is one of the main [symptoms](https://www.fightparkinsons.org.au/understand-parkinsons/signs-symptoms) of Parkinson’s, alongside [tremor](https://www.fightparkinsons.org.au/understand-parkinsons/signs-symptoms/tremor) and slowness of movement. Not everyone will experience all of these symptoms.

In Parkinson’s, rigidity in a person is often most noticeable when they move a joint through a circular movement. The movement often feels as if the joint is moving through a number of cogs, known as ‘cogwheel rigidity’.

Some people also experience a constant resistance to motion throughout the entire range of movement, known as ‘lead pipe rigidity’.

Rigidity can stop muscles from stretching and relaxing. It can cause:

* Stiff muscles
* Inflexible muscles
* Pain and muscle cramps
* Fixed ‘mask-like’ facial expression
* Inability to swing arm or arms when walking
* Difficulties getting out of chairs, turning over in bed and turning around
* Difficulties with fine movements such as writing or doing up buttons
* Postural change
* Fatigue.

#### Managing rigidity

Consult your GP or specialist for medications that can help with rigidity.

#### Useful tips

Below are tips for avoiding postural hypotension:

* **Regular exercise and stretching**  
  Can help you to strengthen muscles and improve flexibility and mobility
* **Physiotherapy**  
  May help with muscle cramps treatment
* **Speech and language therapy**  
  May help you with exercises to keep facial muscles flexible. Seeing a therapist soon after diagnosis may make treatment more effective, too
* **Complementary therapies**  
  Acupuncture or taking a magnesium supplement have been helpful for some people in reducing rigidity.

## Support for you

* Call the Fight Parkinson’s Information Line on [1800 931 031](tel:1800931031)
* Email: [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#88e1e6eee7c8eee1efe0fcf8e9fae3e1e6fbe7e6fba6e7faefa6e9fd)
* Speak to your GP or specialist for changes in medication.

### Related resources for you

![icon](/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/icon_pdf.png)

### Fact sheet: Medications and treatments for Parkinson's

 [Download](/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Medications_and_Treatments_for_Parkinsons.pdf)

Support and services

## Free confidential information line

* [1800 931 031](tel:1800931031)

Open 9am-5pm Mon-Fri AEST

Being diagnosed with Parkinson’s is a personal experience but no one has to face Parkinson’s alone. Support and information can make a significant and positive difference to the lives of those living with Parkinson’s, their families and carers.

* [Call us](tel:1800931031)
* [Email us](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#a6cfc8c0c9e6c0cfc1ced2d6c7d4cdcfc8d5c9c8d588c9d4c188c7d3)

**Please note**: Fight Parkinson’s uses the phrase Parkinson’s rather than Parkinson’s Disease to reflect the community’s preference. Parkinson’s Disease is used only when necessary such as in medical, research or government contents, or in direct quotes.

This is the homepage of Fight Parkinson's, an Australian organization dedicated to supporting the estimated 219,000 Australians living with Parkinson's or Atypical Parkinson's. The organization serves as a central hub connecting medical professionals, researchers, carers, supporters, government, and donors. The website is organized into six main sections:

1. **Understand Parkinson's** - Covers what Parkinson's and Atypical Parkinson's are, signs and symptoms, causes, stages, diagnosis, young onset, and specific conditions (PSP, MSA, CBS). Includes a learning hub and glossary.

2. **Living with Parkinson's** - Resources for recently diagnosed, building a care team, support services, treatments, management/lifestyle, medications, legal/financial rights, carers, and peer support groups.

3. **Advancing Research** - Information on Parkinson's research, the organization's research agenda, research partners, opportunities to participate in research, and donating to research.

4. **Professionals** - Resources for health professionals, researchers, communities of practice, care workers, and professional development.

5. **How You Can Help** - Ways to donate, wills/estates/bequests, fundraising, corporate sponsorship, sharing stories, tributes, volunteering, and naming a hero.

6. **News & Resources** - Downloadable resources, multi-lingual publications, and learning hubs.

The organization also provides a free confidential helpline (1800 931 031) open Monday-Friday 9am-5pm AEST.

A detailed sub-page covers **bradykinesia (slowness of movement) and rigidity** in Parkinson's. Key points include:
- Bradykinesia is a main motor symptom, causing fatigue, reduced arm swing, smaller handwriting, shuffling gait, freezing episodes, and difficulty with daily tasks. Management includes physiotherapy and medications.
- Rigidity presents as stiff/inflexible muscles, often as "cogwheel rigidity" (ratchet-like movement) or "lead pipe rigidity" (constant resistance). It can cause muscle cramps, mask-like facial expression, postural changes, and fatigue. Management includes medication, exercise, physiotherapy, speech therapy, and complementary therapies like acupuncture or magnesium supplements.

Note: The organization uses "Parkinson's" rather than "Parkinson's Disease" to reflect community preference.

# Symptoms of Parkinson’s

[APDA](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/) [Parkinson’s Disease](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/) Symptoms of Parkinson’s![](https://d2icp22po6iej.cloudfront.net/wp-content/themes/apda-2021-ct/icons/big-little-a.png)![](https://d2icp22po6iej.cloudfront.net/wp-content/themes/apda-2021-ct/icons/font-minus.svg)![](https://d2icp22po6iej.cloudfront.net/wp-content/themes/apda-2021-ct/icons/font-plus.svg)

## **Common Symptoms of Parkinson’s Disease**

Below, we discuss the most common Parkinson’s disease symptoms. Remember that although these are the typical symptoms, they can vary greatly from individual to individual—both in terms of their intensity and how they progress. Motor symptoms generally involve movement, while non-motor symptoms do not.

Use the links below to quickly navigate to a symptom:

* [Tremors](#tremors)
* [Rigidity](#rigidity)
* [Bradykinesia](#bradykinesia)
* [Vocal Symptoms](#vocal-symptoms)
* [Oral Dysfunction](#oral-dysfunction)
* [Postural Instability](#postural-instability)
* [Walking or Gait Difficulties](#walking-gait)
* [Cognitive Changes](#cognitive-changes)
* [Depression and Anxiety](#depression-anxiety)
* [Disturbances in the Sense of Smell](#smell)
* [Eye and Vision Issues](#eye-vision)
* [Fatigue](#fatigue)

* [Gastrointestinal Issues](#gastrointestinal-issues)
* [Lightheadedness](#lightheadedness)
* [Melanoma](#melanoma)
* [Pain](#pain)
* [Personality Changes](#personality-changes)
* [Psychosis](#psychosis)
* [Sexual Concerns](#sexual-concerns)
* [Sleep Problems](#sleep-problems)
* [Sweating](#sweating)
* [Urinary Issues](#urinary-issues)
* [Weight Loss](#weight-loss)

---

## What are the primary motor symptoms of Parkinson’s disease?

There are four primary motor symptoms of Parkinson’s disease:

* tremor
* rigidity
* bradykinesia (slow movement)
* postural instability (balance problems)

Observing two or more of these symptoms is the main way that physicians [diagnose Parkinson’s](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/diagnosing/).

### Understanding Parkinson’s Disease

* [Causes of Parkinson’s](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/causes/)
* [Diagnosing Parkinson’s](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/diagnosing/)
* [**Symptoms of Parkinson’s**](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/symptoms/)
* [Treatment & Medication](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/treatment-medication/)
* [Early Onset Parkinson’s](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/early-onset-parkinsons-disease/)

It is important to know that not all of these symptoms must be present for a diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease to be considered. In fact, younger people may only notice one or two of these motor symptoms, especially in the [early stages](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/early-onset-parkinsons-disease/) of the disease. Not everyone with Parkinson’s disease has a tremor, nor is a tremor proof of Parkinson’s. If you suspect Parkinson’s, see a neurologist or movement disorders specialist.

#### Introducing an easier way to track your symptoms and manage your care.

[DOWNLOAD THE APP](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/apda-symptom-tracker)

##### Don’t want to download the app? Use the [non-mobile version here](https://fs9.formsite.com/ekreeger/form290/index.html).

### Tremors

Characteristically occurring at rest, the classic slow, rhythmic tremor of Parkinson’s disease typically starts in one hand, foot, or leg and eventually affects both sides of the body. The resting tremor of Parkinson’s disease can also occur in the jaw, chin, mouth, or tongue. In addition, some people with Parkinson’s disease can experience a feeling of internal tremor, which is not necessarily noticeable to others. [Read more about Parkinson’s tremors.](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/symptoms/tremor/)

### Rigidity

Rigidity refers to a tightness or stiffness of the limbs or torso. Rigidity, especially in the early stages of the disease, may be wrongly attributed to arthritis or orthopedic problems, such as a rotator cuff injury.

### Bradykinesia

Greek for “slow movement,” bradykinesia is a frequent symptom of Parkinson’s disease and related movement disorders. In addition to a general slowness of movement, the bradykinesia of Parkinson’s disease is typically demonstrated by a reduced or [mask-like expression of the face](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/symptoms/facial-masking/) (hypomimia or facial masking), a decreased blink rate of the eyes, and problems with fine motor coordination (for example, difficulties buttoning a shirt). Having trouble turning over in bed and slow, small handwriting (micrographia) are other signs of bradykinesia.

### Vocal Symptoms

In addition to the five core motor symptoms of Parkinson’s, changes in the voice are commonly experienced. These are believed to be at least partly due to bradykinesia. The voice may become softer, or it may start off strong and then fade away. There may be a loss of the normal variation in volume and emotion in the voice, so that the individual may speak in a monotone. In more advanced Parkinson’s, speaking may become rapid, with the words crowded together, or stuttering may occur.

### Oral Dysfunction

Two common and distressing problems that can develop in Parkinson’s disease are swallowing dysfunction and drooling. These issues are very important to diagnose. Impacts on your daily life and your health can range from difficulties with meals to more extreme (but less common) cases where it could lead to choking and aspiration which can be very serious or even fatal. [Read more about swallowing problems and drooling.](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/symptoms/swallowing-difficulties-and-drooling/)

### Postural Instability

More pronounced in the later stages, postural instability includes the inability to maintain a steady, upright posture or to prevent a fall. Such balance problems in Parkinson’s disease are associated with a tendency to list or fall backward (retropulsion); in fact, a light push can cause the individual with Parkinson’s disease to continue stepping backward or to even fall.

### Walking or Gait Difficulties

Bradykinesia and postural instability both contribute to walking—or gait—difficulties in Parkinson’s, particularly as the disease progresses. A common, early symptom of Parkinson’s disease is a decrease in the natural swing of one or both arms when walking. Later, steps may become slow and small, and a shuffling gait (festination) may appear. Gait problems in Parkinson’s disease can also include a tendency to propel forward with rapid, short steps (propulsion). People with advanced Parkinson’s disease may experience episodes of freezing, in which the feet appear to be glued to the floor. [Read more about freezing of gait.](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/symptoms/freezing-of-gait/)

### Find local support & resources

[APDA Chapters](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/resources-support/local-resources/) and [Information and Referral Centers](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/resources-support/local-resources/) offer comprehensive support programs for patients and their caregivers. Exercise groups, educational forums, support groups, and information tailored to meet your changing needs.

[Find an APDA Center near you](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/resources-support/local-resources/) or call [800-223-2732](tel:8002232732).

## What are some of the non-motor symptoms of Parkinson’s?

Because Parkinson’s disease is a type of movement disorder, the associated non-motor symptoms can often be overlooked. However, there are several common symptoms of Parkinson’s disease that do not primarily involve movement.

### Cognitive Changes

Particularly in more advanced Parkinson’s disease or in older people with the disease, problems with thinking, word finding, and judgment are common. If these symptoms occur in the early stages of illness, however, they may be symptoms of a related disorder (e.g., [dementia with Lewy bodies](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/article/understanding-parkinsons-disease-dementia-lewy-bodies/)) rather than idiopathic Parkinson’s. Many individuals report difficulties in multitasking and organizing daily activities. Confusion may also be a side effect of some Parkinson’s disease medications. [Read more about the cognitive changes related to Parkinson’s](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/symptoms/cognitive-changes/)

### Depression and Anxiety

Depression and anxiety are fairly common non-motor symptoms of Parkinson’s. They can range in severity and may improve with Parkinson’s disease treatment, medications, and “talking therapy” or psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). [Read more about depression and anxiety.](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/symptoms/depression/)

### Disturbances in the Sense of Smell

A reduced sensitivity to odors (hyposmia) or a loss of smell (anosmia) is often an early symptom of Parkinson’s. In fact, hyposmia and anosmia may be experienced months or even years before the traditional motor symptoms of Parkinson’s disease emerge.

### Eye & Vision Issues

As a result of Parkinson’s, the eyes can experience diminished movement capabilities. Also, blinking can slow from 16-18 times per minute to 1-2 times per minute, leading to a condition called “dry eyes.” [Read about eye & vision issues associated with Parkinson’s.](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/symptoms/eye-vision-issues/)

### Fatigue

Fatigue is a complex symptom of Parkinson’s disease that is not fully understood. It is known, however, that fatigue is significantly associated with depression and sleep disorders. [Read more about fatigue in Parkinson’s.](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/symptoms/fatigue/)

### Gastrointestinal Issues

Disturbances of the gastrointestinal system are common. Constipation occurs frequently because Parkinson’s disease may slow the automatic movement of the digestive system; however, side effects of medications may also contribute to constipation. [Read more about gastrointestinal issues.](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/article/the-gut-and-parkinsons/)

### Lightheadedness

Separate from the balance problems of postural instability but contributing to gait problems, lightheadedness or a faint feeling occurs often with Parkinson’s. This symptom is related to the body’s inability to quickly regulate blood pressure, particularly when sitting up from a lying position or standing from a sitting position. When severe, lightheadedness may cause blackouts or fainting.

Download our fact sheet to learn more: [Neurogenic Orthostatic Hypotension in Parkinson’s Disease](https://d2icp22po6iej.cloudfront.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/APDA18126-NOH-Factsheet-2018.pdf)

### Melanoma

Individuals with Parkinson’s disease may have an increased risk of melanoma, a serious type of skin cancer. As a result, people with Parkinson’s disease should undergo annual skin examinations with a dermatologist. If you notice any troubling skin lesions, be sure to talk to your physician about them. [Read more about cancer and Parkinson’s.](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/article/cancer-and-parkinsons-disease/)

## Have a question about Parkinson’s disease?

Our Scientific & Medical Affairs Department can provide expertise and resources to answer your questions and address your concerns.

[Ask a Doctor](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/resources-support/ask-the-doctor/)

### Pain

There are particular types of pain that may be unique to people with Parkinson’s. In addition, there are aspects of Parkinson’s that may exacerbate pain that’s originating from another source. [Read our blog post on Pain & Parkinson’s.](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/article/is-pain-a-symptom-of-parkinsons-disease/)

### Personality Changes

The disease can affect the brain in ways that cause modest personality changes over time. Also, Parkinson’s medication can, in some instances, cause [impulse control disorders (ICD)](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/symptoms/impulse-control-disorders/). An ICD can manifest as hypersexuality, pathological gambling, and other impulsive behaviors. [Read more about Parkinson’s effect on personality](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/symptoms/personality-change/)

### Psychosis

Parkinson’s disease psychosis is a non-motor symptom of Parkinson’s disease that causes patients to experience hallucinations and/or delusions. More than half of all patients with Parkinson’s disease eventually develop symptoms over the course of their disease. [Read more about Parkinson’s disease Psychosis.](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/symptoms/psychosis/)

### Sexual Concerns

Reductions in sexual desire, or libido, is another non-motor symptom of Parkinson’s disease that is often under-recognized. Treatment with Parkinson’s disease drugs frequently improves sexual desire and, in some cases, even increases it to a troublesome level. In men, the inability to achieve or maintain an erection (impotence) can occur; however, impotence may also be related to other age-related changes in the body or other conditions. [Read more about the sexual effects of Parkinson’s.](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/symptoms/sexual-effects/)

### Sleep Problems

Sleep problems are commonly experienced by people with Parkinson’s. The inability to fall asleep, or primary insomnia, is less common than the inability to stay asleep, or secondary insomnia. Other individuals with Parkinson’s disease have vivid dreams, although these are more typically due to side effects of medications for PD. [Read more about sleep problems associated with Parkinson’s.](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/symptoms/sleep-problems/)

### Sweating

Excessive sweating is a relatively common sign of Parkinson’s, particularly if the disease is untreated. It happens most often in the upper body. [Read more about sweating and other skin conditions associated with PD.](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/article/sweating-and-skin-problems/)

### Urinary Issues

Urinary frequency (the need to urinate often) and urinary urgency (the feeling that one must urinate right away, even if the bladder is not full) are other possible symptoms. [Urinary problems](https://d2icp22po6iej.cloudfront.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/APDA23364B_BladderSymptomsFS_ESP_TCD4FN_WEB.pdf) may be worse at night when a person is lying flat. There may also be problems with initiating a urine stream (urinary hesitancy), slowness of urination, and overfill of the bladder.

### Weight Loss

Loss of weight is a common symptom, particularly in the later stages of the illness. If weight loss is significant and unintended, your physician should perform an examination to exclude other medical causes of weight loss. [Read more about the relationship between PD and weight loss.](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/what-is-parkinsons/symptoms/weight-loss-parkinsons-disease/)

### Download the APDA Parkinson’s Handbook

Get a deeper understanding of Parkinson’s disease and learn all the basics of the disease, including how to live a better life in spite of a diagnosis.

[Download Our Handbook](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/handbook-download/)

DONATE

args.summary:
This webpage from the American Parkinson Disease Association (APDA) provides a comprehensive overview of the symptoms of Parkinson's disease, categorized into motor and non-motor symptoms.

**Primary Motor Symptoms** (four main symptoms used for diagnosis):
1. **Tremor** - Classic slow, rhythmic resting tremor, typically starting in one hand, foot, or leg; can also affect jaw, chin, mouth, or tongue. Some experience internal tremor not noticeable to others.
2. **Rigidity** - Tightness or stiffness of limbs or torso, often misattributed to arthritis or orthopedic issues in early stages.
3. **Bradykinesia** - Greek for "slow movement"; includes reduced facial expression (hypomimia/facial masking), decreased blink rate, fine motor coordination problems, difficulty turning in bed, and micrographia (small handwriting).
4. **Postural Instability** - More pronounced in later stages; inability to maintain upright posture or prevent falls, often with backward falling tendency (retropulsion).

**Other Motor Symptoms:**
- **Vocal Symptoms** - Softer voice, monotone speech, loss of normal variation in volume and emotion; in advanced stages, rapid speech with crowded words or stuttering.
- **Oral Dysfunction** - Swallowing difficulties and drooling; can lead to choking and aspiration.
- **Walking/Gait Difficulties** - Decreased arm swing, shuffling gait (festination), propulsion, and freezing episodes (feet "glued to the floor").

**Non-Motor Symptoms:**
- **Cognitive Changes** - Problems with thinking, word finding, and judgment, especially in advanced stages; difficulties with multitasking and organizing.
- **Depression and Anxiety** - Common, can improve with PD treatment, medications, and cognitive behavioral therapy.
- **Disturbances in Sense of Smell** - Hyposmia (reduced sensitivity) or anosmia (loss of smell); often an early symptom occurring months or years before motor symptoms.
- **Eye & Vision Issues** - Diminished eye movement, dry eyes from reduced blinking (from 16-18 times/minute to 1-2 times/minute).
- **Fatigue** - Complex symptom significantly associated with depression and sleep disorders.
- **Gastrointestinal Issues** - Constipation from slowed digestive system; medications may also contribute.
- **Lightheadedness** - Related to blood pressure regulation (neurogenic orthostatic hypotension); may cause blackouts or fainting.
- **Melanoma** - Increased risk; annual skin examinations recommended.
- **Pain** - Specific types of pain unique to Parkinson's; disease may exacerbate pain from other sources.
- **Personality Changes** - Modest changes over time; medications can cause impulse control disorders (ICD) including hypersexuality and pathological gambling.
- **Psychosis** - Hallucinations and/or delusions; affects more than half of all patients over the course of their disease.
- **Sexual Concerns** - Reduced libido; erectile dysfunction in men; medications may improve or increase sexual desire.
- **Sleep Problems** - Secondary insomnia (inability to stay asleep) more common than primary insomnia; vivid dreams from medication side effects.
- **Sweating** - Excessive sweating, especially in upper body, common if untreated.
- **Urinary Issues** - Frequency, urgency, hesitancy, slowness, and bladder overfill.
- **Weight Loss** - Common in later stages; should be evaluated to exclude other medical causes.

The page emphasizes that symptoms vary greatly between individuals in intensity and progression, and that not all symptoms must be present for a diagnosis. Observing two or more of the four primary motor symptoms is the main diagnostic method.

There is a lot to know about Parkinson's disease. Learn about symptoms, how it is diagnosed and what treatment options are available.

While living with PD can be challenging, there are many things you can do to maintain and improve your quality of life and live well with Parkinson's disease.

Living well with Parkinson’s disease (PD) means getting the support you need — from tools that help you work alongside your care team to resources that empower you.

Our research has led to breakthroughs in treatment and improved care that bring hope to the entire Parkinson's community.

There are many ways you can support the fight against Parkinson’s. Whatever form your gift takes, you can be confident that it goes toward providing crucial resources for those affected by this disease.

## Breadcrumb

## Breadcrumb

# Bradykinesia (Slowness of Movement)

## 💡 Quick Summary

Bradykinesia is slowness of movement and a key symptom of Parkinson’s.

Affects daily tasks like buttoning shirts or brushing teeth.

Medications such as [levodopa](/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/prescription-medications/levodopa "Levodopa"), dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors, and amantadine help manage slowness and [“off” periods](/library/fact-sheets/managing-off-time "Managing \"Off\" Time in Parkinson's").

[Exercise](/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/exercise "Exercise") and therapies like music therapy can improve movement, reduce bradykinesia and support overall Parkinson’s well-being.

![Man walking on paved path between two areas with grass and plants](/sites/default/files/styles/no_sizing/public/images/bradykinesia.jpg?itok=1UdB4Q4g)

**Bradykinesia** means slowness of movement and speed (or progressive hesitations/halts) as movements are continued. It is one of the cardinal symptoms of Parkinson’s disease (PD). You must have bradykinesia plus at least either tremor or rigidity for a Parkinson’s diagnosis to be considered.

In Parkinson’s, this slowness happens in different ways:

This translates into difficulty performing everyday functions, such as buttoning a shirt, cutting food or brushing your teeth.

Bradykinesia can be particularly frustrating because it is often unpredictable. One moment you can move easily, while in the next moment you may need help.

## Managing Slowness of Movement

[**Levodopa**](/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/prescription-medications/levodopa "Levodopa") is the medication most commonly given to control the movement symptoms of Parkinson’s. [**Dopamine agonists**](/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/prescription-medications/dopamine-antagonists "Dopamine Agonists"), [**MAO-B (monoamine oxidase type B) inhibitors**](/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/prescription-medications/mao-b-inhibitors "MAO-B Inhibitors"), and [**amantadine**](/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/prescription-medications/amantadine "Amantadine") can also be used alone or in combination with other medications to improve slowness, as well as stiffness and tremor.

If you experience [**“off” periods**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=StvzwQnmi3g&list=PLDGRDRM479GsNdWaz4GkJQGeOaN36pYw3) (changes in your ability to move, usually related to medication timing) when bradykinesia and other symptoms are worse, adjusting the dose or schedule of your medication could help. Talk to your healthcare provider before making any changes to your medications.

In addition to medications, [**exercise**](/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/exercise "Exercise") should be part of your treatment plan for all Parkinson’s symptoms. Staying active is an essential element of living well with PD.

Research also suggests that [**music therapy**](/library/podcast/42 "Episode 42: The Benefits of Music Therapy for Parkinson's") can reduce bradykinesia and other Parkinson's symptoms.

--- SOURCE 1: Exploring the Caregiver Role after Deep Brain Stimulation ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10098415

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in Parkinson's Disease (2023) exploring how spouse caregivers make sense of themselves and their caregiver role 1 year and 5 years after their partner's deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery for Parkinson's disease (PD). The study, conducted at UCL Queen Square Institute of Neurology, London, recruited 16 spouse caregivers (8 husbands, 8 wives) of heterosexual couples where the spouse with PD had bilateral STN DBS surgery.

**Methodology:** Semi-structured interviews were conducted using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA). However, 8 of the 16 caregivers struggled to reflect on their own lived experience and focused primarily on their partners, making their transcripts unsuitable for IPA. These 8 were analyzed via content analysis. The remaining 8 interviews (4 from 12-18 months post-DBS, 4 from 5 years post-DBS) were analyzed using IPA.

**Key Findings:**

For the 8 caregivers who did NOT self-reflect (Group 2): They shared less than half as many self-reflections, showed a consistent bias toward discussing their partner's experience rather than their own, and were largely unaware of this bias. Only 1 of the 8 acknowledged preferring to speak about their spouse.

For the 8 caregivers who shared personal reflections (Group 1), three interrelated themes emerged:

1. **DBS allows carers to question and shift the caregiver role:** At 1 year post-DBS, caregivers struggled to envision life without the caregiver role. At 5 years, they were more comfortable reassociating into the role of spouse, consciously stepping back from caregiving duties.

2. **Parkinson's unites and DBS divides:** At 1 year, caregivers showed a "combined self" identity, some even saying "we have Parkinson's." At 5 years, they showed more autonomy and acceptance of separate identities.

3. **Seeing myself and my needs, DBS enhances visibility:** At 1 year, caregivers remained focused on their partner's needs despite DBS improvements. At 5 years, they were better able to recognize and address their own needs.

**Conclusion:** The study suggests that spouses maintain the caregiver role 1 year post-DBS because they struggle to identify themselves in any other way, but become more comfortable transitioning back to the spouse role 5 years post-surgery. The authors recommend further inquiry into caregiver and patient identity roles post-DBS to support psychosocial adjustment after surgery.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This pilot study aimed to explore how caregiver spouses make sense of themselves one and five years after their partner's deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery for Parkinson's disease.", "The results suggested that spouses maintained the role of caregiver one year post DBS because they struggle to identify themselves in any other way but were more comfortable reassociating into the role of spouse 5 years post surgery.", "Half of the 16 participants did not share enough reflections regarding their own lived experience for an IPA analysis. They disregarded, deflected, or chose not to answer many questions about their experience, and chose to speak predominantly about their ill partners.", "DBS allowed carers to question and shift the caregiver role, Parkinson's unites and DBS divides, and seeing myself and my needs, DBS enhances visibility.", "All of the spouses in Group 1 who were interviewed 5 years post DBS, shared this ability to let go of the sense of responsibility to care for all of their partner's needs, allowing them to act like carers less and act like spouses more again."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: IMPORTANT Recovery Tips! Deep Brain Stimulation Surgery | Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) Explained! ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Tmoet0No04

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from SingHealth (published November 29, 2024) provides post-surgery recovery guidance for Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) surgery in Parkinson's Disease patients. It is the second video in a three-part series.

**Post-Surgery Care:**
- Patients typically leave the hospital 5–7 days after DBS surgery
- Light activities only for at least 2 weeks post-operation
- Continue same PD medications and diet as before surgery
- Increase fluids, fruits, and vegetables to prevent constipation
- Low-impact exercises (walking, tai chi, stretching) are encouraged
- Avoid heavy objects or activities that could damage the neurostimulator or connecting wire

**Warning Signs (call doctor or visit ED):**
Blurred vision, loss of speech, weakness in arms/legs, difficulty swallowing, or seizures

**Wound Care:**
- Keep wounds clean and dry; do not touch or scratch
- No ointments, lotions, or powders unless instructed by doctor
- Do not run or swim
- Check temperature; inform surgeon if 38°C or above
- Watch for signs of infection (redness, warmth, pain, swelling, oozing, wound splitting)

**DBS System Activation & Maintenance:**
- System is turned on and programmed about 1 month after surgery
- Patient must stop PD medication 12 hours before programming appointment
- Programming is an outpatient procedure taking 4–5 hours
- PD medications may be adjusted after settings are fixed
- Regular follow-up appointments and fine-tuning may be required
- Patients/caregivers may adjust settings within pre-set limits
- Check DBS battery life monthly
- Non-rechargeable batteries last 3–6 years; rechargeable batteries last up to 15 years (must be recharged at least once a week)
- Neurostimulator needs replacement when battery is ending

**Precautions:**
- Always carry DBS implant card; show to security staff for manual checks when traveling
- Magnets can turn off or damage the DBS system
- Do not place electrical or magnetic devices near neurostimulator or wires
- MRI scans and medical procedures (e.g., diathermy) can affect the device; consult doctor before such tests
- DBS helps control symptoms but is not a cure; patients should continue PD rehabilitation, take medications as advised, attend appointments, and spend time with family and friends.
</summary>

Rechargeable batteries can last up to 15 years and must be recharged at least once a week", "The DBS system is turned on and programmed about 1 month after the surgery", "Patients should always carry their DBS implant card, show it to security staff when traveling, and request a manual check"

--- SOURCE 3: Postoperative rehabilitation after deep brain stimulation surgery for movement disorders ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1388245718300038

SUMMARY:
<summary>
**Postoperative Rehabilitation After Deep Brain Stimulation Surgery for Movement Disorders**

This 2018 review article published in *Clinical Neurophysiology* (Volume 129, Issue 3, Pages 592-601) addresses the lack of standardized guidelines for postoperative care and rehabilitation following deep brain stimulation (DBS) in patients with movement disorders such as Parkinson's disease (PD), essential tremor, and dystonia. The authors, led by Niels Allert, provide a consensus-based synopsis of current clinical practice and propose guidelines for postoperative rehabilitative care.

**Key Points:**

- **Importance of Postoperative Care:** The initial 3 months after DBS implantation are critical for achieving optimal long-term outcomes. No unequivocal algorithms for optimized postoperative care currently exist.
- **Multidisciplinary Approach:** A coordinated therapy within a multidisciplinary team (trained in movement disorders and DBS) is essential for long-range maximal efficiency. Clear information transfer to subsequent caregivers is vital.
- **Rehabilitation Role:** Scientific research on neurorehabilitation after DBS is limited, partly due to differences in national healthcare systems. Rehabilitation goals must be individualized based on residual motor and non-motor symptoms.
- **Assessment Instruments:** Quantification of residual symptoms using standardized scales (e.g., Barthel index, Functional Independence Measure) is mandatory. At least one assessment in the medication OFF state is needed.
- **Disease-Specific Goals:**
  - *Parkinson's Disease:* Stabilization of DBS efficacy takes weeks to months. Programming and medication titration continue during rehabilitation. Physical therapy, occupational therapy, and speech therapy are recommended.
  - *Dystonia:* Improvement is gradual (months to years for generalized dystonia, months for cervical dystonia). Mobile components respond faster than fixed components. Speech and swallowing difficulties may arise.
  - *Tremor:* Symptoms are well-controlled immediately, with essential hand tremor decreasing by 80–90%. Head and voice tremor improve less. Long-term diminishing effects on action tremor may occur.
- **Side Effects:** Perioperative side effects include transient confusion (2–5% of patients), speech disorders (hypophonia, dysarthria), stimulation-induced dyskinesia, and psychiatric effects (apathy, depression, hypomania). Device-related complications include infections, lead migration, and fracture.
- **Medication and Programming:** Medication adjustments post-DBS are essential. Stimulation programming follows a trial-and-error approach guided by clinical signs and existing algorithms.
- **Patient Education:** Psychological adjustment to living with an implanted device, safe handling of equipment, and addressing unfounded fears are important components of rehabilitation.
- **Social Aspects:** Preserving work capacity and evaluating driving ability are important rehabilitation goals for patients of working age.
- **Long-Term Follow-Up:** Sustained improvements in motor function may last 2–5 years. Routine screening of electrode impedance and IPG replacement is recommended. Patients can be trained to make small parameter adjustments within the therapeutic window.
- **New Developments:** Adaptive DBS (closed-loop technology) and directional DBS systems represent promising advancements for improving postoperative care.

**Conclusion:** Rehabilitation after DBS requires a coordinated effort from a team including caregivers, the patient, family, and social environment. Clear roles between DBS centers and postoperative caregivers should be established through standardized communication and follow-up protocols.
</summary>

URL: https://mayfieldclinic.com/pe-dbs.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a surgical procedure to implant a device that sends electrical signals to brain areas responsible for body movement. DBS can help reduce symptoms of tremor, slowness, stiffness, and walking problems caused by Parkinson's disease, dystonia, or essential tremor. Successful DBS allows people to potentially reduce their medications and improve their quality of life.

**Key Components:** A DBS system has three implanted parts: a neurostimulator (battery-powered pacemaker device placed under the skin of the chest), a lead (coated wire with electrodes at the tip placed inside the brain), and an extension wire connecting the lead to the neurostimulator.

**Target Brain Areas:** Electrodes can be placed in the subthalamic nucleus (STN) for tremor, slowness, rigidity, dystonia and dyskinesia; the thalamus (VIM) for tremor; or the globus pallidus (GPi) for tremor, slowness, rigidity, dystonia and dyskinesia.

**Candidacy:** Candidates include those with movement disorders where medications have lost effectiveness, troubling "off" periods, or medication-induced dyskinesias. DBS may not be an option for those with severe untreated depression, advanced dementia, or atypical Parkinson's symptoms.

**Surgery:** The procedure involves two stages. Stage 1 (implanting electrodes, 4-6 hours) uses a stereotactic frame, MRI/CT imaging, and involves placing electrodes while the patient is awake to perform tasks. Stage 2 (implanting the stimulator, about 1 hour) is performed under general anesthesia about a week later.

**Awake vs. Asleep DBS:** Standard DBS is performed awake requiring medication to be held. Asleep DBS is performed under general anesthesia in an MRI or CT scanner, equally effective, and doesn't require holding medications.

**Results:** For Parkinson's disease, DBS of the subthalamic nucleus improves symptoms of slowness, tremor, and rigidity in about 70% of patients. For essential tremor, DBS of the thalamus may reduce hand tremor in 60-90% of patients. Unlike other surgeries (pallidotomy, thalamotomy) that damage brain tissue, DBS is reversible.

**Risks:** Include a 1% chance of bleeding in the brain, infection, seizures, and potential worsening of speech and balance impairments. The battery needs replacement every 3-5 years (non-rechargeable) or 10-15 years (rechargeable).

**Recovery:** Most patients are discharged the day after electrode implantation. Programming begins about 10 days after surgery, often requiring 3-4 visits to optimize settings.

The session was hosted by Professor Tilo Kunath from the University of Edinburgh.

**Panelists:**
- **Benjamin Ster (Ben)**: A patient diagnosed with Parkinson's ~12 years ago, who received adaptive DBS 4 years ago (the first patient in Canada to undergo this procedure). He is now 41 and co-authored the book "Reprogramming the Brain."
- **Dr. Rhonda McFlater**: Junior professor at University Hospital of Würzburg, Germany, studying how DBS modulates the immune system in Parkinson's.
- **Dr. Alfonso Fasano**: Professor of neurology in Toronto and Milan, specializing in DBS and advanced technologies for movement disorders.

**Key Topics Covered:**

1. **What is DBS?** A surgical treatment involving electrodes implanted in the brain connected to a battery (pacemaker) in the chest. It is an established, non-experimental treatment with high-level evidence. It's effective for motor symptoms (tremor, stiffness, slowness, dyskinesias, motor fluctuations) but not for memory problems, balance disorders, or freezing of gait. A general rule: what responds to levodopa will respond to DBS.

2. **How DBS Works**: The electrical stimulation calms overactive neurons (specifically in the subthalamic nucleus, STN) that become hyperactive due to dopamine neuron loss. This helps rebalance brain networks.

3. **Adaptive DBS (aDBS)**: A newer form that adjusts stimulation strength based on brain signals. DBS uses a biomarker (beta frequency) to detect when the brain is more "parkinsonian" and adjusts stimulation accordingly. It can reduce battery consumption and side effects from over-stimulation, though Ben noted it can drain batteries faster in some cases. Some devices can be upgraded to adaptive via software if they are from certain brands and within the last 4 years.

4. **Disease Modification Potential**: 
   - Dr. McFlater's research shows DBS may reduce alpha-synuclein aggregation and modify immune responses, shifting from pro-inflammatory to protective immune cells.
   - Dr. Fasano cautioned that while animal models show promise, there is no definitive human evidence for disease modification. However, indirect benefits (improved sleep, exercise ability, medication reduction) may slow disease progression.
   - Ben emphasized that DBS allows him to exercise daily, which is known to be disease-modifying.

5. **Patient Selection**: 
   - Age is not an absolute cutoff but a proxy for frailty. Different brain targets (STN, GPi, VIM) are preferred at different ages.
   - Three pillars for successful DBS: a great neurological team, a great surgical team, and a supportive home environment.
   - Early-stage DBS is not generally recommended unless the patient has significant fluctuations or resistant tremor.

6. **Health Disparities**: Access to DBS varies significantly. Treatment is expensive (~$100,000), and disparities exist based on race, gender, socioeconomic status, and geography. Women are underrepresented in DBS treatment, partly due to caregiver dynamics and how doctors present options.

7. **Other Topics**: 
   - DBS can be combined with other treatments (e.g., exercise).
   - DBS can be done alongside cardiac pacemakers with proper coordination.
   - Remote programming of DBS devices is possible.
   - Digital biomarkers (e.g., from Apple Watch via the Stripe PD app) may help tailor DBS in the future.

--- SOURCE 21: Challenges in PD Patient Management After DBS: A Pragmatic Review - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6174419

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a pragmatic review article published in *Movement Disorders Clinical Practice* (2018) by Rossi et al. from FLENI, Buenos Aires, Argentina, addressing the most common postoperative management challenges in Parkinson's disease (PD) patients after Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) of the subthalamic nucleus (STN) or internal globus pallidus (GPi).

**Key Issues Covered:**

- **Unrealistic Patient Expectations**: Only 43% of patients perceived DBS outcomes as positive; 25% were disappointed. Patients often overestimate post-surgery function levels. Authors recommend identifying at-risk individuals and providing psychological support pre-and post-surgery.

- **Caregiver Burden**: Multiple studies show no significant reduction in caregiver burden after DBS, despite patient motor improvement. Psycho-educational interventions are recommended.

- **Speech Disturbances**: Common after STN-DBS, including intelligibility issues, hypophonia, and stuttering. Low-frequency stimulation and Lee Silverman Voice Treatment may help.

- **Freezing of Gait & Balance**: Axial symptoms (PIGD) improve less consistently than cardinal motor symptoms. GPi-DBS may better preserve gait and posture. Low-frequency stimulation (60-80 Hz) recommended for FoG.

- **Postural Disorders**: Camptocormia may improve with STN-DBS if treated early (within 1.5 years). No current evidence supports postural disorders as a sole indication for DBS.

- **Apathy**: Affects ~27% of patients one year post-STN-DBS. Often linked to rapid dopaminergic medication reduction. Slow medication tapering is recommended.

- **Anxiety & Depression**: May improve short-term but worsen long-term. Depression is rare immediately after DBS. Suicide rates are higher in the first year post-STN-DBS (~1% completed suicide).

- **Impulse Control Disorders (ICD)**: Relationship is controversial. DBS may worsen or improve ICD. STN target selection and medication reduction are valid strategies for severe ICD.

- **Cognition**: Risk of cognitive decline may be higher with STN- vs. GPi-DBS, affecting verbal fluency, processing speed, and working memory. Authors recommend GPi-DBS if cognitive concerns exist.

- **Weight Gain**: Common after DBS (first year), potentially leading to obesity/metabolic syndrome. GPi-DBS may cause more weight gain than STN-DBS. Nutritional counseling is recommended.

- **Disease Progression vs. DBS Decline**: Sustained motor improvement is typical, but worsening of axial/neuropsychiatric features likely reflects disease progression rather than DBS wearing off.

- **Battery End of Life**: IPG expiration is a movement disorder emergency that can cause life-threatening akinetic crises. Dopaminergic medication is often ineffective; chronic DBS must be urgently restored. GPi-DBS may be safer due to less medication reduction.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the Parkinson's Foundation provides a comprehensive overview of Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) as an advanced treatment for managing Parkinson's disease.

**What is DBS:** DBS is a surgical procedure that implants a system delivering electrical pulses to brain areas controlling movement. It helps control movement symptoms when medications alone are insufficient, improving quality of life by reducing tremor, stiffness, slowness, dyskinesia, and medication-related fluctuations.

**FDA Approval Milestones:** 1997 (Parkinson's tremor), 2002 (advanced Parkinson's symptoms), 2016 (earlier stages, diagnosed ≥4 years), 2025 (adaptive DBS feature for certain systems).

**How DBS Works:** Electrical pulses from thin wires implanted in the brain help reset abnormal brain signals caused by dopamine-producing cell damage in the substantia nigra. It targets three FDA-approved brain areas: GPi and STN.

**DBS System Components:** (1) Neurostimulator/IPG (control center, placed under skin near collarbone, rechargeable or non-rechargeable), (2) Leads (thin wires in brain with 4-16 electrodes, directional stimulation), (3) Controller (handheld device or app for on/off, battery check, limited adjustments, remote programming).

**Symptoms Helped:** Movement symptoms (tremor, stiffness, slowness responsive to levodopa), medication side effects like dyskinesia, some non-movement symptoms (sleep issues, pain, overactive bladder). Tremor may improve even if levodopa-resistant.

**Symptoms May Worsen:** Balance, speech, and swallowing problems, especially if pre-existing.

**Surgery:** Typically involves two procedures (lead placement, then neurostimulator implantation). Requires pre-surgery evaluation including neuropsychological assessment, brain imaging, medication review, and mental health screening.

**Candidate Criteria:** Confirmed PD diagnosis, some levodopa response, persists despite medication adjustments, no serious mood/cognitive problems, healthy enough for surgery, has support network, realistic expectations.

**Key Considerations:** Most people still need some medication post-DBS. Side effects are usually short-term and adjustable. DBS failure can often be fixed (lead placement, hardware, programming issues). Requires ongoing follow-up with regular adjustments.
</summary>

- **Addiction/Substance Use:** About 20% of older adults experience substance misuse. Integrated treatment combining detoxification, CBT, relapse prevention, and management of co-occurring psychiatric conditions.

- **Caregiver Role:** Critical for treatment adherence, monitoring, and social support. Social determinants of health must be addressed.

- **Pain & Osteoporosis:** Pain managed with physical therapy, analgesics, gabapentin/duloxetine, or DBS. Bone density screening, calcium/vitamin D, and fall prevention recommended.

- **Autonomic Dysfunction:** Orthostatic hypotension managed with increased salt/fluid intake, midodrine, or droxidopa. Urinary symptoms and constipation addressed through lifestyle and pharmacologic means.

The guide emphasizes that early screening, integrated behavioral health services, and multidisciplinary collaboration are essential for improving quality of life in seniors with PD.
</summary>

"56% of participants receiving CBT responded to treatment at week 10, vastly outperforming the 8% response in the control group." URL: https://www.caregiver.org/resource/parkinsons-disease-caregiving

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Family Caregiver Alliance provides a comprehensive overview of Parkinson's Disease (PD) and caregiving for those affected by it. Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurological disease resulting from the destruction of dopamine-producing nerve cells in the basal ganglia. By the time motor symptoms appear, approximately 50% of dopamine-producing cells have already been lost, and non-motor symptoms may be noticed up to 10 years prior.

Key facts: PD is the second most common neurodegenerative disease after Alzheimer's, affecting 500,000 to 1,500,000 people in the U.S., with 50,000-60,000 new cases annually. It is most common in people over 60, though some experience symptoms before age 40. Genetic causes are rare, occurring in only 6-8% of cases.

Symptoms include both motor (tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability) and non-motor symptoms (depression, anxiety, sleep disorders, cognitive changes). Treatment primarily involves drug therapy, most commonly levodopa/carbidopa (Sinemet) and dopamine agonists. Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) is a surgical option approved by the FDA in 2002, with over 80,000 patients having undergone the procedure worldwide. Non-medical interventions like dance, yoga, Tai Chi, and physical activity are also beneficial.

The page covers Lewy Body Dementia (LBD), noting that 10-70% of those with PD will develop some degree of dementia. It provides extensive caregiver guidance focusing on five key recommendations: Get prepared, Take care of yourself, Get help, Foster a good relationship, and Encourage the person with PD to stay active. Resources include links to the American Parkinson Disease Association, National Parkinson Foundation, and other support organizations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
By the time a person starts to experience motor symptoms of Parkinson's, they've already lost approximately 50% of their dopamine producing cells, "One common expression is 'genetics loads the gun, but environmental [exposure] pulls the trigger.'", "Quality of life studies show that early treatment with dopaminergic medications improves daily functioning, prevents falls, and improves a person's sense of well-being.", "Studies show that 10% to 70% of those living with PD will develop some degree of dementia (loss of brain function).", "Former caregivers of a loved one with PD suggest doing the following: Get prepared, Take care of yourself, Get help (don't try to do it all yourself), Work to maintain a good relationship with your loved one, and Encourage the person with PD for whom you care, to stay active."
</key_excerpts>
