# Parkinson's Caregiver Resources

When someone is diagnosed with Parkinson's disease (PD), the person is usually able to continue to provide self-care for some time.  However, since Parkinson's is a progressive disorder, over time the person will need more and more assistance. Often someone close to the person with PD will step in to manage care or provide care. Usually this is a spouse or adult child, but it can a sibling, parent, friend, even ex-spouse.

The resources listed here will help you understand what to expect as a Parkinson's caregiver.

We occasionally host webinars with caregivers coping with PD, PD dementia, or other dementia types, with [recordings  you can view](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/authors-advice.html) and [resources for coping with Parkinson's symptoms](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/coping-with-symptoms.html).

![A heart shape carved from sandstone](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/panel_builder_copy/panel_1/image_copy_1587541683.img.620.high.jpg/heart-shape-sandstone.jpg)

Image by Stanford.

## Becoming a PD Caregiver

![Davis Phinney Foundation](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_1293343250.img.620.high.jpg/davis-phinney-logo.jpg)

### [Advice for Parkinson’s Care Partners](https://www.davisphinneyfoundation.org/blog/podcast-advice-for-parkinsons-care-partners-connie-carpenter-phinney/)

*By Davis Phinney Foundation, October 24, 2018*

In this 24-minute podcast, Kelsey Phinney interviews her mom, Connie Carpenter Phinney, about being a Parkinson's care partner for over 18 years. Topics include how Davis was diagnosed, telling their young children, family life changes, self-care and communication, household safety modifications, coping with good and bad days, and maintaining their marriage despite Parkinson's.

![American Parkinson Disease Association](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image.img.620.high.png/apda-newlogo.png)

### [Becoming a Care Partner](https://www.apdaparkinson.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/APDA18127-Keys-to-Caregiving-D3V2-002.pdf)

*Published by American Parkinson Disease Association, 2018*

This two-page educational supplement offers tips on being a care partner for someone with Parkinson's disease and taking care of yourself. Included is a list of online resources useful to families managing long term illness.

![Stanford Medicine](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_1597017464.img.620.high.jpg/stanford-medicine-logo.jpg)

### [Being a PD Caregiver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cQjeL664woM)

*By Stanford APDA Information & Referral Center, March 10, 2025*

In this 90-minute webinar, Lianna Marie, a caregiver who cared for her mother with Parkinson's disease for 30 years (including eight years with dementia), shares lessons learned from her caregiving journey. She has authored several books about Parkinson's caregiving and founded a website offering resources, posts, and a free 22-page ebook with practical tips to make living with Parkinson's easier and safer.

![WellMed](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_882635000.img.620.high.png/WellMed-logo.png)

### [Caring for Someone with Parkinson's Disease](https://soundcloud.com/caregiverteleconnection/caring-for-someone-with-parkinsons-disease-8-5-2020)

*By WellMed Charitable Foundation, 2020*

In this one-hour teleconference, clinical social worker Elaine Book, addresses some of the challenges unique to PD caregiving, by stage of PD.  She also talks about management of caregiving responsibilities and self-care.  And there are some good tips about communication. Sadly, only the first 12 minutes of the teleconference was recorded. Fortunately, staff at the Parkinson's Community Outreach Program attended and took notes of the entire hour.  
  
[Teleconference notes are on the Stanford PD Community Blog](https://parkinsonsblog.stanford.edu/2020/08/caring-for-someone-with-parkinsons-disease-speaker-notes/).

![Stanford Medicine](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_508583221_1722366599.img.620.high.png/logo-stanford-medicine.png)

### [Parkinson's Caregiver Video Series](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLrukR7WKf08QdnsBACT-gUx0QstYd5UZ8)

*By Stanford Parkinson's Community Outreach Program, June 2024*

Ten short videos (three to six minutes) on tips for newly diagnosed, avoiding nausea with Sinemet, adult day care programs, apathy and exercise, low blood pressure, resistance to in-home care, hospitalization, hospital discharge planning, home health vs. home care, and respite grants.

![Davis Phinney Foundation](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_2970822.img.620.high.jpg/davis-phinney-logo.jpg)

### [Parkinson’s Care Partners: Rewriting the Rule Book](https://davisphinneyfoundation.org/parkinsons-care-partner-rulebook/)

*Published by Davis Phinney Foundation, 2025*

This 20-page digital booklet guides care partners in creating a personal rule book for living well with Parkinson's. It helps reset relationships, define decision-making, focus on mutual well-being, clarify challenges and expectations, and avoid anger or guilt from lack of clarity.

![Aging Care](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_249740038.img.620.high.jpg/agingcare-com-logo.jpg)

### [Questions a Caregiver Should Ask about Parkinson’s Disease](https://www.agingcare.com/articles/questions-a-caregiver-should-ask-about-parkinsons-disease-150353.htm)

*By Anne-Marie Botek.  Published by AgingCare.com, 2015*

When faced with the diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease, this list of questions will help you become an advocate.  In addition to commonly asked questions, there are five you should not fail to ask, including questions about treatment options, why a particular treatment path, exercise, diet, and prognosis.

![Connecting Caregivers Radio](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_1725307855.img.620.high.jpeg/Connecting_Caregivers_Radio.jpeg)

### [Top 10 Ways A Care Partner Can Support Someone With Parkinson’s Disease](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1Gy38BUi-KA)

*By Connecting Caregivers Radio, November 2, 2021*

In this one-hour webinar, Yazmil Soriano, with Neuro Challenge, offers tips for caring for a person with PD. This information is especially useful for care partners of someone in early to mid stages.

## Relationship and Communication

![World Parkinson Coalition](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_111126221_1602140590.img.620.high.jpg/wpc-logo.jpg)

### [Communicating and Staying Connected with Parkinson’s in the Relationship](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w0s1TkfK6kM)

*By World Parkinson Coalition, February 3, 2022*

Good communication is key to any healthy relationship, but PD and its common symptoms offer unique communication challenges. In this hour-long webinar, a virtual panel focuses on challenges and solutions related to maintaining effective communication between care partners and their loved one with PD.

## Adult Children PD Caregivers

![Parkinson Association of Alberta](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_970284399_496402143.img.620.high.jpg/Parkinson_Assoc_Alberta.jpg)

### [Adult Children Providing Care for People with PD](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h016VaSoZU4)

*By Parkinson Association of Alberta, May 27, 2020*

In this one-hour webinar, movement disorders specialist Janis Miyasaki, MD, provides insight and information for adult children of people with Parkinson disease, including the rewards and many challenges like changing intergenerational dynamics, difficult decision making, family conflict, balancing everyone's needs and so much more.

![Parkinson's Foundation](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_207490077.img.620.high.jpg/parkinsons-foundation-logo.jpg)

### [Being There for Your Parent with Parkinson’s](https://www.parkinson.org/library/podcast/142)

*Published by Parkinson's Foundation, December 27, 2022*

In this 20-minute episode of the podcast, Substantial Matters, Kelly Arney, MSSW, has several good pieces of advice for different situations, including communicating with the parent about how much help they will accept without giving up their autonomy.

![Davis Phinney Foundation](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_2970822_c_137838324.img.620.high.jpg/davis-phinney-logo.jpg)

### [Care Planning for a Parent Living with Parkinson's](https://davisphinneyfoundation.org/blog/care-planning-for-a-parent-living-with-parkinsons/)

*Published by Davis Phinney Foundation, August 1, 2019*

This article offers seven considerations for planning and managing the care of an aging parent as suggested by a man who cared for his mother with PD. These are elements of care that you will want to understand and plan for prior their need, so you aren't making complex decisions in the midst of a health or safety crisis.

![Parkinson's Foundation](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_207490077_455214092.img.620.high.jpg/parkinsons-foundation-logo.jpg)

### [Living with Uncertainty: Tips for Having a Parent with Parkinson’s](https://www.parkinson.org/blog/tips/parent-with-pd)

*Published by Parkinson's Foundation, November 16, 2023*

In this post from the Parkinson's Today Blog, shares five tips for coping with the uncertainty around having a parent with PD, including concern over whether PD is genetic, how to reduce your risk of also developing PD, ways to maintain a positive outlook and manage anxiety, tending to feelings of grief and loss, and living life to the fullest.

## Manuals and Courses for PD Caregivers

![Parkinson's Foundation](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_2074900771.img.620.high.jpg/parkinsons-foundation-logo.jpg)

### [Caring and Coping](https://www.parkinson.org/library/books/caring-coping)

*Published by Parkinson's Foundation, 2018*

This 176-page comprehensive guide for caregivers of people with Parkinson’s may be helpful at any stage.  There are "Tip sheets" with pointers from every day care to travel concerns.  And there are "Worksheets" to prepare for medical appointments, keep track of medications on a scheduling sheet, maintain a symptoms diary, and preparing to interview and trained hired caregivers.

![Parkinson Society British Columbia](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_1746811675.img.620.high.jpg/PDSocietyBC-logo.jpg)

### [A Comprehensive Guide for Parkinson’s Caregivers](/content/dam/sm/parkinsons/documents/Parkinsons-Caregivers-BC-2018_20181109150050.pdf)

*Published by Parkinson Society British Columbia, March 2018*

This 67-page guide covers building a care team, best practices of daily living, motor and non-motor changes, accessing support, preparing for the future, caring for the caregiver, references for further reading and an index of worksheets for care planning.

![Michael J. Fox Foundation](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_970284399_1239914356.img.620.high.png/mjff-logo.gif)

### [Facing Parkinson's Together](https://www.michaeljfox.org/form/care-partner-guide)

*By The Michael J. Fox Foundation, February 20, 2026*

This free 108-page digital guide supports care partners by combining medical, emotional, and practical advice. Designed to be flexible and easy to use, the guide can be read cover to cover or  quickly find the information most relevant to your stage of the journey by using the built-in navigation and links.

![Davis Phinney Foundation](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_97313705.img.620.high.jpg/davis-phinney-logo.jpg)

### [The Parkinson’s Care Partner’s Digital Toolbox](https://www.davisphinneyfoundation.org/blog/parkinsons-care-partners-digital-toolbox/)

*Published by Davis Phinney Foundation, March 14, 2018*

This blog post provides links to over 30 worksheets for Parkinson's wellness, lifestyle self-assessments, and symptom checklists, plus caregiver tools including calendars, communication aids, digital legacy management, legal information, meal planning, medication management, safety resources, care partner self-care, transportation, and more.

See also the 112-page "[Every Victory Counts...for Care Partners](https://davisphinneyfoundation.org/every-victory-counts-manual/)" 2021 manual.

![Davis Phinney Foundation](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_129334325.img.620.high.jpg/davis-phinney-logo.jpg)

### [Parkinson’s Care Partner Training](https://davisphinneyfoundation.org/programs/care-partner-training/#1695395034422-a3f2c219-ad51)

*By Davis Phinney Foundation, October 24, 2018*

This ten-part program led by a movement disorder specialist, clinical social worker, registered dietician, and care partner mentors offers education, confidence-building tools, and strategies for managing Parkinson's complications. Includes a 56-page digital handbook with journal prompts, educational links, and homework ideas.

![Parkinson's Foundation](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_1340599220.img.620.high.jpg/parkinsons-foundation-logo.jpg)

### [Parkinson’s Foundation Care Partner Program](https://education.parkinson.org/community-education/carepartner)

*By Parkinson's Foundation*

A series of self-paced online courses designed for anyone [caring for someone with Parkinson's](https://www.parkinson.org/resources-support/carepartners), including spouses, partners, family members, and friends. Courses feature clinical experts such as movement disorder neurologists, social workers, psychologists, and rehabilitation therapists, along with experienced care partners who share insights from their lived experiences.

![PMD Alliance](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_2970822_c.img.620.high.png/PMD_Alliance.png)

### [Roadmap to Care: Planning for Your Loved One’s Needs at Each Stage of the Disease](https://www.pmdalliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/RoadMaptoCare.pdf)

*Published by PMD Alliance, 2023*

This comprehensive, easy to read, six-page guide highlights the motor and nonmotor symptoms common in early, mid, and late stage Parkinson's, treatment needs, and what to do at each stage. Because the health of primary care partners often suffers, especially in mid-to-late stages, this guide considers the physical, emotional, and financial needs of both the person with PD and primary care partner so you have the support you need and get ahead of the stressors.

![Lewy Body Dementia Association (LBDA)](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_134059922_301886676.img.620.high.png/LBDA.png)

### [Supporting Meaningful Engagement](https://lewy-learning-center.thinkific.com/courses/supporting-meaningful-engagement?mkt_tok=MTgzLUFLUS01MTcAAAGa-vB0K2sgnID4MgShllAJvo5VHIu9W_nG4nM3sbWLZ38FbNf6nhJQmcK5dodP4J3whY-JHFDHSTfzUm5hDR8H0woOr_ale-SDOuurLvPabQ)

*By Lewy Body Dementia Association*

This free, six-part course is presented by an occupational therapist. Each video focuses on a different aspect of daily life, providing insights into how to adapt activities and environments to meet the unique cognitive and physical needs of those with Lewy Body Dementia. Care partners will learn to encourage participation in ways that foster a sense of accomplishment and well-being.

## Courses for Professionals

![Parkinson Society Southwestern Ontario](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_134059922.img.620.high.png/Parkinson_Society_Southwest_Ontario.png)

### [Parkinson Education Program for Community Caregivers](https://psso.ca/programs-services/pep-online/)

*By Parkinson Society Southwestern Ontario*

This eight-module online educational series is for professionals working in community settings (home health, retirement homes, long-term care homes, and hospitals) who provide care to individuals living with moderate to severe PD.

## Family Conversations About Driving

![AAA](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_696786404.img.620.high.png/AAA.png)

### [Driver Planning Agreement](https://exchange.aaa.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/Driver-Planning-Agreement.pdf)

A printable sheet which both the older driver and family sign.  The family agrees to help the older driver to explore all options to remain mobile, and the older driver agrees to explore other forms of transportation.

![Teepa Snow portrait](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_126516429.img.620.high.jpg/Teepa-Snow.jpg)

![National Highway Traffic Safety Administration](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_691145591.img.620.high.jpeg/NHTSA.jpeg)

*Published by National Highway Traffic Safety Association*

This comprehensive webpage is intended to inform and broaden the discussion about older driver safety and mobility. In it you will find detailed guidance to help older drivers make informed decisions about their driving behavior and suggestions on how to begin a conversation about safety concerns.

![Caring.com](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_126182200.img.620.high.jpg/caring-com-logo.jpg)

*Published by Caring.com*

![The Hartford Insurance Group](https://med.stanford.edu/parkinsons/caregiver-corner/caregiver-resources/_jcr_content/main/panel_builder/panel_0/text_image_846656445.img.620.high.png/Hartford-logo.png)

# Caregiver’s Guide for Parkinson’s Disease

![caregivers-guide-for-parkinsons-disease.jpg](https://cdn.pfizer.com/pfizercom/styles/convert_to_webp/s3/caregivers-guide-for-parkinsons-disease.jpg.webp?VersionId=GAIq08Jyqxq1YL22En3mRJgOuH6OCPjB&itok=hTlYEIdb)

Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a complex neurodegenerative motor disorder, meaning there are many features of the disease that will change over time—slowly in most people. And, while no two people experience the disease the same way, there are a number of common symptoms caregivers can look out for that may help prepare them for the changes likely to occur during early-stage, mid-stage, and advanced-stage Parkinson’s disease.

As PD progresses, patients may have increased difficulty walking, talking, swallowing, or completing daily activities. They may also experience depression, anxiety, sleep disturbances, cognitive problems, mental health problems (caused by medicine) and/or impulse control problems. As a consequence, the role of the caregiver progresses and becomes more demanding, and will require the caregiver—whether a spouse or family member—to anticipate, recognize, and navigate new challenges. The more educated and prepared you are as a caregiver, the more successful you will be at overcoming the various challenges associated with your loved one’s disease.

### Getting Started

PD patient management goes beyond the medications that provide symptom relief. In fact, a great way to prepare for what may lie ahead is to work with a healthcare “team” who can offer you advice about how to help your loved one live better with PD. Your team may include an *occupational therapist*, someone who teaches people with PD alternative ways to perform daily tasks, a *physical therapist* who helps restore, maintain, and promote overall fitness and health, and a *speech therapist*, someone who fixes the difficulties with swallowing food and liquids and communicating.

You also want to consider home safety, this includes removing potential kitchen, bath and bedroom hazards, securing or removing loose rugs, making room for standing or spinning a wheelchair, and asking for a home safety evaluation. Again, as PD progresses, you should periodically make new assessments to keep up with the advancement of the disease.

### Early Stage Disease

It may seem counterintuitive to prepare for late-stage disease when your loved one is in the early stages of PD, but this can actually be the best time to get organized and think about the future. There will come a time when he or she may be unable to tell you what kind of medical care, facility, or end-of life plan is preferred. So this is the time to make everything as clear as possible.

There is often a so-called “honeymoon” period when people with PD first start taking medication, when it can seem like the side effects of the disease are not so disabling. However, most medications are efficacious and then are less effective as the disease progresses. Still, you may be able to keep your loved one active by trading responsibilities when a change in the disease makes a usual task too difficult. For instance, if your loved one is unable to wash and dry the dishes due to grasping or range of motion difficulties, he or she can take over the bill paying. This kind of task-balancing can help to keep things feeling a bit normal.

### Mid-Stage Disease

In mid-stage PD, medicine has an inconsistent effect, and due to fatigue, your loved one may become less active. Physical movement can become much more frustrating as it is unpredictable, and mood changes may affect the way a person feels and thinks. Early signs of dementia may also begin to show and tremors can become greater. Also, a side effect of PD medications called *dyskinesia* may cause your loved one to experience involuntary writhing movements. During Mid-stage PD, your loved one may have impaired balance, difficulty walking, and an increased risk of falling. Interestingly, the person’s handwriting may become very small; this is a condition called *micrographia*, which is common for people with PD.

Additionally, non-motor symptoms may become troublesome to the patient and the caregiver. Medication can help to address these symptoms as they advance; however, fatigue, mood changes, insomnia and depression are not always diagnosed in mid-stage PD. Also, other symptoms provoked by medication use tend to develop. At this stage, a good tip is to learn to be flexible when it comes to managing or working around the loved one’s fatigue. For example, it may be better to schedule fewer activities, break up tasks, errands, or other activities into shorter time periods.

### Advanced Disease

Advanced-stage PD patients are often confined to a wheelchair; however, since the disease progresses differently in different people, many do not progress to the advanced stage. During this stage, patients are not able to live alone and caregiver assistance with all daily activities including dressing, eating, and walking becomes necessary. Medications that treat PD can cause hallucinations, delusions, agitation and mania. One study reported that dementia develops in many people after 9 years. So it is important to have made preparations early on, before reaching the late stages of PD. You may need to make decisions or plans with family members or other professionals on end of life medical care, living wills, or power of attorney.

### Last But Never Least: Caring for Yourself

In my experience as a clinician, I have seen the PD caregiver become consumed in caring for the patient. It’s true that there’s a lot to do for your loved one, but many caregivers do not take enough time to focus on their own needs. Studies show that women caregivers who do not take care of themselves have more health problems (including depression and other mental health disorders) than women who do. If you are a caregiver who forgets to take care of yourself, here are some tips to keep in mind:

args.key_excerpts: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a complex neurodegenerative motor disorder, meaning there are many features of the disease that will change over time—slowly in most people., In my experience as a clinician, I have seen the PD caregiver become consumed in caring for the patient. It's true that there's a lot to do for your loved one, but many caregivers do not take enough time to focus on their own needs., Studies show that women caregivers who do not take care of themselves have more health problems (including depression and other mental health disorders) than women who do., One study reported that dementia develops in many people after 9 years., Interestingly, the person's handwriting may become very small; this is a condition called micrographia, which is common for people with PD.
args.summary:
This is a Pfizer-published caregiver's guide for Parkinson's disease (PD), authored by Dr. Rachel Schindler. It outlines the progression of PD across three stages and provides practical advice for caregivers. Key points include:

**Getting Started:** Recommends assembling a healthcare team (occupational, physical, and speech therapists) and conducting home safety assessments.

**Early Stage:** Encourages advance planning for future medical care and end-of-life decisions. Notes a "honeymoon" period where medication seems effective, and suggests task-balancing to keep the patient active.

**Mid-Stage:** Describes worsening symptoms including inconsistent medication effects, fatigue, impaired balance, micrographia (small handwriting), dyskinesia (involuntary movements from medication), and potential early dementia signs. Advises scheduling flexibility to accommodate fatigue.

**Advanced Stage:** Patients often require full-time care and wheelchair assistance. Dementia may develop after about 9 years. Emphasizes the importance of having made legal and medical care preparations (living wills, power of attorney) earlier.

**Caregiver Self-Care:** Stresses that caregivers must attend to their own health, noting studies showing caregivers who neglect self-care have more health problems including depression.

Parkinson’s disease is a movement disorder that can [progress over time](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/resources/understanding-the-progression-of-parkinsons-disease) and may need long-term care. People with more [advanced stages of Parkinson’s](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/resources/end-stage-parkinsons-disease-what-to-know) often need a caregiver, usually a family member, to help with daily life. These activities can include eating, dressing, bathing, using the bathroom, getting in and out of bed, and moving safely around the house.

Caregivers tending to loved ones with advanced Parkinson’s need to be ready for the changes involved [as the disease progresses](https://www.parkinson.org/understanding-parkinsons/what-is-parkinsons/stages). Many MyParkinsonsTeam members who serve as caregivers for a loved one with Parkinson’s disease report challenges.

One MyParkinsonsTeam member said, “My husband has had Parkinson’s for more than 25 years. He is at stage 4. For over a month, he has been seeing things that are not there. … We don’t share a room anymore. We haven’t for about three months. The reason is that he has very vivid dreams.”

Another member commented, “I’m caring for my husband. … Each day, there is something new and different to deal with.”

Just as people with advanced Parkinson’s need support, so do their [caregivers](https://www.parkinson.org/blog/care/outside-help). This article serves as a caregiver’s guide and talks about five ways to support your loved one while also taking care of yourself.​

## 1. Talk to the Doctor About Adjusting Medication

One important way to support your loved one is by helping ensure their symptoms are managed as well as possible. In advanced stages of Parkinson’s, many people have new or changing symptoms that may mean it’s time to revisit their treatment plan with a neurologist or movement disorder specialist.

![](/pull_quote_full.png)

## “I’m caring for my husband. … Each day, there is something new and different to deal with.”

## — A MyParkinsonsTeam member

You might consider bringing up a medication review if your loved one:

* Has lived with Parkinson’s for many years
* Is experiencing more tremors, rigidity (muscle stiffness), or bradykinesia (slowness) as medications start to wear off
* Shows signs of dyskinesia (involuntary movements), such as slow, twisting motions or sudden jerking of the limbs, face, or torso
* Develops nonmovement symptoms, such as trouble with memory or thinking, depression, anxiety, speech changes, constipation, vivid dreams or [hallucinations](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/resources/how-to-recognize-hallucinations-and-delusions), delusions, increased sweating, sleep problems, or sexual challenges

Doctors may adjust the timing or dosage of current medications or recommend additional treatments to better manage advanced Parkinson’s symptoms. Possible adjustments include:

* Changing the timing or dose of levodopa/carbidopa to reduce “wearing-off” periods between doses
* Using extended-release levodopa ([Crexont](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/treatments/crexont)) to provide a slower release of medication to stabilize dopamine levels
* Adding drugs such as rasagiline ([Azilect](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/treatments/azilect)) or entacapone ([Comtan](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/treatments/comtan)) to help extend dopamine activity
* Introducing treatments such as amantadine ([Gocovri](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/treatments/gocovri)) to help control involuntary movements caused by long‑term levodopa use
* Prescribing rivastigmine ([Exelon](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/treatments/exelon)), which is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to treat dementia (memory and thinking problems) in Parkinson’s
* Trying clozapine (used off label, meaning not officially approved for this use) or pimavanserin ([Nuplazid](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/treatments/nuplazid)) to help manage hallucinations or delusions
* Using medications that can help with sleep, such as clonazepam or melatonin
* Considering devices that deliver medication under the skin like continuous apomorphine infusion ([Onapgo](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/treatments/onapgo)), continuous foslevodopa/foscarbidopa infusion ([Vyalev](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/treatments/vyalev)), or continuous levodopa/carbidopa intestinal gel infusion ([Duopa](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/treatments/duopa)).

Always talk to your loved one’s doctor before making any changes to medications.

## 2. Look Into Device-Assisted Therapy

In addition to adjusting medication, healthcare specialists may suggest device-assisted therapy for those with advanced Parkinson’s disease. These therapies use pumps or surgical implants to deliver more consistent treatment.

The four main options are:

* Continuous levodopa/carbidopa infusion — This treatment can help reduce wearing-off symptoms and dyskinesia by delivering medication directly to the small intestine through a pump. The continuous flow helps keep dopamine levels more stable throughout the day.
* Continuous foslevodopa/foscarbidopa infusion — This treatment is also a pump that provides medication under the skin and treats motor symptoms.
* Apomorphine infusion or injection — Apomorphine is a fast-acting medication used during “off” periods when other Parkinson’s medications stop working as well. It can be given through [subcutaneous (under the skin) injection](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/resources/overcoming-the-fear-of-self-injection-with-advanced-parkinsons-treatment) or delivered continuously using a small pump worn on the body.
* Deep brain stimulation (DBS) — DBS is a surgical treatment where a neurosurgeon places small electrodes in specific parts of the brain. These electrodes deliver gentle electrical pulses that can help manage tremors, stiffness, and other motor symptoms. DBS is [usually recommended](https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/surgical-treatment-options/deep-brain-stimulation) for people who still benefit from levodopa but have serious movement problems or side effects.

Each of these options has benefits and potential risks, and not everyone with Parkinson’s is a candidate. Talk to your loved one’s neurologist or movement disorder specialist to learn more about what might be right for them.

## 3. Consider Physical Therapy for Balance and Gait

Even with the right medication plan, people living with advanced Parkinson’s may still struggle with gait (the pattern or style of how a person walks), balance, and frequent falls. Gait changes in Parkinson’s can include shorter steps, a stooped posture, or difficulty starting or stopping movement. These issues increase the risk of falling, which is why movement-based therapies, including physical therapy, can play a key role in managing symptoms.

Research shows that targeted movement training may help [improve balance](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21674624/) in people with Parkinson’s. For people with mild to moderate Parkinson’s, both resistance exercises and tai chi can reduce the risk of falls, according to a study in The New England Journal of Medicine.

Ask your loved one’s doctor which types of exercise or physical therapy might be safe and helpful based on their symptoms and stage of Parkinson’s. The doctor may also suggest ways you can help your loved one stay active, motivated, and safe while moving.

## 4. Know When You’ve Reached Caregiver Fatigue

Caring for someone with advanced Parkinson’s can take a toll on your physical, emotional, and mental well-being. Many care partners experience [Parkinson’s caregiver fatigue](https://www.parkinson.org/Living-with-Parkinsons/For-Caregivers/Caring-for-the-Caregiver/Caregiver-Stress), a deep, persistent exhaustion that builds over time. It’s important to recognize when you may need help, rest, or additional support.

![](/pull_quote_full.png)

## You are more likely to be able to provide high-quality care for others if you’re taking care of yourself as well.

Signs of caregiver fatigue include:

* Neglecting your own health or daily needs
* Feeling isolated or misunderstood by others
* Worrying constantly about the future
* Feeling frustrated with your loved one, then feeling guilty about those feelings
* Being exhausted even after sleep
* Feeling depressed, hopeless, or overwhelmed

Members of MyParkinsonsTeam often talk openly about the emotional weight of caregiving. “My wife fell yesterday while I was showering, and I couldn’t hear her calls for help,” one member wrote. “Thankfully, she was just bruised. Felt guilty for not being there.”

Another said, “You do what you have to do for their care and your own self-care. One person can’t do it all. Don’t feel guilty.”

### How Parkinson’s Can Affect Relationships

Parkinson’s doesn’t just affect the person diagnosed. It can strain even the strongest relationships. Many care partners are also spouses or long-term partners, and balancing the roles of caregiver and companion can be overwhelming.

“As a person who’s been married for 26 years, with the last four years trying to deal with my husband with this disease and my health issues, just make sure you’re in it for the long haul. It’s a big challenge — be sure you’re educated on this topic,” one MyParkinsonsTeam member shared.

Another wrote, “Hubby is in personal care, and I’m living at our home. His Parkinson’s seems to get worse every day. He’s now having delusions of me being with another man and divorcing him.”

Some members have turned to counseling or relationship therapy for support. Others have found it helpful to take short breaks during emotionally intense moments. Sudden [changes in behavior or personality](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/resources/behavioral-changes-and-parkinsons) can sometimes stem from Parkinson’s-related changes in thinking or memory, not relationship issues alone.

### 5. Incorporate Self-Care Into Your Routine

Caring for someone with Parkinson’s disease is a long-term commitment, and it’s just as important to care for yourself along the way. The Parkinson’s Foundation emphasizes that care partners need support, too. You can call their helpline at 800-473-4636 to find local support groups, educational tools, and resources tailored for caregivers.

Creating a self-care plan can help you stay physically, mentally, and emotionally strong. It also gives you a way to recharge, so you can continue to care for your loved one without losing yourself in the process.

Here are several [types of self-care](https://www.parkinson.org/blog/care/compassion-fatigue) you might include in your routine:

* Physical self-care — Prioritize rest, nutritious meals, and regular movement (even a short daily walk counts).
* Emotional self-care — Talk to a therapist, connect with a Parkinson’s caregiver support group, or simply write your thoughts in a journal.
* Spiritual self-care — Explore practices that bring meaning or peace, such as prayer, meditation, or gratitude reflection.
* Sensory self-care — Take time to tune into your senses. Enjoy a favorite scent, listen to calming music, or walk in nature.
* Intellectual self-care — Stimulate your brain with books, music, puzzles, or creative hobbies.
* Adventurous self-care — Try something new just for you, like taking a class, starting a hobby, or visiting a place you’ve been curious about.

You are more likely to be able to provide high-quality care for others if you’re taking care of yourself as well.

## Join the Conversation

On [MyParkinsonsTeam](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/activities), people share their experiences with Parkinson’s disease, get advice, and find support from others who understand.

Are you caring for someone with Parkinson’s disease? ​Share your experience in a comment below.

args.summary:
This article from MyParkinsonsTeam (updated January 5, 2026) is a caregiver guide for supporting loved ones with advanced Parkinson's disease. It is medically reviewed by Kiran Chaudhari, M.B.B.S., M.D., Ph.D., and written by Andrew J. Funk, DC, DACNB. The guide outlines five key ways to support a loved one while also caring for oneself:

1. **Talk to the Doctor About Adjusting Medication** – As Parkinson's advances, symptoms may change, requiring medication adjustments. Doctors may modify levodopa/carbidopa timing or dosage, add drugs like rasagiline (Azilect), entacapone (Comtan), amantadine (Gocovri), rivastigmine (Exelon), clozapine, or pimavanserin (Nuplazid), or consider device-based delivery systems like Duopa, Vyalev, or Onapgo.

2. **Look Into Device-Assisted Therapy** – Options include continuous levodopa/carbidopa intestinal infusion, continuous foslevodopa/foscarbidopa subcutaneous infusion, apomorphine infusion/injection, and deep brain stimulation (DBS), which uses electrodes to deliver electrical pulses to manage tremors and stiffness.

3. **Consider Physical Therapy for Balance and Gait** – Targeted movement training, resistance exercises, and tai chi can help improve balance and reduce fall risk. Research from The New England Journal of Medicine supports these approaches.

4. **Know When You've Reached Caregiver Fatigue** – Signs include neglecting one's own health, feeling isolated, constant worry, frustration followed by guilt, exhaustion, and hopelessness. The guide emphasizes recognizing these symptoms and seeking support.

5. **Incorporate Self-Care Into Your Routine** – Physical, emotional, spiritual, sensory, intellectual, and adventurous self-care are recommended. The Parkinson's Foundation helpline (800-473-4636) is provided for caregiver support resources.

The article also includes community member quotes illustrating caregiving challenges, such as hallucinations, vivid dreams, and relationship strain. It notes that the full article content is behind a membership/signup wall.

There is a lot to know about Parkinson's disease. Learn about symptoms, how it is diagnosed and what treatment options are available.

While living with PD can be challenging, there are many things you can do to maintain and improve your quality of life and live well with Parkinson's disease.

Living well with Parkinson’s disease (PD) means getting the support you need — from tools that help you work alongside your care team to resources that empower you.

Our research has led to breakthroughs in treatment and improved care that bring hope to the entire Parkinson's community.

There are many ways you can support the fight against Parkinson’s. Whatever form your gift takes, you can be confident that it goes toward providing crucial resources for those affected by this disease.

# Caregiving Tips: Helping a Loved One in the Later Stages of Parkinson’s

![Caregiver assisting an elderly woman with a walker](/sites/default/files/styles/no_sizing/public/images/Caregiving-Tips-blog.jpg?itok=EflrZDgP)

Navigating Parkinson’s disease (PD) can come with many surprises for the person living with the disease and those who love them. Since Parkinson’s progresses, symptoms often begin to complicate daily activities as a person progresses through the [stages](/understanding-parkinsons/what-is-parkinsons/stages "Stages of Parkinson's") of PD.

Learning how to manage Parkinson’s is a constantly evolving learning curve that should always be modified to best suit both the needs of the person with Parkinson’s and the [care partner](/resources-support/carepartners "For Care Partners"). In this article, we highlight tips that can help your loved one adjust to these changes.

## Daily Living

### Moving

[Movement changes](/understanding-parkinsons/movement-symptoms "Movement Symptoms") are common in Parkinson’s and can become more difficult to manage in later PD stages. As a care partner, you can help your loved one [move safely](https://www.parkinson.org/resources-support/carepartners/advanced/daily-living#StandingSitting).

### Freezing and Falls

People with Parkinson’s sometimes experience **[freezing](https://www.parkinson.org/resources-support/carepartners/advanced/daily-living#Walking)** episodes, which is the temporary and involuntary inability to move. Freezing is a significant cause of falls, as it creates a feeling like your feet are glued to the floor.

### Travel and Transportation

[Leaving the home](https://www.parkinson.org/resources-support/carepartners/advanced/daily-living#TravelTransportation) can be difficult, but outings to a doctor’s office or physical therapist are often necessary. Consider methods that promote safety and decrease care partner stress.

[Read More: Traveling with Parkinson’s](/living-with-parkinsons/management/traveling "Traveling with Parkinson's")

### Mealtime and Swallowing

Advanced Parkinson’s can cause difficulty with [eating and drinking](https://www.parkinson.org/resources-support/carepartners/advanced/daily-living#Mealtime) because of movement and swallowing problems. Making adjustments to mealtimes can help your loved one get the [nutrition](/living-with-parkinsons/management/diet-nutrition "Diet & Nutrition") they need.

## Caring for the Care Partner

Parkinson’s symptoms change over time, as will your role as a care partner. The most important thing to remember is that if you do not [take care of yourself](/resources-support/carepartners/caring-for-self "Caring for the Care Partner"), you will not be able to take care of your loved one.

[Caregiver burnout](/blog/care/prevent-burnout "What You Can Do to Prevent Care Partner Burnout") is a state of physical, emotional and mental exhaustion. Burnout can occur when caregivers don't get the help they need, or if they try to do more than they are able, physically or financially. Caregiver burnout symptoms can include:

These tips can help you navigate your own wellbeing as a care partner:

[Read More: Self-Care & Caregiving Tips](/resources-support/carepartners/caring-for-self "Caring for the Care Partner")

## Parkinson’s & Dementia

When [thinking changes](/resources-support/carepartners/advanced/dementia "Thinking Changes & Dementia") are mild, these symptoms often do not impact everyday life. But as Parkinson’s advances, more profound changes in thinking can occur, including dementia. [Dementia](/understanding-parkinsons/non-movement-symptoms/dementia "Dementia") is when someone experiences problems with memory and thinking that are advanced and interfere with daily activities and quality of life.

args.summary:
This webpage from the Parkinson's Foundation provides caregiving guidance for those supporting a loved one in the later stages of Parkinson's disease. Key topics covered include:

**Daily Living Challenges:**
- **Moving:** Movement changes become more difficult to manage in later stages; care partners can help loved ones move safely.
- **Freezing and Falls:** Freezing episodes (temporary inability to move) are a significant cause of falls, creating a sensation of feet being glued to the floor.
- **Travel and Transportation:** Leaving home can be difficult but is often necessary for medical appointments; methods to promote safety and reduce caregiver stress are recommended.
- **Mealtime and Swallowing:** Advanced Parkinson's can cause eating and drinking difficulties due to movement and swallowing problems; mealtime adjustments can help with nutrition.

**Care Partner Self-Care:**
- Highlights the risk of caregiver burnout—a state of physical, emotional, and mental exhaustion that occurs when caregivers don't get needed help or try to do more than they are able.
- Emphasizes that if care partners do not take care of themselves, they cannot care for their loved one.

**Parkinson's & Dementia:**
- Mild thinking changes often don't impact daily life, but as Parkinson's advances, more profound changes can occur, including dementia (problems with memory and thinking that interfere with daily activities and quality of life).
- Strategies for improving communication are provided.

**Additional Resources:**
- Links to related materials including "Caring & Coping: A Care Partner's Guide to Parkinson's Disease," "CareMAP: Managing Advanced Parkinson's," and relevant blog posts.
- The Parkinson's Foundation offers support for care partners across all stages of the journey.

# Advanced Parkinson’s

## 💡 Quick Summary

* Advanced Parkinson’s disease occurs when a person is no longer physically independent and requires help with daily activities.

* Cognition changes, including thinking difficulties and [dementia](/understanding-parkinsons/non-movement-symptoms/dementia "Dementia"), are common in advanced PD and may affect communication and memory.

* Care strategies should be personalized and supported by a local [care team](/living-with-parkinsons/finding-care/building-your-team "Building Your Care Team"), including medical professionals and community resources.

* Key areas of focus include managing movement and communication challenges, adjusting [daily routines](/living-with-parkinsons/management/activities-daily-living "Activities of Daily Living") and planning for end-of-life care.

![Advanced Parkinson’s](/sites/default/files/styles/no_sizing/public/images/advancedparkinsons.jpg?itok=IyOyJvPk)  

There is no single definition of “advanced” Parkinson’s disease (PD). While the disease progresses differently from person to person, there are several scales healthcare professionals use to measure the disease is and its progression. In general, when a person with Parkinson’s is no longer physically independent, the disease is considered advanced.

This means that the person has problems with mobility and cannot complete activities of daily living without help. Cognition changes, specifically [dementia](/understanding-parkinsons/non-movement-symptoms/dementia "Dementia"), are also a hallmark of advanced PD.

Suggestions and tips for helping your loved one manage advanced PD should always be modified to best suit both of your needs. We strongly recommend building a care team in your local area to help you on your caregiving journey. For referrals, talk to your loved one’s PD doctor or call our [Helpline](/resources-support/helpline "Helpline") at 1-800-4PD-INFO (1-800-473-4636).

## Get Informed

### Activities of Daily Living

Advanced Parkinson’s often complicates daily activities. We highlight tips to help you adjust your home and lifestyle.

[EXPLORE OUR TIPS](/resources-support/carepartners/advanced/daily-living)

### Thinking Changes & Dementia

A broad range of thinking and memory changes can occur in Parkinson’s. How can you help your loved one along the way?

[LEARN MORE](/understanding-parkinsons/non-movement-symptoms/dementia)

### Planning for End of Life

As difficult as it is to discuss, it is important for you and your loved one to plan for and talk about options end-of-life plans.

[FIND OUT MORE](/resources-support/carepartners/advanced/end-life)

## Addressing Challenges in Advanced Parkinson's

* ### 

  As Parkinson’s advances, your loved one will likely need greater hands-on assistance. Talk to your loved one’s PD doctor for a referral for a physical therapist (PT). PTs can provide an evaluation and teach you safe and effective ways to safely help while avoiding injury.

  + **Help ensure your loved one is regularly exercising.** [Exercise](/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/exercise "Exercise") helps people with Parkinson’s stay strong and flexible, improve circulation and helps maintain the ability to do daily tasks. [Online classes](/resources-support/online-education/pdhealth "PD Health @ Home") and in-person chair exercise classes can be worth exploring.
  + **Ask an expert.** Work with a physical or occupational therapist to design an exercise program tailored to your loved one’s particular needs and challenges.
  + **Build a routine.** Encourage regular movement of arms and legs as part of the daily routine. It may be necessary to split exercise into several short sessions, or to incorporate a few exercise activities during dressing or bathing tasks. Use small, inexpensive equipment like balls or balloons throughout the day to help stimulate movement, and practice repeating common words or phrases, focusing on maintaining loudness in between tasks or activities.
  + **Think big.** Encourage your loved one to focus on maintaining large, exaggerated motions whenever possible.
  + **Stay active together.** Get your loved one up and walking with assistance whenever possible to maintain leg strength and strong, healthy bones. Engage in activity with your loved one through music (dancing, marching, singing, swaying, etc.). Encourage participation, when possible. Give just enough assistance as required.
* ### 

  In addition to the natural changes like hearing loss and cognitive changes that come with aging, it can be even more challenging to communicate when your loved one has advancing Parkinson’s.

  A person with Parkinson’s is more than 33 percent more likely to experience a conversation breakdown due to [non-movement PD symptoms](/understanding-parkinsons/non-movement-symptoms "Non-Movement Symptoms") — such as changes to speech, decreased facial expression (also called "facial masking") and anxiety.

  + **Work on speech**. Ask your doctor for a referral to a speech pathologist to design a breathing and speech practice program.
  + **Pick times of day to have specific conversations**. Consider [medication](/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/prescription-medications "Prescription Medications") times and times when the person with PD is less prone to [fatigue](/understanding-parkinsons/non-movement-symptoms/fatigue "Fatigue").
  + **Eliminate distractions**. It helps to see and hear as you communicate. Turn off the TV and sit face to face to make out mouth movement and voice loudness.
  + **Remain calm**. Resist raising your voice or giving up. People may withdraw and become nervous with an elevated voice. Stay engaged and be persistent. You will find strategies that work for you.
  + **Negotiate preferences ahead of time**. Care partners who are often just trying to help can talk over or interrupt their loved one. This often leads to unintentional negative effects and can end up taking away from identity and voice. ASK for permission to speak for them or fill in information.
  + **Acknowledge conversation difficulties**. Verify that you understood the message. Discuss openly the type of help needed and how you would like to give and receive it.

### For Care Partners

Read our care partner tips for Activities of Daily Living.

[LEARN MORE](/resources-support/carepartners/advanced/daily-living)

Parkinson’s disease can affect many different parts of the body. But perhaps one of the scariest symptoms is when it starts to affect breathing. People with Parkinson’s may face various respiratory problems. Some are easier to treat than others. Here’s more information about which breathing problems may be related to Parkinson’s disease and what you can do about them.

🗳️ How much do your symptoms impact your daily life?

Very much

## Thanks! You've successfully submitted your vote.

Sign up to view the results!

[![](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/assets/f-b439e07abadb195cd140b2e2c34f75478a896ce0cd8979f6a87a39e2f1070650.png) Continue with Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/oauth/?response_type=code&scope=public_profile,email&display=page&client_id=717303681729411&redirect_uri=https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/facebook&)  [Continue with Google](https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth?client_id=566547933063-pokg6gnpblfucc0vudgjksbmbbhdul52&redirect_uri=https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/google&response_type=code&scope=email profile&)

Already a member? [Log In](/users/sign_in)

## 1. Aspiration Pneumonia

People living with Parkinson’s disease have a higher risk of aspiration pneumonia. This is due to the disease’s effects on motor coordination, which is associated with dysphagia (swallowing difficulties). Aspiration pneumonia happens when food or fluid gets into the lungs. If left untreated, this causes a pneumonia infection.

Pneumonia is more common in [advanced Parkinson’s disease](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/resources/end-stage-parkinsons-disease-what-to-know) than in the [early stage](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/resources/understanding-the-progression-of-parkinsons-disease) because swallowing becomes more challenging with time. According to a recent study from 2021, [80 percent](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8147845/#:~:text=Studies%20have%20reported%20that%2080%25%20of%20patients%20with%20Parkinson%E2%80%99s%20disease%20develop%20dysphagia) of people with Parkinson’s disease have trouble swallowing. This symptom generally gets worse as the disease progresses.

Trouble swallowing makes it more likely that foods and beverages will go down the windpipe instead of the throat. This is called aspiration. Aspiration promotes lung inflammation and makes breathing more difficult. It’s also a big risk factor for aspiration pneumonia.

Untreated aspiration pneumonia is the main cause of mortality (death) for people with Parkinson’s disease. It can be diagnosed with a chest X-ray. Fortunately, doctors can treat aspiration pneumonia with antibiotics if caught in time. The person with Parkinson’s or a loved one should consider asking a healthcare provider the following questions:

* When and how often do we need to perform standard screening of swallowing abilities?
* What precautions or steps can help prevent aspiration pneumonia?
* What changes to the medication regimen can help manage swallowing difficulties, and when should I start exploring these options?
* Is there a standard protocol I should be aware of?

People who get aspiration pneumonia frequently can meet with a speech and language pathologist for help. They may suggest strategies like thickening liquids before drinking them to reduce the risk of aspiration.

## 2. Respiratory Dyskinesia

“Respiratory dyskinesia” refers to an involuntary lung movement. It causes rapid, shallow, and irregular breathing related to muscle spasms or tremors.

Being consistent with your Parkinson’s disease treatment plan can help minimize motor fluctuations that affect breathing. [Studies show](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7447545/#:~:text=Significantly%20increased%20motor%20symptoms%2C%20including%20bradykinesia%20and%20rigidity%2C%20which%20worsen%20when%20patients%20are%20off%20levodopa%2C%20have%20been%20shown%20to%20be%20associated%20with%20reduced%20lung%20function%20and%20impaired%20respiratory%20mechanics) that people with Parkinson’s who stay on the medication levodopa have fewer respiratory problems than those who go off their medication.

However, respiratory dyskinesia can also be a side effect of levodopa — usually when levodopa reaches its maximum effect. If your medication causes respiratory dyskinesia, your doctor may consider adjusting your dose. Your healthcare team can help you find the right balance of medication to control your symptoms while avoiding side effects, thereby improving your quality of life.

## 3. Restrictive Lung Disease

When a person’s lungs cannot fully open up or expand, they can develop what’s called restrictive lung disease. Muscle stiffness from Parkinson’s disease can restrict chest muscles and slow down their movement. One MyParkinsonsTeam member said, “I have tightness and compression in my chest when I lie down. I’m gasping with shortness of breath when I try to speak more than three words at a time.”

People with Parkinson’s disease may also struggle to stand up straight. Hunching over can limit the lungs’ capacity to take in air.

“I sleep for two or three hours most nights. Then I wake up and cannot get back to sleep in bed due to problems with breathing,” said a MyParkinsonsTeam member. “I go to the living room and fall back to sleep in my electronically adjustable chair and can usually sleep another five or six hours due to a breathing problem. Sitting more erect helps.”

A doctor can diagnose restrictive lung disease by doing a pulmonary function test, which entails measuring the volume of air that a person can exhale after taking a deep breath. A round of steroids may be enough to treat restrictive lung disease in the short term. However, supplemental oxygen is a longer-term treatment option that’s sometimes also combined with inhaled steroids to prevent hypoxia (low blood oxygen levels).

## 4. Shortness of Breath

“Dyspnea” is the medical term for shortness of breath. It is a feeling of difficult or labored breathing that can make you feel as though you’re not getting enough air, even at rest.

Shortness of breath can develop in people with Parkinson’s when their medication starts wearing off or doesn’t work as well as it once did. If you’re on the same medication and dosage for a long time, it may start to be less effective. This can affect the brain chemicals responsible for movement and memory, causing issues like shortness of breath. To avoid this complication, your healthcare provider may suggest changing your medication dose or schedule.

Another possible cause of shortness of breath is uncontrolled anxiety. Anxiety is a common symptom of Parkinson’s. It can cause physical responses that need to be managed. One MyParkinsonsTeam member described how shortness of breath and anxiety are a cycle. “Shallow breathing is scary. It makes me think I’m going to suffocate, which makes me stress more,” they shared.

Treatments for anxiety include:

* Speaking with a therapist
* Learning behavioral strategies
* Using anti-anxiety medication

Once you have a better handle on anxiety, you may notice a reduction in episodes of dyspnea.

## 5. Obstructive Sleep Apnea

Parkinson’s disease may affect muscle function in the airways and cause obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). With OSA, a person stops and starts breathing throughout the night. For some people with Parkinson’s, their brain isn’t able to adequately direct their body to breathe, due to Parkinson’s-related brain lesions.

OSA can lead to symptoms and complications such as:

* Excessive daytime sleepiness
* Loud snoring
* Abrupt awakening at night with gasping and choking
* Dry mouth when waking up
* Morning headaches
* Difficulty focusing or concentrating
* Mood changes leading to depression, anxiety, or irritability
* Complications such as poor memory
* Heart disease
* Stroke

To determine if you have OSA, your healthcare provider may recommend a sleep study, which typically includes a polysomnogram. During the sleep study, you will wear various sensors and electrodes that record your brain waves, oxygen levels, heart rate, breathing patterns, and muscle activity while you sleep. Once diagnosed, sleep apnea can be treated with a continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) machine, which helps maintain open airways and improve respiratory function throughout the night. Discuss sleep posture, medication timing, and exercise options with your healthcare provider to help manage sleep apnea effectively.

## Finding Solutions for Your Breathing Troubles

Members of MyParkinsonsTeam have reported feeling misunderstood by those who are not fully aware of the various [symptoms associated with Parkinson’s disease](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/resources/symptoms-of-parkinsons). However, by advocating for themselves and communicating their concerns, they have been able to receive appropriate care and support. “I’m back to the local hospital today for another chest X-ray,” explained one member. “My general practitioner has no idea why my breathing is so bad, although I saw another provider yesterday who feels it could well be Parkinson’s or my Parkinson’s medication. Hooray! Finally, someone agrees with me.”

Parkinson’s diagnosis comes with a lot of unpredictable changes and ongoing challenges. Understanding the potential complications and your treatment options can help you communicate with your healthcare team and take control of your health.

## Talk With Others Who Understand

On [MyParkinsonsTeam](https://www.myparkinsonsteam.com/), people share their experiences with Parkinson’s, get advice, and find support from others who understand.

Do Parkinson’s-related issues like the effects of levodopa impact your breathing? If so, how does respiratory dysfunction affect your daily life? Let others know in the comments below.

args.summary:
This article from MyParkinsonsTeam (updated January 5, 2026) outlines 5 potential respiratory complications associated with Parkinson's disease. The article is medically reviewed by Dr. Kiran Chaudhari and written by Anastasia Climan, RDN, CDN.

**1. Aspiration Pneumonia** – Due to dysphagia (swallowing difficulties), which affects 80% of people with Parkinson's per a 2021 study. Food/fluid enters the lungs, causing pneumonia. Untreated aspiration pneumonia is the main cause of death for people with Parkinson's. Treatable with antibiotics if caught early. Speech and language pathologists may recommend strategies like thickening liquids.

**2. Respiratory Dyskinesia** – Involuntary lung movement causing rapid, shallow, irregular breathing due to muscle spasms or tremors. Staying consistent with levodopa treatment helps, but respiratory dyskinesia can also be a side effect of levodopa at maximum effect. Dose adjustments may be needed.

**3. Restrictive Lung Disease** – Lungs cannot fully expand due to muscle stiffness from Parkinson's, compounded by hunching posture. Diagnosed via pulmonary function test. Short-term treatment may include steroids; longer-term options include supplemental oxygen.

**4. Shortness of Breath (Dyspnea)** – Can occur when medication wears off or becomes less effective, or due to uncontrolled anxiety (common in Parkinson's). Treatment includes adjusting medication, therapy, behavioral strategies, and anti-anxiety medication.

**5. Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)** – Parkinson's affects airway muscle function and brain's ability to direct breathing. Diagnosed via sleep study (polysomnogram). Treated with CPAP machine. Complications include daytime sleepiness, heart disease, stroke, and mood changes.

The article includes community member testimonials and emphasizes the importance of advocating with healthcare providers for proper respiratory care.

# Rehabilitation Treatment for Airway Protection in Parkinson's Disease

**Study Rationale:**Aspiration pneumonia is a leading cause of death in persons with Parkinson's disease (PD). One of the main reasons people with PD develop aspiration pneumonia is that they often have both swallowing dysfunction (dysphagia) and cough dysfunction (dystussia). If food or liquid enters the airway, a cough is not elicited and the material remains in the airway (silent aspiration). It is then possible for the material to enter the lungs, resulting in an infection called aspiration pneumonia. Currently, there are no tested treatment approaches that specifically target silent aspiration.

**Hypothesis:**The goal of this study is to determine how well two different rehabilitation treatments, expiratory muscle strength training (EMST) and sensorimotor treatment for airway protection (smTAP), work to improve cough and swallowing function in persons with PD and dysphagia.

**Study Design:**This study will include two participant groups; one group will receive EMST and the other will receive smTAP. There will be initial baseline testing of swallowing, coughing, respiratory and laryngeal function. We will also measure their perception of their cough and swallowing problem. Then, participants will be randomly assigned to either the EMST or smTAP training groups. They will be further randomized to receive immediate training or delayed training where there is a five-week wait to start with a second baseline performed at the end of the five-week delay. Once training is complete they will once again complete measures of swallowing, coughing, respiratory and laryngeal function.

**Impact on Diagnosis/Treatment of Parkinson's Disease:**We anticipate that this study will help us better understand what treatments work best to improve swallowing and cough in people with PD, resulting in an immediate shift in the clinical management of swallowing and cough dysfunction in PD. We also believe that participants will have improvements in their own swallowing and cough function, therefore, reducing the risk of aspiration pneumonia.

**Next Steps for Development:**This clinical trial will help us determine if one of the two treatments is best for treating these sorts of swallowing and cough problems in people with PD. We will then follow up by testing the long-term impact of these treatments on health and quality of life.

args.summary:
This webpage from The Michael J. Fox Foundation describes a funded research study on "Rehabilitation Treatment for Airway Protection in Parkinson's Disease." The study addresses the critical problem of aspiration pneumonia, a leading cause of death in people with Parkinson's disease (PD). The research focuses on the dual issues of swallowing dysfunction (dysphagia) and cough dysfunction (dystussia) that often lead to silent aspiration.

**Study Rationale:** Aspiration pneumonia is a leading cause of death in PD due to combined swallowing and cough dysfunction, with no current treatments specifically targeting silent aspiration.

**Hypothesis:** The study aims to determine how well two rehabilitation treatments—expiratory muscle strength training (EMST) and sensorimotor treatment for airway protection (smTAP)—improve cough and swallowing function in PD patients with dysphagia.

**Study Design:** Two participant groups will receive either EMST or smTAP. Baseline testing of swallowing, coughing, respiratory, and laryngeal function will be conducted, along with patient perception measures. Participants will be randomized to treatment groups and further randomized to immediate or delayed (five-week wait) training. Post-training measures will be repeated.

**Impact on Diagnosis/Treatment:** The study aims to identify the best treatments for improving swallowing and cough in PD, leading to immediate changes in clinical management and reducing the risk of aspiration pneumonia.

**Next Steps:** The clinical trial will determine which treatment is most effective, followed by testing the long-term impact on health and quality of life.

**Lead Researcher:** Michelle S. Troche, PhD, CCC-SLP, based in New York, NY. The study was funded in 2016 under the Therapeutic Pipeline Program.

# Exploring the Link Between Pneumonia & PD

![Abstract illustration of lungs](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/67f1f2e5f33de00b029ea079/67f3b2f42257354a5875c68c_Abstract%20Lungs.jpg)



According to a [2020 study](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022510X20302860#:~:text=Introduction,in%20such%20patients%20%5B3%5D.), pneumonia is the leading cause of death and the most common reason for hospital admissions in people living with Parkinson’s disease.Understanding the connection between Parkinson's disease and pneumonia, including its causes, treatments, and the [latest research](https://pcla.org/lets-talk-parkinsons-the-latest-in-parkinsons-research-2023/), is vital for improving care and outcomes for individuals living with PD.

## Connection Between Parkinson's Disease and Pneumonia

Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurological disorder affecting movement and causing symptoms like tremors, stiffness, and bradykinesia (slowness of movement). As the disease advances, it can lead to a range of complications, one of the most serious being pneumonia.Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the air sacs in one or both lungs. It can be particularly perilous for individuals with Parkinson's disease due to the various factors related to PD that increase susceptibility to respiratory infections.The link between Parkinson's disease and pneumonia is primarily rooted in the motor and non-motor symptoms associated with PD that compromise the respiratory system. Historically, chronic immobilization and difficulties with swallowing  (dysphagia) put people living with PD at a higher risk of pneumonia, particularly aspiration pneumonia.Individuals with Parkinson's often experience dysphagia due to weakened throat muscles. This increases the risk of aspiration — the inhalation of food, liquid, or saliva into the lungs — which can lead to aspiration pneumonia, a specific type of pneumonia.Further, the reduced mobility and ability to cough effectively in people with PD can prevent the proper clearance of respiratory secretions, elevating the risk of developing aspiration pneumonia.

## Causes of Pneumonia in Parkinson's Disease

Pneumonia in people living with PD may be triggered in several ways, most relating to the motor symptoms associated with Parkinson’s disease.

### Aspiration due to Dysphagia

Swallowing difficulties make aspiration one of the leading causes of pneumonia in people living with PD. Dysphagia typically occurs in the later [stages of PD](https://pcla.org/the-stages-of-parkinsons-disease-explained-2023/) and [is reported to increase in severity each year after diagnosis](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7988066/).Regular assessments by speech and language therapists can help in managing dysphagia, but the risk remains significant.

### Impaired Cough Reflex

PD can weaken the cough reflex, making it harder to clear the lungs of harmful particles, including bacteria and viruses.

### Decreased Mobility

Reduced physical activity can lead to a weaker immune system and poorer overall lung health, making it easier for infections to take hold.

### Medication Side Effects

Some medications used to treat PD may cause drowsiness or sedation, increasing the risk of aspiration.

## Treatments for Pneumonia in Parkinson's Disease

Treatment for pneumonia in people with PD typically involves a combination of approaches tailored to the individual's symptoms and the severity of their condition.

### Antibiotics

Bacterial pneumonia, such as aspiration pneumonia, requires antibiotics, which must be chosen carefully to avoid interactions with PD medications.

### Physical Therapy

Respiratory physiotherapy can help improve lung function by teaching exercises to strengthen the muscles involved in breathing and coughing.

### Swallowing Interventions

Speech and language therapists can provide strategies to reduce the risk of aspiration and help prevent aspiration pneumonia, such as modifications to diet texture or swallowing techniques.

### Adjustment of PD Medications

In some cases, adjusting PD medications can help manage symptoms contributing to pneumonia risk under the guidance of a neurologist.

## Research Directions

Recent research into the connection between Parkinson's disease and pneumonia has focused on prevention, early detection, and management strategies. Studies are exploring:**Vaccination Strategies:** Research into the effectiveness of vaccines, such as the pneumococcal and influenza vaccines, in reducing the incidence of pneumonia in people living with PD.**Innovative Therapies:** The development of new therapies aimed at improving swallowing function and reducing aspiration risk.**Early Detection and Monitoring:** The use of technology and clinical tools for the early detection of swallowing disorders and respiratory issues in people living with PD.**Understanding Mechanisms:** Investigating the underlying mechanisms linking PD to increased pneumonia risk could lead to targeted interventions.

## Understanding Pneumonia & PD: An Ongoing Effort

The connection between Parkinson's disease and pneumonia represents a significant challenge in the management of PD.The increased risk of pneumonia is due to a combination of factors inherent to Parkinson's, including difficulties with swallowing and impaired cough reflex. Treatment approaches are multifaceted, aiming to treat pneumonia when it occurs and address the underlying risk factors associated with PD.Ongoing research is critical to developing more effective prevention, detection, and management strategies, aiming to improve quality of life and outcomes for individuals living with Parkinson's disease.PCLA is dedicated to supporting Parkinson’s research and providing resources to our community. [Check out our upcoming Let’s Talk Parkinson’s feature on Choking and Swallowing Issues with Parkinson’s](https://pcla.org/event/choking-and-swallowing-issues-with-parkinsons/) with speech-language pathologist Julia Nicholls. This is a free online event thanks to our sponsors Boston Scientific, Acadia, and Abbott.[Register for the May 10th LTP event on Choking and Swallowing Issues here](https://pcla.org/event/choking-and-swallowing-issues-with-parkinsons/).
