[![Image 1](https://emcrit.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/ibcclogo.jpg)](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/toc/ "ibcclogo")

# Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS; including Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndr.)

August 7, 2025 by [Josh Farkas](https://emcrit.org/author/pulmcrit/)

### **CONTENTS**

*   [Causes of NMS](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#causes_of_NMS)
*   [Clinical features](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#clinical_features)
*   [Laboratory abnormalities](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#laboratory_abnormalities)
*   [Differential diagnosis](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#differential_diagnosis)
*   [Evaluation](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#evaluation)
*   [Diagnostic criteria](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#diagnostic_criteria)
*   [Management overview](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#overview_of_NMS_management)
    *   [Bromocriptine pharmacology](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#bromocriptine)
    *   [Amantadine pharmacology](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#amantadine)
    *   [Dantrolene pharmacology](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#dantroline)

*   [Pathophysiology](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#pathophysiology)

###### * * *

### causes of NMS

[(back to contents)](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#top)

* * *

* * *

##### **[#1/2] addition of a dopamine antagonist**

*   **The risk** of NMS is on the order of ~0.01-0.04% among people exposed to antipsychotics. ([32659853](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32659853/))
*   **Timing**: 
    *   NMS usually develops during the first 1-2 weeks after drug initiation, and virtually always within a month. ([32722730](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32722730/), DSM-5-TR)
    *   There are a few case reports of NMS arising _within_ the ICU as a nosocomial complication of antipsychotic administration. Diagnosis of nosocomial NMS is challenging (e.g., the development of fever and altered mental status may initially be attributed to sepsis).

*   **Risk factors**: 
    *   Personal or family history of NMS.
    *   Parkinson’s disease or Lewy body dementia. ([28144147](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28144147/))
    *   Rapid up-titration of neuroleptic, parenteral administration routes, and higher total drug doses may increase risk. However, most NMS cases occur within the therapeutic dose range. (DSM-5-TR)
    *   Multiple anti-dopaminergic agents (e.g., antiemetic + antipsychotic).
    *   Drug-drug interactions that elevate antipsychotic levels.
    *   Coadministration with lithium.
    *   Iron deficiency.
    *   (There doesn’t appear to be any dramatic age or sex predominance. ([30743298](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30743298/)) Historical trends towards higher rates among young men may simply represent patients treated with higher doses of neuroleptics.)

*   **Causative agents (D2-receptor antagonists)**
    *   First-generation (“typical”) antipsychotics have the greatest risk. 
        *   About half of all reported cases are associated with haloperidol. ([32722730](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32722730/)) This might relate to haloperidol’s high potency for D2 inhibition (as compared with chlorpromazine, which is the quintessential low-potency first-generation antipsychotic).

    *   Atypical antipsychotics have a lower risk (clozapine and quetiapine have the lowest risk). (Shutter, 2019)
    *   D2-inhibiting antiemetics, e.g.: 
        *   Prochlorperazine (Compazine™️).
        *   Promethazine (Phenergan™️).
        *   Metoclopramide.

    *   Tetrabenazine causes dopamine depletion. (Frucht 2022)

* * *

##### **[#2/2] withdrawal of exogenous dopamine stimulation (Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome)**

#### **causes of Parkinsonism-Hyperpyrexia Syndrome**

*   Discontinuing dopaminergic medications, dose reduction, or nonadherence. For example: 
    *   Due to dysphagia.
    *   Inappropriately holding medications before a procedure.
    *   Following incarceration.

*   Changing from immediate-release to extended-release formulations.
*   Reduced absorption of levodopa due to coadministration with high-protein tube feeds. (Frucht 2022)
*   Discontinuing anticholinergics or COMT inhibitors (e.g., entacapone).
*   Dysfunction of a deep brain stimulator (if the patient has a device, it should be immediately interrogated). (Shutter 2019; [27907965](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27907965/))
*   Infection or dehydration. ([26110802](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26110802/))

#### **⚠️ differential diagnosis: dyskinesia-hyperpyrexia syndrome**

*   This results from an _overdose_ of dopaminergic agents or occasionally physiological stress (e.g., infection, dehydration, heat exposure). This involves dyskinesias, rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia, and confusion. Management requires a judicious _reduction_ of dopamine agonists. ([27907965](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27907965/))
    *   Dyskinesia-hyperpyrexia syndrome is extremely rare, with only a few cases reported. (Freucht 2022)
    *   Treatment involves aggressive supportive care and down-titration of Parkinson’s medications.

#### **(related: withdrawal of chronic dopaminergic stimulation)**

*   Cessation of chronic cocaine use. ([28660166](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28660166/))

###### * * *

### clinical features

[(back to contents)](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#top)

* * *

* * *

##### **three hallmark features**

#### **overall architecture of the clinical syndrome**

*   Symptoms usually develop gradually over 1-3 days, but timing is _extremely variable_. NMS likewise takes a while to improve, with resolution usually occurring over two weeks.
*   Mental status changes and extrapyramidal symptoms often precede hyperthermia and autonomic instability. Initially, many patients will only have mental status changes and extrapyramidal features, which may render early diagnosis challenging.
*   Parkinsonism-Hyperpyrexia syndrome often occurs with prominent extrapyramidal symptoms, since these patients are very sensitive to this manifestation. ([30743298](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30743298/))Symptoms may begin 18 hours to a week after changing therapy. (Shutter 2019)
    *   Rigidity and tremor are often the first symptoms.
    *   Hyperpyrexia and mental status changes may subsequently evolve.

#### **#1/3: altered mental status (~70%)**

*   Agitation may initially occur, progressing to mutism, catatonia, and coma. ([30459031](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30459031/), [30743298](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30743298/))
*   Patients often appear alert but dazed and unresponsive, consistent with _catatonic stupor_. (DSM-V-TR)

#### **#2/3: extrapyramidal symptoms**

*   Rigidity is the most common and hallmark extrapyramidal symptom: 
    *   The most severe manifestation is _lead-pipe rigidity_ (stable resistance _throughout_ the range of motion).
    *   Rigidity may be _less prominent_ with second-generation antipsychotics. ([39321364](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39321364/))
    *   May be more notable in the upper extremities. ([40746904](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40746904/))

*   Tremor (similar to Parkinson’s disease), chorea.
*   Oculogyric crises (gaze may be fixated upwards).
*   Dystonia (which may be refractory to anticholinergic therapies).
*   Dysphagia or dysarthria may occur.

#### **#3/3: sympathetic hyperactivity**

*   Hyperthermia: 
    *   ~87% of patients have temperatures >38 °C.
    *   ~40% of patients have temperatures >40 °C.
    *   Delayed onset of hyperthermia may promote diagnostic confusion.
    *   Similar to other forms of hyperthermia, this is usually _not_ associated with chills, nor is it responsive to antipyretic therapy.

*   Profuse diaphoresis (~44%).
*   Hemodynamic instability: 
    *   Sinus tachycardia and other arrhythmias (~62%).
    *   Labile hypertension (~42%).

*   Pallor.
*   Urinary incontinence.

* * *

##### **complications are responsible for the ~10% mortality rate**

*   Most common complications: ([32659853](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32659853/))
    *   Aspiration, pneumonia, and respiratory failure may occur. This may relate in some cases to dysphagia and hypersalivation caused by NMS.
    *   Renal failure due to rhabdomyolysis occurs commonly.
    *   Venous thromboembolic events may result from immobility and systemic inflammation.

*   Takotsubo cardiomyopathy may result from autonomic instability.
*   Disseminated intravascular coagulation and multiorgan failure may ultimately evolve, secondary to the above processes.

###### * * *

### laboratory abnormalities

[(back to contents)](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#top)

* * *

*   **Creatinine kinase** is often >1,000 U/L. 
    *   Creatinine kinase may be normal early in the disease course, before rigidity emerges. One literature review found a CK level above 300 IU/L in 94% of patients.([32659853](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32659853/))
    *   For a differential diagnosis of the causes of elevated creatinine kinase, see the chapter on rhabdomyolysis [_here_](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/rhabdo/#causes_of_rhabdomyolysis). There are _numerous_ causes of creatinine kinase elevation, but marked elevation without another explanation might point to NMS in the appropriate clinical context.

*   **Leukocytosis** (as high as 40,000), with left shift and elevated neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio. 
    *   C-reactive protein is often also elevated.

###### * * *

### differential diagnosis

[(back to contents)](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#top)

* * *

#### **toxicological/metabolic**

*   **Extrapyramidal side-effect of a neuroleptic medication**: 
    *   **Neuroleptic-induced Parkinsonism**: Much more common than neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Clinical features may include rigidity or dystonia. ([39321364](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39321364/))
    *   **Acute dystonic reaction**.

*   **Serotonin syndrome**, which may be sorted out since: 
    *   These two disorders are caused by different medications.
    *   Serotonin syndrome is marked by _clonus_ and _hyperreflexia_.
    *   If present, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea point towards serotonin syndrome.

*   **Malignant hyperthermia** (usually caused by inhalational anesthetics or succinylcholine, with a more rapid onset than NMS).
*   **Muscle relaxant withdrawal** (e.g., intrathecal baclofen, carisoprodol). ([27625493](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27625493/))
*   Sympathomimetic intoxication.
*   Anticholinergic intoxication.
*   Ethanol/sedative withdrawal.
*   Lithium intoxication.
*   Strychnine poisoning.
*   **Environmental heat stroke**can be _aggravated_ by neuroleptics.Heat stroke shouldn’t cause rigidity or diaphoresis.
*   **Hyperthyroidism** (may cause tremor, but shouldn’t cause extrapyramidal motor abnormalities).

#### **infection**

*   Meningitis, encephalitis.
*   Sepsis of any etiology.
*   Tetanus.

#### **primary neurologic**

*   Stroke involving the brainstem and basal ganglia. ([28144147](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28144147/))
*   Nonconvulsive status epilepticus.
*   Autoimmune encephalitis (may cause catatonia; antipsychotics may serve as a trigger).

#### **malignant catatonia due to another underlying etiology**

*   NMS represents a subtype of _malignant catatonia_, which is triggered by neuroleptics.
*   Thus, neuroleptic malignant syndrome can be indistinguishable from malignant catatonia due to other etiologies. Other potential triggers of catatonia should therefore be considered (discussed [here](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/catatonia/#causes_of_catatonia_&_evaluation)).
*   Features that may suggest an additional or alternative cause of catatonia may include: 
    *   Behavioral prodrome for weeks involving psychosis, agitation, or apathy. ([28144147](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28144147/))
    *   More _positive_ motor symptoms (e.g., waxy flexibility, stereotyped repetitive movements, automatisms).

###### * * *

### evaluation

[(back to contents)](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#top)

* * *

#### **evaluation may involve the following:**

*   Neurological examination and measurement of core temperature.
*   Creatinine kinase level.
*   Complete blood count with differential.
*   Thyroid-stimulating hormone (if features of possible thyrotoxicosis).
*   Evaluation for infection (e.g., blood cultures, chest radiograph).
*   Depending on the context, neuroimaging and lumbar puncture might be considered.

###### * * *

### diagnostic criteria

[(back to contents)](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#top)

* * *

*   Diagnostic criteria are currently not very helpful.
*   The DSM-4 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual) contained diagnostic criteria for NMS. However, DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR _removed_ any formal criteria for diagnosing NMS. This reflects that no simple, cut-and-dry definition of NMS exists. _Many articles continue to refer to “DSM criteria” for NMS, but the most recent DSM contains no such criteria._

###### * * *

### overview of NMS management

[(back to contents)](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#top)

* * *

#### **[#1/8] discontinue offensive medication(s)**

*   [a] **Stop and avoid medications that antagonize the D2 receptors**, e.g.: 
    *   Antipsychotics.
    *   Many antiemetics (e.g., metoclopramide, promethazine, prochlorperazine).

*   [b] **In Parkinsonism-Hyperpyrexia syndrome**: 
    *   _Restart_ Parkinsons medications immediately (more on this [here](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/move/#managing_Parkinson's_disease_medications_in_the_ICU)). 
        *   In patients who are strictly NPO, a transdermal or parenteral dopamine agonist may be needed (e.g., apomorphine 2 mg SC q3hr, or rotigotine). (Freucht 2022)

    *   Additional medical therapy with bromocriptine [💉](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#bromocriptine_is_1st_line) (a dopamine agonist) should be considered, although there is no evidence regarding this. (Freucht 2022)
    *   Ensure that any deep-brain stimulator is functioning properly.

#### **[#2/8] supportive care for hyperthermia**

*   Physical cooling measures are often required (e.g., cooling blankets, ice packs, evaporative cooling).
*   Antipyretics are _not_ effective. Giving some acetaminophen is fine, but don’t expect it to really work.
*   (General supportive care for the hyperthermic patient is discussed [_here_](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/hyperthermia/#general_supportive_care).)

#### **[#3/8] respiratory support**

*   Intubation may be necessary, for example: 
    *   Some patients may develop respiratory failure due to muscular rigidity.
    *   For severe hyperthermia, intubation with paralysis and sedation will accelerate control of the hyperthermia.

*   Sialorrhea is a feature of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. If this is causing clinical problems (e.g., aspiration), it may be managed with glycopyrrolate. [💉](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/bradycardia/#glycopyrrolate)

#### **[#4/8] manage fluid, electrolytes, and rhabdomyolysis**

*   Rhabdomyolysis is common (its treatment is discussed further [_here_](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/rhabdo/#treatment_basics)). Even if CK levels are _initially_ normal, continue to monitor CK levels, as rhabdomyolysis often develops over time.
*   Avoid nephrotoxins (high risk of acute kidney injury).
*   Follow electrolytes & manage appropriately. Common abnormalities include: ([39321364](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39321364/))
    *   Hypocalcemia.
    *   Hypomagnesemia.
    *   Dysnatremia.
    *   Hyperkalemia.
    *   Metabolic acidosis.

*   Volume depletion may result from insensible losses and the inability to tolerate oral intake. Monitor and treat this accordingly.

#### **[#5/8] hemodynamic stabilization**

*   Causes of hemodynamic instability are numerous, including: 
    *   Sympathetic lability due to NMS.
    *   Volume depletion.
    *   Medication-induced (e.g., dexmedetomidine, propofol, etc.).
    *   Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.

*   Evaluate with POCUS and ensure adequate fluid resuscitation.
*   Hemodynamics can be labile. Treat cautiously with short-acting medications.

#### **[#6/8] benzodiazepines (or propofol)**

*   **Benzodiazepines**: 
    *   Benzodiazepines are generally regarded as a front-line therapy for catatonia (including NMS).
    *   Benzodiazepines may help control agitation and promote muscle relaxation.
    *   A starting dose is often lorazepam 2 mg IV q8hr.
    *   For refractory malignant catatonia, the dose may need to be escalated as high as 16-24 mg/day. Unfortunately, there is a risk that benzodiazepines could cause or promote the development of delirium. This risk may be minimized by using moderate doses.

*   **Propofol**: For intubated patients, propofol may be used as a benzodiazepine equivalent (since it stimulates GABA-A receptors).
*   (Further discussion of GABA-ergic medications in catatonia is here: [📖](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/catatonia/#lorazepam)).

#### **[#7/8] manage agitation if needed**

*   This may be challenging, since antipsychotics must be avoided.
*   Treatment options may include: 
    *   Benzodiazepines may be helpful (see #6 above).
    *   Central alpha 2 agonists (e.g., [dexmedetomidine](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/sedate/#dexmedetomidine) or [clonidine](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/sedate/#oral_alpha-2_agonists)).
    *   [Valproate](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/sedate/#valproate) is probably a reasonable treatment for hyperactive delirium in this context. Some case reports have questioned whether valproate might promote NMS, but valproate alone doesn’t cause NMS. ([28138117](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28138117/))

#### **[#8/8] treat the underlying neurotransmitter imbalance causing NMS**

*   Options here include bromocriptine and/or amantadine. 
    *   Bromocriptine is a direct dopamine agonist.
    *   Amantadine indirectly increases the dopaminergic/cholinergic balance.

*   Retrospective data suggest that patients with NMS treated with one of these agents had better outcomes.Patients with moderate-severe NMS should arguably receive one of these agents. In extremely refractory cases, both drugs could be combined.
*   The selection of bromocriptine vs amantadine may be based on patient-specific factors: 
    *   Factors supporting the use of bromocriptine: [💉](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#bromocriptine)
        *   Renal failure.
        *   Epilepsy.
        *   More severe cases?

    *   Factors supporting the use of amantadine: [💉](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#amantadine)
        *   Liver failure.
        *   CYP3A4 inducers/inhibitors.
        *   Milder cases: Amantadine is useful for the treatment of drug-induced Parkinsonism. Even if the patient doesn’t have frank, full-blown NMS, the use of amantadine may still be justifiable and beneficial.

*   When in doubt, amantadine may be a good selection due to its _safety_ and _tolerability_.

* * *

##### **[#9/8] other treatments that may rarely be needed**

#### **(dantrolene may be used for refractory rigidity)**

*   Dantrolene is a direct-acting muscle relaxant. Dantrolene can be used to treat refractory rigidity, but it’s suboptimal because it doesn’t treat the underlying neurotransmitter abnormalities involved in NMS.
*   Dantrolene shouldn’t be used as monotherapy for NMS (without coadministration of bromocriptine and/or amantadine).
*   The ideal niche for dantrolene might be for an _intubated_ patient with NMS and ongoing muscular rigidity despite IV lorazepam. IV dantrolene may help control rigidity while waiting for other therapies to take effect (e.g., enteral amantadine and/or enteral bromocriptine).

#### **(ECT; electroconvulsive therapy)**

*   ECT has been used for NMS, analogous to its use in malignant catatonia in general.
*   For patients with severe NMS refractory to medical therapy, ECT could be considered. For patients with underlying schizophrenia or psychotic depression, ECT could be particularly helpful (since it may treat the NMS and the underlying disorder).

### bromocriptine

[(back to contents)](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#top)

* * *

* * *

##### **bromocriptine: contraindications, drug interactions, side effects 👎**

#### **contraindications**

*   Psychosis or severe psychiatric disorders (may exacerbate).
*   Uncontrolled hypertension.
*   Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (including preeclampsia, eclampsia, pregnancy-induced hypertension).
*   Breastfeeding.

#### **drug-drug interactions**

*   CYP3A4 inducers or inhibitors.
*   Dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics, some antiemetics) – drugs oppose the activity of bromocriptine.

#### **side effects**

*   D2 dopamine agonism: 
    *   Nausea/emesis (due to stimulation of D2 receptors in the area postrema).
    *   Psychosis, including exacerbation of the patient’s underlying psychiatric illness.

*   Dyskinesia.
*   Hypotension.
*   Retroperitoneal fibrosis, pleural and pulmonary fibrosis, cardiac valve fibrosis.

* * *

##### **bromocriptine:****indications, advantages 👍**

#### **bromocriptine for NMS**

*   Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist, which should reverse the antidopaminergic effect of antipsychotic medications.
*   There is no high-quality evidence for any therapy in NMS. However, enhancing dopamine signaling is a rational strategy that should improve the underlying pathophysiology and is supported by some case-report-level evidence. A systematic literature review suggested that NMS-specific therapy (e.g., bromocriptine and dantrolene) might reduce mortality in severe cases, when compared to purely symptomatic therapy with benzodiazepines. ([32659853](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32659853/))

#### **bromocriptine for postpartum cardiomyopathy**

*   Bromocriptine therapy remains controversial. There is some evidence supporting bromocriptine, but it is of low quality. Bromocriptine may promote thrombosis; therefore, anticoagulation should be considered in patients receiving bromocriptine.([30704579](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30704579/)) Bromocriptine will suppress lactation.
*   American sources are less enthusiastic about bromocriptine, recommending that it be considered if the ejection fraction is <35%.([38197818](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38197818/))
*   European Society of Cardiology 2018 guidelines state the following regarding bromocriptine: “Addition of bromocriptine to standard HF therapy may improve LV recovery and clinical outcome in women with acute severe PPCM. Bromocriptine (2.5 mg once daily) for at least

 1 week may be considered in uncomplicated cases, whereas prolonged treatment (2.5 mg twice daily for 2 weeks, then 2.5 mg once daily for 6 weeks) may be considered in patients with EF <25% and/or cardiogenic shock. Bromocriptine treatment must always be accompanied by anticoagulation with heparin (LMWH or UFH), at least in prophylactic dosages. The essential therapies for patients with acute PPCM have been summarized under the BOARD label: Bromocriptine, Oral heart failure therapies, Anticoagulants, vasoRelaxing agents, and Diuretics.”([30165544](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30165544/))

#### **other indications**

*   Neurogenic fever**[📖](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/fever/#neurogenic_fever)**: Bromocriptine has been described as helpful in some case reports. ([33344618](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33344618/),[28348904](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28348904/))
*   Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity[📖](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/psh/)(PSH, aka sympathetic storm):Bromocriptine may be used for refractory hyperthermia.
*   Parkinson’s disease.
*   Restless leg syndrome.
*   Type II diabetes.
*   Cocaine withdrawal syndrome.

* * *

##### **bromocriptine:****dosing**

#### **dosing of bromocriptine for NMS**

*   The usual dose range is 2.5-5 mg orally every 8 hours.
*   Starting dose is 2.5 mg PO q8hr, may titrate up to 5-10 mg q6-8hr.
*   The maximal dose is 40 mg/day (10 mg every 6 hours).
*   Continue for 10 days after NMS resolution to avoid recurrence, then taper off very gradually.

#### **dosing of bromocriptine for neurogenic fever**

*   There is no well-defined optimal dose.
*   The commonly reported dose across various studies is 2.5 mg three times daily. However, some reports have required a need to use higher doses (e.g., up-titration to 30 mg/day). ([33344618](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33344618/))
*   This dosing range is similar to that described above for NMS.

#### **dosing for paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity**

*   The starting dose is 1.25 mg PO q12hr, with up-titration to a maximal cumulative dose of 40 mg/day. (Naidech 2022)

* * *

##### **bromocriptine:****pharmacology**

*   **Chemical properties**: 
    *   Molecular weight: 751 g/mol.
    *   LogP: 3.9

*   **Absorption**: 
    *   Oral bioavailability is only ~7% due to high first-pass metabolism.
    *   There is no difference in absorption between bromocriptine capsules and bromocriptine tablets.
    *   Recommended to be taken with food to reduce nausea/vomiting side effects.

*   **Distribution**: 
    *   Protein binding is 90-96%.
    *   Vd is ~60 L.
    *   Crosses the blood-brain barrier into the CNS.

*   **Metabolism**: 
    *   Metabolism is via CYP3A4.

*   **Elimination**: 
    *   Primarily eliminated via biliary secretion.

*   **Half-life & duration of action**: 
    *   Half-life is 5-6 hours.

###### * * *

### amantadine

[(back to contents)](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#top)

* * *

* * *

##### **amantadine: contraindications, drug interactions, side effects 👎**

#### **contraindications**

*   Major psychotic disorder, suicidality, or severe depression.
*   GFR <15 ml/min (not an absolute contraindication, but exercise extreme caution – if there is an adverse effect, the drug will persist for days).
*   Untreated angle-closure glaucoma.
*   Epilepsy.

#### **drug-drug interactions**

*   Overall, there are _minimal drug-drug interactions_.
*   Urine pH: 
    *   Urine alkalinization causes systemic drug accumulation (e.g., sodium bicarbonate, acetazolamide).
    *   Urine acidification causes accelerated drug clearance.

#### **side effects**

*   Neuropsychiatric side-effects: 
    *   Insomnia or hypersomnia.
    *   Confusion, agitation.
    *   Psychotic symptoms (E.g., delusions, hallucinations, paranoid ideation).

*   Anticholinergic side-effects. 
    *   Dry mouth.
    *   Constipation.
    *   Urinary retention.

*   Withdrawal syndrome (if abruptly withdrawn).
*   Livedo reticularis.
*   Orthostatic hypotension, syncope, and peripheral edema.
*   Reduced seizure threshold.
*   Corneal edema.
*   Dysphagia.
*   (QT prolongation risk seems to be minimal.) ([34678171](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34678171/))

* * *

##### **amantadine:****indications, advantages 👍**

*   **Neuroleptic malignant syndrome**: 
    *   Amantadine also has dopaminergic effects and may be used as an alternative dopaminergic agent if bromocriptine is contraindicated.
    *   For severe and refractory NMS, amantadine could be combined with bromocriptine. ([33896535](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33896535/))
    *   Low-level case-control data do support the use of amantadine, even suggesting that its use correlates with reduced mortality. ([1685592](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1685592/))

*   **Parkinson disease**: 
    *   Amantadine decreases rigidity, bradykinesia, and tremor.
    *   Amantadine is less effective than levodopa-carbidopa.

*   **Drug-induced Parkinsonism**: 
    *   Front-line therapy is often considered to be an anticholinergic agent (e.g., benztropine or trihexylphenidyl). Amantadine may be useful, especially in older patients, because it causes fewer anticholinergic side effects. However, among patients with _chronic psychotic disorders_, amantadine increases the risk of recurrent psychosis.

*   **Restless leg syndrome**.
*   **Tardive dyskinesia**.
*   **Catatonia**.
*   **Traumatic brain injury**.
*   **Fatigue in multiple sclerosis**: Amantadine is a front-line therapy. This emphasizes that amantadine tends to have an activating effect on patients, so it may be best when given early in the day (to avoid insomnia).
*   **(Influenza therapy)**Amantadine historically was used to treat or prevent influenza A. This is no longer recommended, due to increasing levels of viral resistance. The primary significance of this is that it illustrates that amantadine has a pretty favorable toxicity profile (patients were put on 100 mg BID amantadine for months during influenza season solely to prevent influenza!).

* * *

##### **amantadine:****dosing**

*   **Dosing in neuroleptic malignant syndrome**: 
    *   The initial dose is 100 mg twice daily (may dose in the early AM and early afternoon to avoid insomnia, noting the half-life is very long). Starting amantadine at a dose of 100 mg twice daily seems pretty common across a range of indications (e.g., drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms, influenza prophylaxis, multiple sclerosis-related fatigue, traumatic brain injury, Parkinson’s disease for patients not taking additional dopaminergic medications).
    *   May titrate up to a maximal dose of 200 mg BID (dosing range of 200-400 mg/day).
    *   Once stabilized, consider a taper over days to weeks (abrupt discontinuation may cause recrudescence).

*   **Renal dosing**of the immediate release formulation (based on a usual recommended dose of 100 mg BID) 
    *   GFR >50 ml/min: No adjustment (100 mg BID).
    *   GFR 30-50 ml/min: 200 mg on day 1, then 100 mg/day.
    *   GFR 15-30 ml/min: 200 mg on day 1, then 100 mg every other day.
    *   GFR <15 ml/min or hemodialysis: 200 mg every 7 days.

* * *

##### **amantadine:****pharmacology**

*   **Chemical properties**: 
    *   Molecular weight: 151 g/mol.
    *   LogP: 2

*   **Absorption**: 
    *   Well absorbed.
    *   Immediate release: peak concentration in 2-4 hours.

*   **Distribution**: 
    *   Vd 3-8 L/kg.
    *   Protein binding is ~60%.

*   **Metabolism**: 
    *   Minimal metabolism.

*   **Elimination**: 
    *   Renal clearance of unchanged drug (via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion).

*   **Half-life & duration of action**: 
    *   Normal renal function: 16 +/- 6 hours.
    *   Healthy older patients: 20-40 hours.
    *   End-stage renal disease: 8 days.

*   **Mechanism of action**: 
    *   The primary site of action appears to be NMDA receptors, where amantadine is a weak, noncompetitive antagonist.
    *   This (indirectly) increases dopamine release and prevents dopamine reuptake.
    *   Amantadine also has indirect anticholinergic activity (despite not actually interacting with acetylcholine receptors).
    *   Amantadine’s indirect mechanism of action may be especially helpful for patients with neuroleptic malignant syndrome who still have residual antipsychotics on board, because amantadine doesn’t need to directly compete for binding to dopamine receptors.

### dantroline

[(back to contents)](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#top)

* * *

* * *

##### **contraindications, drug interactions, side effects 👎**

#### **contraindications (relative; there are no contraindications to the use of dantrolene for malignant hyperthermia)**

*   [1] Hepatic dysfunction (may lead to prolonged dantrolene activity).
*   [2] Acute liver injury (dantrolene can cause severe, potentially fatal hepatotoxicity).
*   [3] Myasthenia gravis.
*   [4] Borderline respiratory muscle status. This includes patients with planned extubation within the near term (relative contraindication, but note that dantrolene can take a long time to clear fully, which may impair extubatability).

#### **drug-drug interactions**

*   [1] Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers: The combination is strongly contraindicated due to a risk of cardiovascular collapse and marked hyperkalemia (due to pharmacodynamic synergism).
*   [2] CNS depressants (may potentiate sedation).
*   [3] Muscle relaxants (may potentiate blockade, increase risk of prolonged weakness).

#### **side effects**

*   Muscle weakness. It’s unclear whether dantrolene may reduce diaphragmatic strength, but theoretically, higher doses might. ([28660166](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28660166/)) Occasional patients may have prolonged weakness following exposure to dantrolene.
*   Neurological side-effects: sedation, seizure, visual disturbance, diplopia, and insomnia.
*   Hyperkalemia.
*   Rash.
*   Diarrhea.
*   Side effects associated with _chronic, oral_ use (but not acute IV use): 
    *   Hepatotoxicity (idiosyncratic; can be fatal). (Wellington 3e)
    *   Seizures.
    *   Pleural effusion with pericarditis.
    *   Heart failure.
    *   Aplastic anemia, leukopenia.
    *   Lymphocytic lymphoma.

* * *

##### **indications, advantages 👍**

*   **Malignant hyperthermia is the primary indication**
    *   Dantrolene is a cornerstone intervention.

*   **NMS (neuroleptic malignant syndrome)**: 
    *   Dantrolene is a direct-acting muscle relaxant. It might help reduce heat production and rigidity.
    *   Dantrolene _shouldn’t_ be used as _monotherapy_ for NMS because it doesn’t directly target the underlying disease process.
    *   Dantrolene should only be used if it’s unequivocally required, since it’s dubious whether its benefits outweigh risks for most patients.

*   **Chronic spasticity**.

* * *

##### **dosing**

#### **dosing in malignant hyperthermia**

*   2.5 mg/kg IV immediately, then administer an additional 1-2.5 mg/kg IV q5min until symptoms subside: 
    *   Target a reduction in etCO2, rigidity, tachycardia, and hyperthermia.
    *   The average dose required to reverse MH is 2.5 mg/kg. (Paw & Shulman 2025)
    *   Large doses (>10 mg/kg) may be needed. However, if 10 mg/kg are given _with absolutely no improvement_, consider an alternative diagnosis and stop giving additional dantrolene. ([29600483](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29600483/))

*   How to reconstitute the dantrolene vials: 
    *   DANTRIUM®/REVONTO®– Each 20 mg vial is reconstituted with 60 ml of sterile water and shaken until the solution is clear. About a dozen vials may need to be reconstituted initially!_Seek an assistant to help with this._
    *   RYANODEX®– Each 250 mg vial is reconstituted with 5 ml of sterile water and shaken to ensure an orange-colored, uniform, opaque suspension.

*   Once stabilized, continue a maintenance dose of 1 mg/kg dantrolene IV q4-6hr (although fulminant cases may require a continuous infusion at 0.25 mg/kg/hour). Continue maintenance therapy until the patient has been stable and improving for 24 hours.
*   ⚠️ Avoid calcium channel blockers, which may interact with dantrolene. However, dantrolene shouldn’t be withheld from patients who have _already_ received calcium channel blockers.

#### **dosing in neuroleptic malignant syndrome**

*   The ideal dose is unclear. The dosing range is 1-2.5 mg/kg q6-8hr hours IV (with a maximal daily dose of 10 mg/kg/day). It may be reasonable to start with 1 mg/kg IV and repeat as needed.
*   There is disagreement about how rapidly this should be discontinued. It might be ideal to wean off dantrolene rapidly, once other therapies are taking effect.

* * *

##### **pharmacology**

*   **Chemical properties**: 
    *   Molecular weight: 314 g/mol.
    *   LogP: 2

*   **Absorption**: 
    *   Oral bioavailability is ~70% with slow absorption over 3-6 hours.

*   **Distribution**: 
    *   Significant protein binding.
    *   Vd is poorly characterized (36-144 L).
    *   Dantrolene does cross the blood-brain barrier and cause sedation.

*   **Metabolism**: 
    *   Hepatic metabolism occurs, but doesn’t involve CYP enzymes.
    *   Metabolites have muscle relaxant properties.

*   **Elimination**: 
    *   80% is eliminated in the urine, primarily as metabolites.

*   **Half-life & duration of action**: 
    *   The biological half-life may be longer than the half-life of dantrolene itself due to active metabolites.
    *   The mean elimination half-life may be ~8-11 hours.
    *   The active metabolite (5-hydroxydantrolene) has an elimination half-life of 15 hours.

*   **Mechanism of action**: 
    *   Blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum within muscles.

###### * * *

### pathophysiology

[(back to contents)](https://emcrit.org/ibcc/nms#top)

* * *

As its name implies, NMS is often related to neuroleptic agents (i.e., antipsychotic medications) and is manifest by mental status changes, hyperthermia, rigidity, and autonomic dysfunction. It can present as a life-threatening emergency and is often challenging to diagnose.

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome seems to result from a deficiency of signaling via D2 dopamine receptors in the brain:

*   Dopamine deficiency within striatal dopamine pathways in the basal ganglia may cause Parkinsonian-type symptoms (e.g., lead-pipe rigidity).
*   Dopamine deficiency in the hypothalamus may cause autonomic dysfunction.
*   Dopamine alterations within the reticular activating system may cause alterations in consciousness (e.g., mutism, coma).([28144147](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28144147/))

A _combination_ of excess motor tone plus dysautonomia may precipitate other features of neuroleptic malignant syndrome, including rhabdomyolysis and hyperthermia.

Treatment involves both augmentation of D2 signaling in the brain, as well as providing muscle relaxants to reduce peripheral muscle tone.

# Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) & Parkinsonism-Hyperpyrexia Syndrome

## Overview
This is a chapter from the **Internet Book of Critical Care (IBCC)** by Josh Farkas, updated August 7, 2025. It covers NMS, a life-threatening neurological emergency characterized by altered mental status, rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic dysfunction, with ~10% mortality.

## Causes
- **#1: Dopamine antagonist exposure** (e.g., antipsychotics, antiemetics like metoclopramide/prochlorperazine). Risk ~0.01-0.04% with antipsychotics. Usually develops within 1-2 weeks of drug initiation. First-generation (typical) antipsychotics carry highest risk; ~50% of cases involve haloperidol.
- **#2: Withdrawal of dopamine stimulation (Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome)** — from discontinuing Parkinson's medications, reduced absorption, deep brain stimulator dysfunction, infection, dehydration.

## Clinical Features
Three hallmark features developing gradually over 1-3 days:
1. **Altered mental status** (~70%) — agitation progressing to mutism, catatonia, coma
2. **Extrapyramidal symptoms** — lead-pipe rigidity (hallmark), tremor, oculogyric crises, dystonia
3. **Sympathetic hyperactivity** — hyperthermia (>38°C in ~87%, >40°C in ~40%), diaphoresis (~44%), tachycardia (~62%), labile hypertension (~42%)

## Laboratory
- Creatinine kinase often >1,000 U/L (elevated in 94% of patients)
- Leukocytosis (up to 40,000), elevated CRP

## Differential Diagnosis
Includes serotonin syndrome (clonus/hyperreflexia), malignant hyperthermia, malignant catatonia, infection, stroke, sympathomimetic intoxication, environmental heat stroke, autoimmune encephalitis.

## Diagnostic Criteria
DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR removed formal criteria; no simple definition exists.

## Management (8 Steps)
1. **Discontinue offensive medications** (dopamine antagonists); for Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia, restart Parkinson's medications
2. **Supportive care for hyperthermia** — physical cooling; antipyretics are ineffective
3. **Respiratory support** — intubation may be needed; glycopyrrolate for sialorrhea
4. **Fluid/electrolyte/rhabdomyolysis management** — monitor CK, avoid nephrotoxins
5. **Hemodynamic stabilization** — use POCUS, short-acting medications
6. **Benzodiazepines or propofol** — front-line therapy (e.g., lorazepam 2 mg IV q8hr, up to 16-24 mg/day)
7. **Manage agitation** — avoid antipsychotics; use benzodiazepines, dexmedetomidine, clonidine, or valproate
8. **Treat neurotransmitter imbalance** — bromocriptine (dopamine agonist) or amantadine (indirect dopaminergic). Retrospective data suggests better outcomes with these agents.

## Key Medications
- **Bromocriptine**: 2.5-5 mg PO q8hr, max 40 mg/day. Contraindicated in psychosis, uncontrolled hypertension. Metabolized via CYP3A4.
- **Amantadine**: 100 mg PO BID, max 400 mg/day. Renally cleared (require dose adjustment for GFR <50). Minimal drug interactions. May be preferred for safety/tolerability.
- **Dantrolene**: 1-2.5 mg/kg IV q6-8hr. Direct muscle relaxant; not for monotherapy. Contraindicated with non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers. Primary indication is malignant hyperthermia.

## Pathophysiology
D2 dopamine receptor deficiency in the brain: striatal deficiency causes Parkinsonian symptoms; hypothalamic deficiency causes autonomic dysfunction; reticular activating system deficiency causes altered consciousness.

# Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome

## Overview

### What is neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a rare and life-threatening reaction to the use of any neuroleptic medication. Neuroleptics, also known as [antipsychotic medications](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/24692-antipsychotic-medications), treat and manage symptoms of many psychiatric conditions.

Advertisement

Cleveland Clinic is a non-profit academic medical center. Advertising on our site helps support our mission. We do not endorse non-Cleveland Clinic products or services.[Policy](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/advertising)

NMS is characterized by the following:

*   High fever ([hyperthermia](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/22111-hyperthermia)).
*   Stiff, rigid [muscles](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/21887-muscle) that can lead to eventual muscle breakdown.
*   Altered mental status.
*   Autonomic nervous system dysfunction ([dysautonomia](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/6004-dysautonomia)).

Your autonomic [nervous system](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/21202-nervous-system) regulates certain body processes, such as [blood pressure](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/17649-blood-pressure) and your rate of breathing. Autonomic dysfunction leads to wide swings in blood pressure, excessive sweating (secondary [hyperhidrosis](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/17113-hyperhidrosis)) and excessive secretion of saliva (spit).

NMS is potentially life-threatening and requires immediate medical attention in a hospital setting.

### What are neuroleptic medications?

Neuroleptics, also known as antipsychotic medications, fall into two classes: first-generation or “typical” antipsychotics and second-generation or “atypical” antipsychotics.

Healthcare providers prescribe first- and second-generation antipsychotics for various neuropsychiatric conditions, including:

*   Behavioral disturbances in [dementia](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/9170-dementia).
*   [Bipolar disorder](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/9294-bipolar-disorder).
*   [Depression](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/9290-depression).
*   [Eating disorders](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/4152-eating-disorders).
*   [Generalized anxiety disorder](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/23940-generalized-anxiety-disorder-gad).
*   Geriatric agitation.
*   [Insomnia](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/12119-insomnia).
*   [Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/9490-obsessive-compulsive-disorder).
*   [Personality disorders](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/9636-personality-disorders-overview).
*   [Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/9545-post-traumatic-stress-disorder-ptsd).
*   [Schizoaffective disorder](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/21544-schizoaffective-disorder).
*   [Schizophrenia](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/4568-schizophrenia) and related disorders.

### Which drugs cause neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

The following medications are associated with NMS:

Advertisement

Typical neuroleptic (antipsychotic) medications:

*   Bromperidol.
*   Chlorpromazine.
*   Clopenthixol.
*   [Fluphenazine](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/20254-fluphenazine-tablets).
*   [Haloperidol](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/19626-haloperidol-tablets).
*   [Loxapine](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/19996-loxapine-capsules).
*   Promazine.
*   [Thioridazine](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/19684-thioridazine-tablets).
*   [Thiothixene](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/19352-thiothixene-capsules).
*   [Trifluoperazine](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/18325-trifluoperazine-tablets).

Atypical neuroleptic (antipsychotic) medications:

*   Amisulpride.
*   [Aripiprazole](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/18424-aripiprazole-dissolving-tablets).
*   [Clozapine](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/19561-clozapine-tablets).
*   [Olanzapine](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/18192-olanzapine-tablets).
*   [Quetiapine](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/19288-quetiapine-tablets).
*   [Risperidone](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/20391-risperidone-tablets).
*   [Ziprasidone](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/18590-ziprasidone-capsules).
*   Zotepine.

Antiemetic medications:

*   Domperidone.
*   [Droperidol](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/20016-droperidol-injection).
*   [Metoclopramide](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/18008-metoclopramide-tablets).
*   [Prochlorperazine](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/20614-prochlorperazine-tablets).
*   [Promethazine](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/19812-promethazine-tablets).

Dopaminergic (antiparkinson) medications (from withdrawal):

*   [Amantadine](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/19249-amantadine-oral-capsules-or-tablets).
*   [Dopamine agonists](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/24958-dopamine-agonists).
*   [Levodopa](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/20349-carbidopa-levodopa-tablets).
*   [Tolcapone](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/18780-tolcapone-tablets).

### What is the difference between neuroleptic malignant syndrome and malignant hyperthermia?

[Malignant hyperthermia](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/17945-malignant-hyperthermia) is a rare and severe reaction to general [anesthesia](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/15286-anesthesia) drugs and [muscle relaxants](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/24686-muscle-relaxers).

Common symptoms include muscle rigidity, slow/decreased reflexes ([hyporeflexia](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/24176-hyporeflexia)) and changes in skin, including bluish discoloration or flushing.

These symptoms may look similar to NMS. However, in most cases, healthcare providers can tell the two conditions apart based on the medical history of the affected person — whether they recently had exposure to an anesthetic or a neuroleptic medication.

### What is the difference between neuroleptic malignant syndrome and serotonin syndrome?

[Serotonin syndrome](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/17687-serotonin-syndrome) is caused by serotonergic agents such as antidepressants, amphetamines, antihistamines and mood stabilizers. Serotonin syndrome happens when there’s too much serotonin in your body.

Symptoms of serotonin syndrome include muscle rigidity, increased/faster reflexes ([hyperreflexia](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/24967-hyperreflexia)), diarrhea, sweating, muscle jerks ([myoclonus](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/15301-myoclonus-muscle-twitch)) and altered mental state. High fever (hyperthermia) and muscle rigidity are usually less severe with serotonin syndrome than with NMS.

Your healthcare provider can distinguish between serotonin syndrome and NMS by both your history and your symptoms.

### Who does neuroleptic malignant syndrome affect?

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) can affect anyone taking neuroleptic (antipsychotic) medications.

Although two-thirds of NMS cases are thought to occur within the first week of starting neuroleptic medications, the syndrome may happen at any time during treatment.

### How common is neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is rare. Approximately 0.01% to 3.2% of people taking neuroleptic (antipsychotic) medications develop NMS.

Cases have been decreasing due to newer medications that are less likely to cause NMS and increased awareness of the syndrome.

## Symptoms and Causes

### What are the symptoms of neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

Symptoms of neuroleptic malignant syndrome typically develop over one to three days and include:

*   Very high [fever](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/10880-fever) (102 to 104 degrees Fahrenheit).
*   Irregular heartbeat ([arrhythmia](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/16749-arrhythmia)).
*   Fast heart rate ([tachycardia](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/22108-tachycardia)).
*   Rapid breathing (tachypnea).
*   Muscle rigidity (stiffness).
*   Altered mental status.
*   [High blood pressure](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/4314-hypertension-high-blood-pressure) or [low blood pressure](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/21156-low-blood-pressure-hypotension).
*   Excessive sweating.

Advertisement

If you’re experiencing these symptoms, it’s important to call 911 and get medical treatment as soon as possible.

### How do neuroleptics cause NMS?

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) can happen from a single dose, increasing dose or the same dose of neuroleptic (antipsychotic) medication. NMS is primarily associated with first-generation antipsychotics but can occur, to a lesser degree, with second-generation antipsychotics, antiemetics, and the withdrawal of anti-Parkinson, or dopaminergic, medication.

Scientists are still learning about the exact cause of neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), but it’s currently hypothesized that it’s caused by dopamine D2 receptor antagonism. Dopamine is a neurotransmitter (chemical substance) that acts to convey messages from one cell to another. Neuroleptics block this messenger from entering cells at a specific receptor.

When the dopamine receptors in your hypothalamus and/or your [spinal cord](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/21946-spinal-cord) are blocked, it causes increased muscle stiffness. The interference with the dopamine receptors in your [hypothalamus](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/22566-hypothalamus) is also responsible for high fever as well as significant changes in blood pressure, as seen in NMS.

## Diagnosis and Tests

### How is neuroleptic malignant syndrome diagnosed?

In order for healthcare providers to diagnose NMS, you must have all of the following symptoms or conditions:

Advertisement

*   You’re taking a neuroleptic medication or have suddenly stopped a dopaminergic medication.
*   You have severe muscle rigidity (stiffness), which is causing muscle breakdown.
*   You have a high fever.
*   You have altered mental status.

In addition, you must have at least two of the following symptoms:

*   Excessive or abnormal sweating.
*   Difficulty swallowing.
*   Incontinence (loss of bladder or bowel control).
*   Rapid heart rate ([tachycardia](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/17616-ventricular-tachycardia)).
*   Sudden inability to speak.
*   Elevated or frequently fluctuating blood pressure.
*   Leukocytosis (increased white blood cell count).
*   Elevated creatine phosphokinase (CPK) due to muscle breakdown.
*   Slow or limited reflexes (hyporeflexia).

### What tests will be done to diagnose neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

Your healthcare provider may order the following tests if they suspect you have neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS):

*   [Comprehensive metabolic panel](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diagnostics/22058-comprehensive-metabolic-panel-cmp).
*   [Urinalysis](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diagnostics/17893-urinalysis).
*   Arterial or venous [blood gas test](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diagnostics/22409-arterial-blood-gas-abg).
*   CPK (creatine phosphokinase) blood test.

## Management and Treatment

### How is neuroleptic malignant syndrome treated?

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a medical emergency, so quick diagnosis and treatment are essential. If you have NMS, you’ll need to receive care in a hospital setting — most likely an intensive care unit (ICU).

In all cases of NMS, healthcare providers discontinue the use of the neuroleptic (antipsychotic) medication that caused NMS. Treatment also involves treating the symptoms of NMS and preventing complications. Treatments could include:

Advertisement

*   Maintaining cardiorespiratory stability through [mechanical ventilation](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/15368-mechanical-ventilation), [antiarrhythmic medications](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/19886-amiodarone-tablets) and/or pacemakers.
*   Maintaining your [electrolyte](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diagnostics/21790-electrolytes) balance through IV fluids.
*   Lowering your fever using cooling blankets, ice water and/or ice packs.
*   Lowering your blood pressure, if it’s elevated, through medication.
*   Treating or preventing blood clots through [heparin](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/19322-heparin-injection) (blot clot medication).
*   Providing medications that can reverse your low dopamine state.
*   Providing muscle or skeletal relaxants.

Care at Cleveland Clinic

[Neurology Care for Adults](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/services/neurology-care)

[Neurology Care for Children](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/pediatrics/services/neurology-care)

[Make an Appointment](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/webappointment/what-to-expect)

## Outlook / Prognosis

### What is the prognosis (outlook) for neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

If neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is diagnosed quickly and treated aggressively and appropriately, most people recover within two to 14 days.

Delayed treatment can result in significant complications, such as muscle, kidney, heart and/or lung issues.

NMS can result in death if it’s not treated quickly enough. The mortality (death) rates for NMS range from 5% to 20%. However, the mortality rate has improved over the past few decades due to awareness of NMS and the use of new antipsychotic medications.

Many people can successfully restart neuroleptic (antipsychotic) medications under guidance from their healthcare provider.

### What are the complications of neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

Unfortunately, complications of neuroleptic malignant are common and severe. While some complications result from the characteristic symptoms of NMS and autonomic dysfunction, others, especially infections, may occur from a prolonged stay in an intensive care unit (ICU).

Complications of NMS include:

*   [Rhabdomyolysis](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/21184-rhabdomyolysis) (most common complication).
*   Dehydration.
*   Acute [kidney failure](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/17689-kidney-failure).
*   Acute respiratory failure.
*   [Seizures](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/6998-seizures-first-aid).
*   [Heart attack](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/16818-heart-attack-myocardial-infarction) (myocardial infarction).
*   [Blood clots](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/17675-blood-clots) throughout your body ([disseminated intravascular coagulation](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/21836-disseminated-intravascular-coagulation-dic)).
*   Acute [liver failure](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/17819-liver-failure).
*   [Pneumonia](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/4471-pneumonia).
*   [Sepsis](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/12361-sepsis).
*   [Urinary tract infection (UTI)](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/9135-urinary-tract-infections).
*   [Pulmonary embolism](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/17400-pulmonary-embolism) (blood clot in your lung).

Because the complications are severe and life-threatening, it’s important to call 911 and seek medical care as soon as possible if you’re experiencing symptoms of NMS. Again, NMS is a life-threatening emergency and may require ICU (intensive care unit) admission.

### When should I see my healthcare provider?

If you take one or more neuroleptic (antipsychotic), antiemetic and/or dopaminergic (antiparkinson) medications, it’s important to see your healthcare provider regularly to make sure the medication is working for you. It’s also important to ask your healthcare provider about the side effects of the medications you’re taking and what symptoms to look out for.

#### When should I go to ER for neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

If you’re experiencing symptoms of neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), such as a very high fever and stiff muscles, it’s absolutely critical to call 911 or get to the nearest hospital as soon as possible. NMS requires immediate medical treatment and can result in death if it’s not treated quickly and properly.

## Prevention

### What are the risk factors for developing neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

Risk factors for developing neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) include the initiation (starting) or increase in the dosage of neuroleptic (antipsychotic) medication. The use of more than one neuroleptic medication or [lithium](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/18665-lithium-tablets-or-capsules) also increases the risk. Finally, abrupt cessation (stopping) of a dopaminergic medication (such as a Parkinson’s medication) may cause NMS.

### A note from Cleveland Clinic

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a serious and life-threatening condition, so if you’re experiencing symptoms, getting medical care as soon as possible is crucial. It’s much easier to treat NMS in its early phase. Even though NMS is rare, it’s important to talk to your healthcare provider or pharmacist about side effects and symptoms to look out for if you take neuroleptic (antipsychotic) medications. They’re there to help you.

# Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) - Cleveland Clinic

## Overview
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a rare and life-threatening reaction to neuroleptic (antipsychotic) medications. It is characterized by high fever (hyperthermia), severe muscle rigidity that can lead to muscle breakdown, altered mental status, and autonomic nervous system dysfunction (dysautonomia). NMS is potentially life-threatening and requires immediate medical attention in a hospital setting.

## Medications Associated with NMS
NMS can be caused by:
- **Typical antipsychotics** (e.g., haloperidol, fluphenazine, chlorpromazine)
- **Atypical antipsychotics** (e.g., clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone, aripiprazole, quetiapine)
- **Antiemetic medications** (e.g., metoclopramide, droperidol, prochlorperazine)
- **Withdrawal of dopaminergic/antiparkinson medications** (e.g., levodopa, dopamine agonists, amantadine)

## Key Facts
- **Prevalence:** Approximately 0.01% to 3.2% of people taking neuroleptic medications develop NMS. Cases have been decreasing due to newer medications and increased awareness.
- **Timing:** About two-thirds of cases occur within the first week of starting neuroleptic medications, but the syndrome can happen at any time during treatment.
- **Mortality:** Ranges from 5% to 20%, though mortality rates have improved due to awareness and newer medications.
- **Recovery:** With prompt diagnosis and aggressive treatment, most people recover within two to 14 days.

## Symptoms (develop over 1-3 days)
- Very high fever (102-104°F)
- Irregular heartbeat (arrhythmia) and fast heart rate (tachycardia)
- Rapid breathing (tachypnea)
- Muscle rigidity/stiffness
- Altered mental status
- High or low blood pressure
- Excessive sweating

## Diagnosis
Requires ALL of the following: taking a neuroleptic medication (or sudden stoppage of dopaminergic medication), severe muscle rigidity causing muscle breakdown, high fever, and altered mental status. Plus at least two additional symptoms (e.g., sweating, swallowing difficulty, incontinence, tachycardia, elevated blood pressure, leukocytosis, elevated CPK).

## Treatment
NMS is a medical emergency requiring ICU care. Treatment includes: discontinuing the causative medication, maintaining cardiorespiratory stability, IV fluids for electrolyte balance, fever reduction (cooling blankets, ice packs), blood pressure management, blood clot prevention, and medications to reverse the low dopamine state.

## Complications
Severe complications include rhabdomyolysis (most common), dehydration, acute kidney failure, respiratory failure, seizures, heart attack, blood clots (DIC), liver failure, pneumonia, sepsis, UTIs, and pulmonary embolism.

## Risk Factors
Starting or increasing dosage of neuroleptic medication, using more than one neuroleptic or lithium, and abrupt cessation of dopaminergic (Parkinson's) medications.

## Distinction from Similar Conditions
- **Malignant hyperthermia:** Similar symptoms but caused by exposure to anesthesia drugs, not neuroleptics.
- **Serotonin syndrome:** Caused by serotonergic agents (antidepressants, etc.); typically has less severe hyperthermia and muscle rigidity than NMS.

# Premature drug reduction after subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation leading to worse depression in patients with Parkinson's disease

Yu Diao 1

Tianqi Hu 1

Hutao Xie 1

Houyou Fan 1

Fangang Meng 1,2

Anchao Yang 1,2

Yutong Bai 1\*

Jianguo Zhang 1,2\*

1. Department of Neurosurgery, Beijing Tiantan Hospital, Capital Medical University, Beijing, China

2. Department of Functional Neurosurgery, Beijing Neurosurgical Institute, Capital Medical University, Beijing, China

Article metrics

## Abstract

**Background:**

Reduction of medication in Parkinson's disease (PD) following subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation (STN-DBS) has been recognized, but the optimal timing for medication adjustments remains unclear, posing challenges in postoperative patient management.

**Objective:**

This study aimed to provide evidence for the timing of medication reduction post-DBS using propensity score matching (PSM).

**Methods:**

In this study, initial programming and observation sessions were conducted over 1 week for patients 4–6 weeks postoperatively. Patients were subsequently categorized into medication reduction or non-reduction groups based on their dyskinesia evaluation using the 4.2-item score from the MDS-UPDRS-IV. PSM was employed to maintain baseline comparability. Short-term motor and neuropsychiatric symptom assessments for both groups were conducted 3–6 months postoperatively.

**Results:**

A total of 123 PD patients were included. Baseline balance in motor and non-motor scores was achieved between the two groups based on PSM. Short-term efficacy revealed a significant reduction in depression scores within the non-reduction group compared to baseline (*P* < 0.001) and a significant reduction compared to the reduction group (*P* = 0.037). No significant differences were observed in UPDRS-III and HAMA scores between the two groups. Within-group analysis showed improvements in motor symptoms, depression, anxiety, and subdomains in the non-reduction group, while the reduction group exhibited improvements only in motor symptoms.

**Conclusion:**

This study provides evidence for the timing of medication reduction following DBS. Our findings suggest that early maintenance of medication stability is more favorable for improving neuropsychiatric symptoms.

## Introduction

Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the subthalamic nucleus (STN) is the first-line surgical treatment for Parkinson's disease (PD), it can effectively improve Parkinson's disease patients' motor and non-motor symptoms (1, 2), reduce motor fluctuations, reduce dopaminergic drug use and adverse drug reactions, and improve patients' quality of life (3–5). In recent years, an increasing number of studies have discovered that non-motor symptoms, particularly emotional aspects such as anxiety and depression, have a significant impact on the quality of life of Parkinson's disease patients (6).

The success of DBS is critically dependent on delivering the appropriate dose of stimulation at the best location within the target region (7). DBS programming is the process of choosing the appropriate electrical stimulation dose at the individual electrode placement and anatomy to achieve the greatest clinical benefit (8). DBS programming is a process that relies on clinical observation and repeated empirical attempts by programming doctors (9). A large number of parameter combinations, including frequency, pulse width, and stimulation voltage selection, as well as contact selection, are usually insufficient to test the best curative effect in a clinical routine treatment (10, 11). If the patient experiences drug side effects such as dyskinesias, apart from the stimulation parameters, the drug may also be adjusted (12). This will result in a greater number of test parameters being combined. Furthermore, while real-time observation and adjustment of stimulation parameters and contacts can improve motor symptoms, most non-motor symptoms cannot be effectively adjusted through real-time observation (13, 14). As a result, the curative effect of programming is highly dependent on the programming doctor's experience and the number of times the patient has gone through trial and error. This has resulted in patients' uncontrollable postoperative clinical benefit, with individual differences in clinical benefit.

In addition to improving the clinical symptoms of patients, STN-DBS has the effect of reducing dopamine drug use (15). Existing research indicates that after DBS, a high dose of LEDD reduces quality of life, and that there is a negative correlation between the two (16). As a result, postoperative drug adjustment, especially the reduction of drug, is critical. Compared with drug therapy alone, the adjustment of drug dosage and type after STN-DBS can better improve the patients' motor and non-motor symptoms (4, 17, 18). For example, after surgery, appropriate medication reductions improved the patient's depressive symptoms and reduced motor fluctuations (19, 20). Medication is reduced based on response to stimulation according to existing drug reduction strategies. If there is a clear response to stim, even a partial response, medication can be gradually reduced. If there is not a response to stimulation because the stimulation parameters are still being determined, medication should not be reduced (21). However, the current drug reduction strategy only relies on clinical response and doctor experience, which has some limitations. If the patient's first-time programming effect is satisfactory, it is an unresolved issue whether the drug dosage should be reduced immediately or maintained in the early stage. If the dosage, type, or timing of the adjustment of the drug is improper, it may cause dopamine dysregulation syndrome (DDS), mental symptoms, depression, mania, etc. (22–24). Improper adjustment of dopamine agonists within 3 months after DBS can lead to the development of manic symptoms or impairment of impulse control (25). In addition, reducing dopamine agonist medications and levodopa immediately after surgery can lead to depression and anxiety (26). As a result, the current DBS postoperative drug adjustment is also based on trial-and-error results of the programmed parameters and the experience of the programmed doctor, and the current postoperative drug adjustment lacks clinical evidence support. When the curative effect of the patient's first programming is acceptable or dyskinesias occur, the programming doctor usually chooses to reduce the drug dosage or stimulation parameters, however, there is no evidence to suggest which method is superior.

In the present study, we included 123 patients treated with STN-DBS and compared early drug reduction (drug reduction at the initial programming after surgery) and late drug reduction (reduction of drug after 3–6 months after surgery) differences in motor and mental symptoms, with the goal of providing clinical evidence support for drug adjustment after DBS and reducing the number of programming trial and error.

## Methods

### Study design and ethical approval

This study was a single center retrospective study. Baseline visit was conducted between August 2018 and February 2021 in Beijing Tiantan Hospital. The programming parameter of the first time was high frequency stimulation, as used by most centers.

The patients in this study were all treated at Tiantan Hospital, and the study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and authorized by Tiantan Hospital Ethics Committees. Our study followed the STROBE guidelines, and the selection of clinical problems followed the PICOS principle.

### Patients

The PD diagnosis was based on UK Brain Bank criteria (27). Patients were screened for bilateral STN-DBS according to the International PD and Movement Disorders Society and National Neurological Society guidelines (28). Levodopa challenge tests were considered satisfactory if there was >30% Movement Disorders Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS)-III improvement, and the patients were treated with DBS.

Patient medication adjustments were jointly decided by neurologists and programming doctors. Initial programming for patients commenced at 4–6 weeks post-surgery (T1) and spanned a duration of 1 week, involving 2–3 programming sessions. During this period, medication adjustments were based on the patients' MDS-UPDRS Part IV item 4.2 scores. Patients with scores ≥2 points after 2–3 programming sessions underwent medication reduction, while those scoring 0–1 points had their medication maintained at a stable level. Short-term follow-up at 3–6 months post-surgery (T2) involved maintaining medication dosages unchanged from T1. Patients were categorized into reduced and non-reduced groups based on whether medication adjustments were made at T1. We excluded patients with clinically relevant severe neuropsychiatric disorders and if neuropsychological impairments were found in the preoperative multi-disciplinary assessments by specialized neuropsychologists and neuropsychiatrists (29). All participants provided written informed consent to take part in the study.

### Clinical assessment

Clinical assessments were conducted at preoperative baseline (within 1 month before surgery) in the ON-medication state (MedON) and OFF-medication state (MedOFF), with at 3–6 months follow-up (medication and stimulation ON/medication OFF and stimulation ON, MedON-StimON/MedOFF-StimON). Due to the best efficacy of DBS achieved within 3–6 months after surgery, 3–6 months was the time point for short-term efficacy analyses of this cohort study at our center (30).

With the following scales:

Motor disorder: MDS-UPDRS-III (31) and Hoehn-Yahr Stage were used to investigate motor impairment. MDS-UPDRS-III involved video collections and was scored by two experienced doctors in a single-blind way, back-to-back (32, 33). Higher scores indicated higher impairment in all scales.

The therapeutic medical regimen was recorded to calculate the levodopa equivalent daily dose (LEDD) according to the method of Tomlinson et al. (34).

The Hamilton Rating Scale for Anxiety/Depression (anxiety/depression, HAM-A/-D) were used for anxiety and depression (35). The 24 items of HAMD were grouped into the following seven factors: (1) anxiety/somatization (six items: psychic anxiety, somatic anxiety, gastrointestinal symptoms, hypochondriasis, insight, and general symptoms); (2) weight loss (one item); (3) cognitive disturbances (six items: self-guilt, suicide, agitation, depersonalization and derealization, paranoid, and obsessive compulsive symptom); (4) circadian fluctuations (one item); (5) retardation symptoms (four items: depression, work and interests, retardation, and sexual symptoms); (6) sleep disturbances (three items: difficulty falling asleep, superficial sleep and early awakening); (7) hopelessness symptoms (three items: helplessness, hopelessness, and worthlessness) (36). The 14 items of HAMA were grouped into the following two factors: (1) somatic anxiety (seven items: somatic anxiety muscular, somatic anxiety sensory, cardiovascular symptoms, respiratory symptoms, gastro-intestinal symptoms, genito-urinary symptoms, and autonomic symptoms); (2) psychic anxiety (seven items: anxious mood, tension, fears, insomnia, cognitive, depressed mood, and behavior at interview). Higher scores indicated higher impairment in all scales.

## Programming and follow-up

In Tiantan Center, there is a special team responsible for PD patients' evaluation. They did not participate to the programming or surgery procedure. So they were unaware of the programming parameters or whether the drug was reduced. At each follow-up, an appointment was made for the patients to be evaluated first, followed by programming. We considered these results were less bias for acute programming parameter changes. As a result, the evaluation results were guaranteed to reflect the patient's true effects within 3–6 months.

The programming doctor performs trial and error on the patient's programming parameters based on the patient's motor symptoms, non-motor symptoms, dyskinesias, and other side effects. The initial programming parameters primarily employ monopolar stimulation of the STN's dorsal contact, 130 Hz high-frequency stimulation, 60 μs pulse width, and a voltage of approximately 2.0 V. Adjust the combination of contacts and parameters based on the patient's immediate motor response and stimulus-related side effects to the programming when the patient is not taking anti-parkinsonian drugs.

Following 1 week of programming and observation, patients conclude their initial programming phase. Subsequently, they return to the hospital for short-term follow-up 3–6 months postoperatively. Throughout the T1-T2 timeframe, the patients' programming parameters and medication regimens remain consistent with those at T1. After the conclusion of the short-term follow-up, patients undergo another 1 week programming and medication adjustment session. We define 1-year post-surgery as the milestone for long-term follow-up, at which point we conduct an assessment of the patients' long-term therapeutic efficacy.

### Statistical analysis

The normality of distribution was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Differences of baseline characteristics and the follow-up between the two groups were analyzed using Mann-Whitney U-tests or unpaired *t*-tests, if parametric tests were applicable. Outcome changes from baseline to follow-up of each group were tested using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests or paired samples *t*-tests, and the results from the two groups were tested with Mann-Whitney U-tests or unpaired *t*-tests. The threshold was *P* < 0.05, unless stated otherwise. All statistical tests were two-tailed. The magnitude of clinical responses was evaluated with relative changes [(mean Testfollow − up-mean Testbaseline)/mean Testbaseline] and Cohen's effect size [(mean Testbaseline-mean Testfollow − up)/SD Testchangescores]. Confidence intervals were calculated for effect sizes based on non-central *t*- distribution (29). Multiple comparisons of the domines of HAMA and HAMD, resulting from the two groups and the use of multiple tests, were corrected using the FDR method. Corrected *P*-values adjusted to the significance threshold of *P* < 0.05 are presented unless otherwise stated.

Furthermore, as our study included data from an observational perspective cohort study of MDS-UPDRS-III, we screened all patients who met the enrollment criteria of this study, and who were enrolled from August 2018 to February 2021, and excluded patients who were lost to follow-up. We used propensity score matching (PSM) to increase causal inference and minimize selection bias. PSM is therefore also called a post-random method. The aim here was to find sub-cohorts of patients in the reducing LEDD group and non-reducing LEDD group with accurately balanced preoperative demographic and clinical characteristics. Variables included for propensity score matching were baseline MDS-UPDRS-III (MedOFF), LEDD, HAMD, HAMA, age at intervention, sex, and duration to reduce confounding factors between categories. Nearest-neighbor matching with a 0.03 caliper without replacement was conducted using a 1:1 ratio (37–39). Subsequently, all analyses of clinical changes from baseline to follow-up were also conducted for the identified matched cohort. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS statistical software for Windows, version 25.0 (SPSS, Chicago, IL, USA) and R 3.6.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing. Analyses were performed using the R statistical software version 3.6.1 (available online at <http://www.R-project.org>) and propensity score analysis using the “MatchIt” package (40).

## Results

A total of 123 patients were included, and one patient who was not returning for the 3–6 months follow-up were excluded. Finally, a total of 122 patients (64 males) with PD patients undergoing bilateral STN-DBS were included in the statistical analyses ([Figure 1](#F1)). The patients were divided in two groups involving the reducing LEDD group (*n* = 75) and non-reducing LEDD group (*n* = 47). The 122 patients in the final analysis were aged 61.93 ± 8.41 years with 13.21 ± 4.75 years disease durations. The Hoehn and Yahr was 2.9 ± 0.2. The average MMSE was 26.19 ± 4.04 and the cores of PDQ-39 were 60.83 ± 24.21 for all patients.

### Differences of outcomes at follow-up

Both groups showed improvement in HAMD total scores and HAMD sleep disturbance scores improved, but more improvement was found in the non-reducing group. Compared to the group with reduced LEDD, the group without LEDD reduction exhibited a significant decrease in the total HAMD score (*P* = 0.037). As expected, the LEDDs were significantly lower ([Table 2](#T2)). Programming parameters are listed in [Table 3](#T3) and were balanced in both groups. Long-term follow-up is shown in [Supplementary Table 1](#SM1). The patient's anxiety (*P* = 0.011) and depression (*P* = 0.013) improved significantly, but there is no different significantly between the two groups.
