## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343)Abstract

In Parkinson’s disease (PD) patients, the progressive nature of the disease and the variability of disabling motor and non-motor symptoms contribute to the growing caregiver burden of PD partners and conflicts in their relationships. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) improves PD symptoms and patients’ quality of life but necessitates an intensified therapy optimization after DBS surgery. This review illuminates caregiver burden in the context of DBS, framing both pre- and postoperative aspects. We aim to provide an overview of perioperative factors influencing caregiver burden and wish to stimulate further recognition of caregiver burden of PD patients with DBS.

**Keywords:**caregiver burden, Parkinson’s disease, deep brain stimulation, neuropsychiatric symptoms, depression

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343)1. Introduction

Caregiver burden (CB) is defined as “the extent to which caregivers perceive that caregiving has an adverse effect on their emotional, social, financial, physical and spiritual functioning” [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B1-brainsci-12-00238)] and occurs in the context of providing informal care for relatives with chronic diseases. Since Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a complex disorder with increasing disabling motor and non-motor symptoms over time, partners of PD patients are at risk of increased CB. The interplay of motor disabilities such as bradykinesia or tremor and non-motor impairments such as cognitive decline, depression or urinary dysfunction challenges both caregiver and recipient. Along with disease progression, higher CB occurs in advanced stages of the disease with higher symptom severity [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B2-brainsci-12-00238)], with non-motor symptoms impacting CB more than motor impairments [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B3-brainsci-12-00238)]. General risk factors for CB are female sex, cohabilitation with the care recipient, the amount of caregiving time and effort and lack of choice [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B4-brainsci-12-00238)]. Female caregivers of PD patients have worse quality of life (QOL) along with impaired mobility, emotional well-being and non-motor symptoms of the PD patient as predictors of CB [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B5-brainsci-12-00238)]. CB can have detrimental effects on the quality of caregiving, as well as the mental health of the caregiver. Therefore, it is pivotal to engage further family members to uncover and reduce CB [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B4-brainsci-12-00238)] and prevent premature institutionalization, as this does often not meet the wishes of caregiver and recipient [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B6-brainsci-12-00238)].

In advanced disease stages, oral drugs fail to sufficiently control PD symptoms, with motor and non-motor fluctuations leaving the patient and caregiver with uncertainty and helplessness in part due to the loss of control of unpredictable symptoms. Therefore, device-aided therapies such as deep brain stimulation (DBS) represent a therapeutic option to provide a substantial long-term improvement of fluctuating PD symptoms, QOL [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B7-brainsci-12-00238)] and probably longer life expectancy [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B8-brainsci-12-00238)]. The DBS operation defines a turning point in the long course of the disease and comes along with high hopes and fears of the patient and caregiver. However, the difficult postoperative adjustments of medication and stimulation can result in severe side effects such as accentuated neuropsychiatric symptoms, potentially resulting in higher risk of suicide [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B9-brainsci-12-00238)], which could affect postoperative CB. Little is known whether informal caregivers actually profit from DBS in terms of CB reduction along with postoperative motor and non-motor symptom control.

This review aims to provide a concise overview of factors contributing to CB in PD in the context of DBS. We retrieved relevant literature published in the PubMed database from 1 January 1993, to 2 February 2022. Database searches were limited to articles published in English. The search terms were as follows: “Caregiver Burden” and “Deep Brain Stimulation” or “DBS”. ([Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#brainsci-12-00238-f001)) ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#brainsci-12-00238-t001)). Additionally, studies of reference were also manually retrieved with the following search terms: “Caregiver Burden” or “Caregiver” or “Caregiving” and “Parkinson” or “Parkinson’s disease” or “Neuropsychiatric symptoms”. Titles and abstracts were screened, and more details were retrieved from the main manuscript. The following information was extracted from the included studies: first author, year of publication, study design, patient’s age, sample size, PD duration, gender distribution, number of caregivers enrolled and outcome parameters/domain of interests.

We first discuss preoperative aspects of PD influencing CB. Here, we concentrate on preoperative mediators of CB and then focus on care recipient and caregiver expectations of DBS. Second, we address postoperative issues arising from the DBS-induced symptom relief or DBS side effects and how that impacts postoperative CB. We discuss how DBS interferes with the long-built relationship of care recipient and caregiver when suddenly the burden of disease fades. Our target is to raise attention to this significant clinical problem and mitigate postoperative CB of PD patients’ caregivers.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343)2. Preoperative Caregiver Burden—DBS Yes or No?

### 2.1. Caregiver Burden Due to Insufficient PD Symptom Control in Advanced Stages

Optimal control of both motor and non-motor symptoms becomes difficult as the therapeutic window narrows in advanced stages of the disease. The combination of oral antiparkinsonian drugs results in a highly complex medication intake with tight timetables but often insufficient symptom control. Along with disease progression, caregiver demands increase, with the highest estimated cost for PD patients in Hoehn and Yahr stage IV [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B2-brainsci-12-00238)]. Motor symptoms become more severe with occurrence of unpredictable motor fluctuations such as peak-dose dyskinesia, wearing off, gait dysfunction, freezing of gait, postural instability and higher risk of falls. Accordingly, caregiver burden is positively correlated with PD motor symptoms, overall disability and Hoehn and Yahr stage, as well as a decrease in PD patients’ activities in daily living (ADL) [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B2-brainsci-12-00238),[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B10-brainsci-12-00238)]. In fact, motor symptoms are a relevant factor for the prediction of CB in nonsurgical PD patients [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B11-brainsci-12-00238)]. Among the diverse non-motor aspects of PD, neuropsychiatric symptoms such as depression, psychosis or impulse control disorders play a substantial role in the daily living of PD patients. These neuropsychiatric symptoms even contribute more to the caregiver burden of PD partners than motor impairment [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B2-brainsci-12-00238),[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B5-brainsci-12-00238),[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B12-brainsci-12-00238)]. Caregiver distress increases along with worsening neuropsychiatric symptoms and lower quality of life of PD patients [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B13-brainsci-12-00238)]. In a cross-sectional observational study of 89 PD patients and 84 caregivers, neuropsychiatric symptoms, such as mood changes and apathy but also MDS-Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) II, caregiving hours per day and caregivers’ Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), had the most impact on CB [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B14-brainsci-12-00238)]. Apart from that, cognitive disturbances correlate with PD patients’ quality of life and caregiver burden [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B11-brainsci-12-00238)]. There are even extreme examples where PD patients cannot tolerate being alone at all [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B2-brainsci-12-00238)]. Neuropsychiatric complications can result in physical aggression against the caregiver, also being directly connected with CB in advanced PD patients [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B15-brainsci-12-00238)]. The 25-item self-reported Alzheimer’s Patient Partners Life Impact Questionnaire (APPLIQue) identified in 74 informal caregivers of advanced-stage PD patients in Hoehn and Yahr stage IV–V the three most rated aspects: “feel of guilt if not there” (71% affirmed), “situation wears me down” (65%) and “always on my mind” (61%) [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B16-brainsci-12-00238)]. Factors associated with higher caregiver QOL were female PD patient gender, better PD patients’ cognition, lower non-motor symptom burden of PD patients and not being the partner of the patient [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B16-brainsci-12-00238)]. In conclusion, PD challenges informal caregivers due to the multitude of different symptoms and caregiver responsibilities, with neuropsychiatric symptoms exerting the probably most severe impact on CB.

### 2.2. Caregiver Expectations of DBS

When oral antiparkinsonian drugs fail to sufficiently control motor symptoms, advanced device-aided therapies such as DBS serve as rescue options. Subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation (STN-DBS) is a well-established therapy for PD and now considered even earlier in the course of the disease when the first clinical signs of motor fluctuations and medically refractory symptoms such as tremor appear [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B17-brainsci-12-00238),[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B18-brainsci-12-00238),[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B19-brainsci-12-00238)]. DBS treatment is associated with substantial symptomatic relief and maintenance of activities of daily living (ADL) even over 10 years [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B7-brainsci-12-00238)]. The lower the preoperative quality of life (QOL), the higher the improvement in QOL after 24 months [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B20-brainsci-12-00238)]. The combined effect of STN-DBS and L-dopa reduces motor severity in PD even more than either treatment alone [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B21-brainsci-12-00238)], with a reduction in L-dopa equivalent following surgery of 55.9%, a 69.1% reduction in dyskinesia and an average reduction of off-periods of 68.2% [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B22-brainsci-12-00238)]. Apart from motor improvement, non-motor symptom reduction was associated with QOL and ADL in a 24-month follow-up [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B23-brainsci-12-00238)]. This is of great importance, as caregiver burden is highly dependent on non-motor symptomatology [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B24-brainsci-12-00238)].

Therefore, DBS is often considered a “game changer” for both PD patients and their caregivers and raises high expectations of DBS effects on QOL. As to the great involvement of spouses in caregiving, the decision to undergo DBS surgery should take into account the caregiver’s expectations and fears. DBS represents an invasive operation of the brain with potential intraoperative complications such as intracranial bleeding, infection and the need for electrode revision [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B25-brainsci-12-00238)], which might elicit fears and concerns in terms of intraoperative adverse events in patients and caregivers. Complication rates are low but must be disclosed to the caregiver and care recipient. It is discussed that unrealistic, unmet expectations contribute to postoperative caregiver dissatisfaction and increased CB [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B26-brainsci-12-00238)]. Despite caregiving responsibilities, the PD subject and caregiver have an overall satisfying relationship preoperatively, but this relationship will be challenged by the sudden DBS-induced changes of motor capabilities of the care-receiving PD patient [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B27-brainsci-12-00238)]. Both patients’ and caregivers’ treatment expectations should be preoperatively addressed and the risk–benefit ratio and perioperative demands of the procedure communicated [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B28-brainsci-12-00238)]. A study from a single tertiary care hospital in India revealed a profound lack of knowledge and misconceptions regarding DBS among PD patients and caregivers [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B29-brainsci-12-00238)]. Thereby, false expectations and postoperative disappointment can occur. In fact, a computer application (DBS-Edmonton app) improved DBS-related knowledge and patient satisfaction [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B30-brainsci-12-00238)]. It is also important to discuss with patients and caregivers that regular postoperative follow-up visits are mandatory for DBS programming, hardware evaluation or battery checks and changes in medication [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B31-brainsci-12-00238)]. In a large, multicenter cohort of movement disorder patients, 12.3% of caregivers recharged the impulse generator of the patient due to caregiver integration in the postoperative process that the caregiver should be aware of preoperatively [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B32-brainsci-12-00238)]. Apart from that, PD patients’ as well as caregivers’ fear the idea of “becoming another person”, so the concept of an individual identity and possible, mostly transient, disease- and medication-related mood changes should be discussed prior to surgery [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B26-brainsci-12-00238),[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B33-brainsci-12-00238)]. In fact, PD patients’ and caregivers’ awareness of possible mood changes after DBS is still limited [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B26-brainsci-12-00238)]. Nevertheless, a perioperative caregiver survey showed that two-thirds of caregivers feel fully prepared for DBS surgery but suggests more information on postoperative care and more communication with the family during surgery [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B34-brainsci-12-00238)]. Importantly, a better understanding of the disease in PD caregivers is associated with lower CB [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B3-brainsci-12-00238)], which supports the effort of intensified preoperative education of PD patients and caregivers. A perioperative psychoeducation program can reduce the anxiety of both PD patients and caregivers up to 2 years after surgery and can help to avoid postoperative maladjustment [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B35-brainsci-12-00238)]. In summary, PD patients’ and caregivers’ expectations of DBS effects are high and must be adjusted by preoperative information and counseling.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343)3. Postoperative Aspects of Caregiver Burden

### 3.1. Caregiver Burden Due to PD Neuropsychiatric Symptoms after STN-DBS

Since PD neuropsychiatric symptoms represent generally one of the most challenging symptoms of CB, neuropsychiatric postoperative changes are highlighted here. Dopaminergic medication and STN-DBS act on the motor, limbic and associative basal ganglia circuit [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B36-brainsci-12-00238)]. However, the corresponding segments of the subthalamic nucleus have their own dose–response curves with partly opposing pathological symptoms [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B36-brainsci-12-00238)]. Postoperative titration of stimulation and medication primarily centers around optimal motor symptom control. On the one hand, neuropsychiatric symptoms such as apathy, anxiety and depression reflect hypodopaminergic states of the limbic and associative loops as a result of withdrawal of dopaminergic drugs. On the other hand, hyperdopaminergic symptoms such as mania or impulse control disorders may occur when stimulation spreads either in other basal ganglia circuits or surrounding anatomical fiber tracts. In fact, at the time of DBS surgery, dopaminergic denervation and drug-induced sensitization have already advanced due to long-term dopaminergic, pulsatile treatment with consequently more severe neuropsychiatric symptoms [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B37-brainsci-12-00238)]. The focal effect of neurostimulation in contrast to the global systemic effect of L-dopa contributes to the imbalance of motor and neuropsychiatric symptom control [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B36-brainsci-12-00238)]. Therefore, within the first few postoperative months, PD patients are at risk of neuropsychiatric adverse effects of STN-DBS, with consequently higher, but transient, CB [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B38-brainsci-12-00238)]. In contrast, in a long-term follow-up of 3–10 years of patients with STN-DBS, neuropsychiatric symptoms such as impulse control disorders and dopaminergic addiction were significantly reduced except for apathy and depression in 25% of PD patients after surgery [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B36-brainsci-12-00238),[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B39-brainsci-12-00238)]. Apathy is directly associated with decreased patient satisfaction [[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B40-brainsci-12-00238)] and might be related to delayed, postoperative dopamine agonist withdrawal [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B41-brainsci-12-00238)] and, as a consequence, can lead to caregiver overload [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B42-brainsci-12-00238)]. Importantly, suicide behavior can occur after STN-DBS in the first 3 years, with a higher risk of patients with psychotic symptoms and depression [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B9-brainsci-12-00238)]. In conclusion, careful assessment of neuropsychiatric symptoms is recommended as they represent one of the main reasons for hospitalization of PD patients postoperatively [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B43-brainsci-12-00238)]. Notably, neuropsychiatric symptoms such as depression, compulsivity and impulsivity increase post-DBS caregiver burden.

### 3.2. Caregiver Burden Outcome after STN-DBS Implantation of PD Dependants

There are unexpected, heterogeneous results of CB outcome after implantation of STN-DBS in PD. Despite improvement in motor function and higher social functioning of PD patients postoperatively, CB was variable and did not change in all caregivers 6 months after STN-DBS [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B38-brainsci-12-00238),[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B44-brainsci-12-00238),[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B45-brainsci-12-00238),[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B46-brainsci-12-00238)]. In a qualitative study with narrative semi-structured interviews and self-made drawings of PD patients and caregivers, heterogeneous reports were obtained [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B47-brainsci-12-00238)]. Many patients and caregivers perceived the DBS “as the beginning of a new life”, “rebirth with clouds” and “renewal”, with improved “communication” and “better participation in everyday routines”. However, it was also conceived that “DBS is not perfect”, and, postoperatively, life still means “living with a sick person” [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B47-brainsci-12-00238)] ([Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#brainsci-12-00238-f002))

The divergent effects of STN-DBS on CB are already obvious in early reports of potential behavioral modifications in PD patients and its impact on familiar relations. In a cohort of 15 PD patients 6 months after DBS, 70% were reported to develop a euphoric mood due to symptom reduction but also fear of potential DBS failure and to return back to the preoperative level. This was associated with hostile behavior of the caregivers in the sense of worries to lose the newly acquired social and relative role again [[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B48-brainsci-12-00238)]. In another cohort of 29 PD patients, several difficulties of social adjustment despite marked motor improvement were observed 18–24 months after STN-DBS, resulting in disturbances of marital relationships [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B49-brainsci-12-00238)]. Although DBS therapy was shown to improve QOL of PD patients without increasing CB in a group of 275 DBS patients [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B31-brainsci-12-00238)], QOL and CB were rated worse by a considerable portion of caregivers [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B45-brainsci-12-00238)]. An unfavorable caregiver satisfaction was even described, with approximately 50% of caregivers being disappointed with DBS outcomes [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B46-brainsci-12-00238)]. This finding is astonishing since one would expect CB of relatives to decrease along with QOL and motor improvement of PD patients.

There might be several factors contributing to this incongruent development of QOL of patients and caregivers postoperatively.

1.   The preexisting neuropsychiatric and medical condition of the caregivers themselves might play a role in the development of postoperative CB. In a prospective, longitudinal study of 25 patients and caregivers with follow-ups at 3 and 12 months, predictive factors for postoperative CB in a logistic regression model were assessed for both caregivers and PD patients [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B50-brainsci-12-00238)]. Interestingly, at the 3-month follow-up, the caregivers were more indecisive about their own well-being but at the 1-year follow-up determined. There were caregivers with improved postoperative CB, often reporting “more freedom and better QOL” and that “PD patients showed less unpleasant side effects of medication”. Caregivers with worsening of postoperative CB reported “more conflicts between patients and caregivers”, “more anxiety concerning welfare of the patient” and “more sadness, stress and less freedom”. There were predicting risk factors of caregivers’ characteristics at baseline for increased postoperative CB, such as older age, greater depression, enhanced anxiety and lower quality of life of the caregivers [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B50-brainsci-12-00238)]. This finding was interpreted as decreased ability of coping strategies or capabilities in those caregivers to adapt to the new postoperative situation [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B50-brainsci-12-00238)]. Higher age of the caregiver is one important mediator of postoperative CB and caregivers’ satisfaction with the DBS operation. [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B46-brainsci-12-00238)]. One has to remember that the caregiver grows older along with the PD patient and might also suffer from illnesses. The older the caregiver, the more exhausting the caregiving. Importantly, the preoperative BDI score is the predictor of postoperative caregiver depression one year after DBS surgery [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B46-brainsci-12-00238)]. Thus is why the well-being of the caregiver should also be regularly addressed both pre- and postoperatively.

2.   The postoperative extent of neuropsychiatric symptoms within PD patients significantly influences the CB of their relatives, as described above. Interestingly, CB was not associated with the extent of motor symptom improvement [[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B44-brainsci-12-00238)] but the patient’s degree of apathy and depression [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B2-brainsci-12-00238),[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B50-brainsci-12-00238)]. In 64 PD patients and caregivers, postoperative caregiver burden, as measured by the Zarit Burden Interview (ZBI), was significantly related to PD patients’ Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) score, caregiver-rated attentional impulsiveness of PD patients, impaired PD set-shifting, prepotent PD inhibition, patients’ hypersexuality and dopaminergic medication dose [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B2-brainsci-12-00238)]. Higher postoperative CB, indexed by ZBI, was correlated with lower relationship quality [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B2-brainsci-12-00238)]. In a second step, it was then assessed whether the new onset of stimulation-induced neuropsychiatric side effects in the early perioperative period of 6 weeks was a predictive factor for increased postoperative CB. There was a significant difference between caregivers of PD patients with and without DBS-induced neuropsychiatric side effects. CB decreased after 6 weeks compared to baseline in caregivers of PD patients without DBS-induced neuropsychiatric side effects but increased in a considerable portion of caregivers of PD patients with DBS side effects [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B2-brainsci-12-00238)].

3.   Postoperative marital conflicts due to changes in the relationship affect CB. DBS surgery profoundly changes caregiver responsibilities and disease-related symptoms due to the sudden relief of disability. Following STN-DBS, social maladjustment as a result of a dramatic improvement in clinical status and identity challenges can occur as part of the “burden of normality” syndrome [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B35-brainsci-12-00238)]. Interestingly, partners of patients with device-aided therapies report more often changes in relationship satisfaction than patients and show more attachment-related avoidance [[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B51-brainsci-12-00238)]. Surprisingly, 65% of PD patients experience a conjugal crisis within 2 years of undergoing DBS [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B26-brainsci-12-00238)]. Marital conflicts occurred in 17/24 couples, with three couples being divorced postoperatively and 33% of spouses becoming depressed within the 2-year follow-up [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B49-brainsci-12-00238)]. Caregivers rate the change in their partnership 1 year post-DBS surgery as negative, with three main sources for marital disturbances: (1) neuropsychiatric changes, as described above with the new onset or ongoing neuropsychiatric symptoms in PD patients; (2) communication problems, e.g., caregivers feel uncertain of how to speak of residual PD symptomatology while the spouse feels healthy postoperatively; (3) caregivers’ overload of responsibilities for the partner and uncertainty about how the load of caregiving develops in the future [[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B52-brainsci-12-00238)]. About 54.5% of caregivers of PD patients with and without DBS suffer from caregiver overload [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B42-brainsci-12-00238)]. During the time that partners spend together because of caring responsibilities, they feel emotionally more distanced [[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B53-brainsci-12-00238)]. These factors might contribute to an increase in marital conflicts [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B46-brainsci-12-00238)]. Marital conflicts are further due to additional changes of social roles within the partnership postoperatively. On the one hand, there is a loss of the caregivers’ attention to the disease condition and the re-emerged responsibility in everyday duties for the PD patients, that PD patients might complain about [[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B48-brainsci-12-00238)]. Additionally, it was hypothesized that marital conflicts are due to role conflicts according to adaption to the new situation. On the other hand, PD patients rejected their spouse because they regained autonomy by DBS-induced motor improvement, but the spouse could not give up the caregiver role, overprotecting the patient and trying to maintain the patients’ dependency. Besides, patients were also rejected by their spouses, who expected them to resume a normal life with all their duties and social matters after the operation, whereas the patients still felt not able to do this [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B49-brainsci-12-00238)]. However, some PD patients with good clinical outcomes also experience a restoration of the “old premorbid self” confirmed by their caregivers. Consequently, in those specific couples with satisfying DBS outcome, CB is lowered, and the relationship flourishes with greater socialization [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B26-brainsci-12-00238)]

4.   DBS is a symptomatic, but not disease-modifying therapy; thus, in the long-term, disease progression with re-emergence of motor symptoms, onset of cognitive impairment and loss of autonomy of PD patients might result in the reoccurrence of increased CB [[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B54-brainsci-12-00238)]. This might contribute to the observation that CB increases in caregivers of some PD patients within the first 2 years after STN-DBS [[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B55-brainsci-12-00238)]. However, in another 2-year follow-up of younger (<65 years) and elderly (>65 years) STN-DBS patients, CB decreased in relatives of both patient groups, even in caregivers of elderly PD patients [[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B56-brainsci-12-00238)]. Observations of long-term results of chronically stimulated patients are of particular interest in the growing numbers of operated and aging PD patients. In terms of PD symptomatology, there is increasing knowledge of long-term effects [[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B57-brainsci-12-00238)]. There is evidence that subthalamic nucleus DBS improves motor function for up to 10 years, although the magnitude of improvement, particularly of levodopa-resistant symptoms, tends to decline over time. Dyskinesia, motor fluctuations and activities of daily living in off-periods remain improved at 5 years, but quality-of-life scores usually decrease [[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B57-brainsci-12-00238)]. Nonetheless, in an observational period of about 14 years after STN-DBS surgery, the risk for recurrent falls and psychotic symptoms is lower in PD patients with STN-DBS compared to patients without DBS surgery [[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B58-brainsci-12-00238)]. Overall, patients’ satisfaction with DBS remains high at long-term follow-up of more than 6 years [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B7-brainsci-12-00238),[59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B59-brainsci-12-00238)]. In a small cohort of late-stage PD patients (Hoehn and Yahr stage ≥4) with marked motor and cognitive impairment treated with STN-DBS for >14 years, patients still benefit partly from stimulation [[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B60-brainsci-12-00238)]. Interestingly, in this specific patient cohort, caregivers had mild to moderate stable caregiver burden. When the medical decision was made to discontinue DBS stimulation due to the clinical impression of poor stimulation response in this advanced disease stage, PD patients’ global motor state and dysphagia declined with delayed onset, while caregivers’ QOL and CB worsened after DBS discontinuation slightly, but without statistical significance [[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B60-brainsci-12-00238)]. The observation of mild-moderate CB in this small cohort of very advanced PD patients with a long disease duration of up to 43 years is astonishing and could be due to acceptance of the CB and habituation to the caregiving situation. Still, long-term observations of CB are scarce and need to be obtained in larger cohorts of long-term caregivers ([Figure 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#brainsci-12-00238-f003)).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343)4. Caregiver Burden in PD Patients with Globus Pallidus Internus Stimulation

The globus pallidus internus (Gpi) is an alternative DBS target for PD patients besides STN implantation as the Gpi is supposed to have a lower risk of dysarthria, neuropsychiatric complications and impaired cognition [[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B61-brainsci-12-00238)]. The discussion of the favorable target in PD is still controversial [[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B61-brainsci-12-00238)]. There is also scarce information on caregiver burden in Gpi patients [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B31-brainsci-12-00238),[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B62-brainsci-12-00238)]. In a cohort with 275 DBS patients, including PD patients implanted both in STN and Gpi, caregiver burden measured by the Multidimensional Caregiver Strain Index (MCSI) was associated with PD age at surgery and interval since surgery [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B31-brainsci-12-00238)]. Overall, QOL increased in this specific DBS cohort, whereas CB did not [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B31-brainsci-12-00238)]. In a parallel two-arm clinical trial with 44 DBS patients, of which 81% were implanted in the Gpi, postoperative home health management with standard of care (SOC) postoperative management was compared [[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B62-brainsci-12-00238)]. In this cohort, caregiver burden measured by MCSI was reduced in both groups 6 months after surgery [[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B62-brainsci-12-00238)]. Interestingly, the MCSI was more reduced in the SOC than in the home health group, although the result did not reach significance [[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B62-brainsci-12-00238)]. In a large multicenter study on 1835 PD patients with a ≥10-year disease duration, 411 patients with DBS were included without further distinction of DBS targets. QOL worsened parallel to increased CB, which can mostly be explained by more severe symptom severity in advanced PD stages [[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B63-brainsci-12-00238)]. In summary, it appears that CB of partners of PD patients with STN and Gpi is mostly reduced shortly after DBS implantation but can increase over time with disease progression and reduced QOL. Further research in larger cohorts is needed on CB in caregivers of PD patients with Gpi stimulation.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343)5. What Is Next? Future Caregiving Challenges

DBS research is further advancing and new promising technologies are in the pipeline. Closed-loop systems with beta oscillations as internal biomarkers for independent, self-regulated adaption of stimulation are one example of current technological developments, which might improve PD patient outcome, reduce neuropsychiatric side effects and thus could decrease CB [[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B64-brainsci-12-00238),[65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B65-brainsci-12-00238)]. Still, these new systems might lead to increased DBS programming burden which might increase caregivers’ burden due to management of medical appointments and transportation. Another promising field is telemedicine with remote access for DBS programming. An obstacle in the treatment of PD patients is the fact that the optimization of DBS parameters is often performed only by movement disorders specialists at specific, far-away university hospitals, resulting in difficult transport and care coordination [[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B66-brainsci-12-00238)]. Telemedicine has already proven to reduce CB due to more flexible patient treatment and reduction of transportation issues to outpatient clinics [[67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B67-brainsci-12-00238)]. Telemedicine comprises teleconsultation, telemonitoring and teletreatment [[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B68-brainsci-12-00238)]. Telehealth with teleprogramming of DBS has become particularly important during the COVID-19 pandemic with overall satisfactory patient experience [[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B69-brainsci-12-00238),[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B70-brainsci-12-00238)]. Providing caregiver support via an online telecare system with constant monitoring of PD symptoms might improve QOL of DBS patients in the future [[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B71-brainsci-12-00238)]. Still, heterogeneous results of virtual house calls or telemedicine were observed in a general group of PD patients [[72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B72-brainsci-12-00238)], thus the benefit of telemedicine and DBS teleprogramming for PD patients and caregivers needs to be proven in larger, multicentric studies. Another rising field represents trained PD nurses as part of an integrated care concept to reduce CB [[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B73-brainsci-12-00238)]. To face the rising demand for intensified caregiving, new models of care are implemented to empower patients and caregivers and personalize care management [[74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B74-brainsci-12-00238)]. These efforts are reasonable to prevent institutionalization since a higher caregiver burden has been associated with higher risk of rehospitalization [[75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B75-brainsci-12-00238)]. Interestingly, home health postoperative management of DBS patients revealed a decrease in clinic visits but without change in CB [[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B62-brainsci-12-00238)], indicating the need to optimize an integrated, multimodal concept in the postoperative management of DBS patients.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343)6. Conclusions

Informal caregivers play an important role in the daily care of PD patients before and after DBS surgery. Caregiver burden does not improve in all caregivers after STN-DBS and GPI-DBS in contrast to dramatic improvement of motor and non-motor symptoms and quality of life in PD patients. Relevant factors for postoperative CB are caregiver coping capabilities, postoperative onset of neuropsychiatric symptoms of PD patients, marital conflicts and the awareness of the symptomatic nature of DBS therapy. But, There is still a lack of information on long-term caregiver burden and predictors after STN-DBS.

Potential tools to reduce postoperative CB represent “preparedness of the caregivers”, which could be protective against postoperative caregivers distress [[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B76-brainsci-12-00238)]. Caregivers should be informed about the specific postoperative aspect of STN-DBS and the potential effect on their own QoL. They should be more intensively integrated into the pre- and postoperative processes. Another option to reduce CB of STN-DBS patients could be cognitive behavioral therapy for caregivers [[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B77-brainsci-12-00238)], which could substantially modify CB prior to and after STN-DBS surgery. Additionally, self-management programs to retain social participation can help the caregiver to maintain well-being during the course of the disease [[78](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B78-brainsci-12-00238),[79](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8870343#B79-brainsci-12-00238)].

To sum it up, there are heterogeneous results on CB changes after STN-DBS, but there are therapeutic approaches to reduce CB in the future. Increased awareness of the special perioperative demands of PD patients with STN-DBS and caregivers is fundamental for an optimized future approach.

args.summary:
This scientific review article published in Brain Sciences (2022) by Gülke and Pötter-Nerger from the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf examines caregiver burden in partners of Parkinson's disease (PD) patients who undergo deep brain stimulation (DBS). The review covers both pre- and postoperative factors influencing caregiver burden.

**Key Preoperative Findings:**
- Caregiver burden is defined as the adverse effect of caregiving on emotional, social, financial, physical, and spiritual functioning.
- In advanced PD, motor symptoms (bradykinesia, tremor, gait dysfunction) and non-motor symptoms (depression, psychosis, cognitive decline) contribute to caregiver burden, with non-motor symptoms having a greater impact than motor impairments.
- Risk factors for caregiver burden include female sex, cohabitation, amount of caregiving time, and lack of choice.
- DBS is considered a "game changer" but raises high expectations; unrealistic expectations contribute to postoperative dissatisfaction.
- Preoperative education and counseling are crucial, as a better understanding of the disease is associated with lower caregiver burden.

**Key Postoperative Findings:**
- Despite significant motor improvement and quality of life gains for PD patients after DBS, caregiver burden does not improve in all caregivers and can even worsen.
- Neuropsychiatric symptoms (depression, apathy, impulsivity, mania) post-DBS significantly increase caregiver burden.
- Caregiver burden is not associated with motor symptom improvement but with patient depression, apathy, and neuropsychiatric side effects.
- Approximately 65% of PD patients experience a conjugal crisis within 2 years of DBS; marital conflicts stem from neuropsychiatric changes, communication problems, and role conflicts.
- Predictors of worsening caregiver burden include older caregiver age, greater caregiver depression, enhanced anxiety, and lower caregiver quality of life at baseline.
- Long-term, DBS is symptomatic but not disease-modifying, so disease progression may lead to re-emergence of caregiver burden.

**Future Directions:**
Closed-loop DBS systems, telemedicine for remote programming, and integrated care models (including trained PD nurses) are promising approaches to reduce caregiver burden.

**Conclusions:** Caregiver burden does not uniformly improve after DBS despite dramatic patient symptom relief. Key factors affecting postoperative burden include caregiver coping capabilities, postoperative neuropsychiatric symptoms, marital conflicts, and the symptomatic nature of DBS therapy. Better caregiver preparedness, psychoeducation, and cognitive behavioral therapy may help reduce burden.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263)Abstract

### Objective:

This study aimed to identify caregiver burden (CB) and contributing factors to CB for Parkinson’s disease (PD) patients under Subthalamic Nucleus Deep Brain Stimulation (STN-DBS) treatment, and investigation the factors, affecting the caregivers’ quality of life (QoL).

### Methods:

Twenty-four PD patients under STN-DBS treatment and their caregivers participated in this study. Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) was applied for the clinical assessment of the patients. Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI), Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), and Minnesota Impulse Control Disorders Interview (MIDI) were used to screen for neuropsychiatric symptoms of the patients. CB was evaluated with the Caregivers Burden Inventory (CBI) and the Burden Scale for Family Caregivers (BSFC-s). The health-related QoL of caregivers was assessed with the Short Form Survey-36 (SF-36).

### Results:

Mean total CBI and BSFC-s scores of caregivers were 32.53 ± 19.71 and 11.66 ± 8.86, respectively. Nineteen caregivers defined moderate or severe caregiver burden according to BSFC-s. Both CBI and BSFC-s scores were significantly associated with UPDRS-part-1 scores, but not with the age and gender of both the patients and their caregivers, disease duration, PDQ39, BDI, HADS, LARS scores, and scores of patients for other UPDRS parts. The presence of impulse control behaviors (ICBs) significantly increased the total CBI score and total BSFC-s (_P_< 0.01). The caregivers’ total and all domain scores of SF-36 were significantly affected by higher CBI and BSFC-s scores.

### Conclusions:

The CB of the patients under STN-DBS treatment was severe. Non-motor symptoms, particularly impulsivity, significantly increased CB and worsened the caregivers’ mental and physical health.

**Keywords:**Caregiver burden, deep brain stimulation, Parkinson’s disease, quality of life

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263)I NTRODUCTION

Parkinson’s disease (PD) is characterized by both motor symptoms and non-motor symptoms (NMS), comprising cognitive, psychiatric, and behavioral disorders. The interaction of motor symptoms and non-motor symptoms has a negative impact on both patients and their caregivers.[[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R1)] Caregiver burden (CB) is defined as the multifaceted level of stress, perceived by the caregiver from caring for a family member and/or loved one.[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R2)] CB is closely associated with disease duration, disability, falls, and particularly psychiatric symptoms such as mental impairment, depression, confusion, and hallucinations in patients with PD.[[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R3)] Also, CB is strongly associated with highly prevalent psychiatric symptoms, such as depression and anxiety among caregivers.[[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R4)] The caregiver’s poor understanding of the disease is also correlated with increased CB.[[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R5)]

Subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation (STN-DBS) is an advanced and effective treatment, in particular in PD patients who have had motor fluctuations and/or dyskinesia despite the best pharmaceutical therapies.[[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R6)] However, it has been reported that despite improvements in patients’ motor function and QoL, DBS did not change or improve CB.[[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R7)[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R8)[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R9)[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R10)] Moreover, a previous study has shown that despite improvements in patient-rated outcomes, as many as 50% of caregivers rated their well-being as negative following STN-DBS.[[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R11)] Several studies have reported that CB was correlated with non-motor symptoms rather than motor symptoms for patients with PD under STN-DBS treatment.[[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R9)[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R10)[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R12)] It has been reported that CB increased following DBS surgery due to neuropsychiatric symptoms, such as impulsivity, behavioral changes, apathy, and depression.[[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R4)[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R11)[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R13)] In the study, we aimed to identify CB and contributing factors to CB for PD patients under STN-DBS treatment and also to evaluate the factors, affecting the caregivers’ QoL.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263)M ETHODS

This cross-sectional study was approved by the University of Akdeniz Ethics Committee (2012-KAEK-20). All patients and their caregivers signed informed consent for data collection. Twenty-four patients with PD, who had undergone DBS surgery and their caregivers participated in this study during routine follow-up visits. The patients without an identified caregiver were not enrolled in the study. History of any severe comorbid disease and presence of severe dementia, as defined by a Mini-Mental State Examination Score (MMSE) of <25, were considered as exclusion criteria due to their possible effects on caregivers’ burden.

The data, including the patients’ social demographic and clinical features, were collected. For clinical assessment of the patients, a modified Hoehn and Yahr Scale, and Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) were applied. The UPDRS has 4 parts; Part I concerns ‘‘non-motor experiences of daily living,’’ Part II concerns ‘‘motor experiences of daily living,’’ Part III is defined as the ‘‘motor examination,’’ and Part IV concerns ‘‘motor complications.” UPDRS part III was tested in both medication ON (Med-ON) and medication OFF (Med-OFF) conditions, when stimulation was on. The med-ON condition was accepted as at least an hour after taking their usual dopaminergic drugs, Med-OFF condition was accepted as at least 12 hours without taking their anti-Parkinson’s medications. The patients’ medications for PD were evaluated using levodopa-equivalent daily dose (LEDD). The patients’ UPDRS scores before surgery were taken from the patient’s medical electronic database.

The QoL of the patients was evaluated with a Parkinson’s disease quality of life questionnaire (PDQ-39). The PDQ-39 consists of 39 items and measures “quality of life” in eight domains, namely mobility, stigma, life activities, communication, emotional well-being, social support, cognition, and pain. The score for each question ranges from 0 to 4. The total score of PDQ39 is calculated by the following equation: the sum of each question score divided by 4, divided by the total number of questions, and multiplied by 100. The total score ranges from 0 to 100 on a linear scale, where higher scores define more serious health problems.[[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R14)]

The patients’ depressive symptoms were evaluated Beck Depression Inventory-I (BDI), a self-report psychometric test, consisting of 21 questions. A higher total BDI score shows more severe depressive symptoms. The patients were also evaluated with Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), which is a self-assessment scale for determination of the level of depression and anxiety in a hospital outpatient clinical setting.[[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R15)] Minnesota Impulse Control Disorders Interview (MIDI) was used to screen for the diagnosis of impulse control behaviors (ICBs) of the patients.[[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R16)] The apathy of the patients was measured using Lille Apathy Rating Scale (LARS) based on a semi-structured interview, comprising 33 items, divided into 9 domains, namely, daily productivity, interests, taking initiative, novelty-seeking, voluntary actions, emotional responses, concern, social life, and self-awareness. The total score of LARS ranges between [−36 to +36], with severe apathy between [−9 and +36], moderate apathy between [−16 and −10], slight between [−21 and −17], and no apathy between [−36 and −22].[[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R17)]

Caregivers were asked to provide sociodemographic information, including age, gender, level of education, work status, and health status. Caregiver burden was evaluated with the Caregivers Burden Inventory (CBI). The CBI is a 24-item questionnaire that measures caregiver burden in five dimensions: time-dependence, developmental, physical, social, and emotional burden. There are five items in each dimension with the exception of the physical burden, which has four items. The score for each item ranges between 0 (not descriptive at all) and 4 (very descriptive). The total scores of the first, second, fourth, and fifth factors can score between 0 and 20. The score for physical burden factors can be calculated by multiplying the sum of items in this dimension by 1.25. Total CBI score ranges between 0 and 100 and higher scores represent greater caregiver burden.[[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R18)] The short version of the Burden Scale for Family Caregivers (BSFC-s) was used to evaluate the caregiver’s total subjective burden. The BSFC-s consists of 10 items with scores between 0 and 3 and total score ranging between 0 and 30. Higher scores show greater caregiver burden.[[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R19)] The BSFC-s scale was classified as (0–4) points “none to mild”, (5–14) points “moderate”, and (15–30) points “severe to very severe”.[[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R20)] The caregivers were also asked to answer “how did caregiver burden change after DBS surgery?” question as positive, negative, or unchanged.

The health-related QoL of caregivers was assessed with the Short Form Survey-36 (SF-36). The SF-36 consists of 36 items, which cover following eight domains of health: vitality, physical functioning, bodily pain, general health perceptions, physical role functioning, emotional role functioning, social role functioning, and mental health. Each scale is directly converted to a scale from 0 to 100, assuming each question has an equal weight. Higher scores indicate a better health state.[[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R21)]

Study data were analyzed using the “Statistical Package for Social Science for Windows (SPSS 23.0)” program. Ordinal variables were evaluated as arithmetic mean, standard deviation, and minimum and maximum values. Spearman correlation analysis was used to determine the relationship between the assessed parameters. Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used to compare two related samples, and the Mann–Whitney _U_ test was used to compare differences between two independent groups. The _P_ value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Seven of 24 patients had ICBs before and after DBS surgery; four patients had both excessive buying and hypersexuality, two patients had excessive buying, and one patient had hobbyism. The ICB symptoms worsened in four of seven patients, which caused critical socio-economic consequences following DBS surgery. A new-onset ICBs was not observed in 17 patients without ICBs before the surgery following DBS surgery.

The mean age of caregivers was 46.7 ± 13.4 (15–68) years. The caregivers provided care for a mean of 10.6 ± 5.6 years. The mean total CBI score and BSFC-s of caregivers were 32.53 ± 19.71 and 11.66 ± 8.86 respectively. Nineteen caregivers (79%) defined moderate or severe caregiver burden according to BSFC-s.

Ten (41%) caregivers described a negative influence of DBS treatment on caregiver burden. Two caregivers reported that the caregiver burden did not change after DBS surgery. Twelve (50%) caregivers defined that DBS treatment affected caregiver burden positively. The clinical characteristics of the patients whose caregivers defined that DBS treatment positively affected caregiver burden were compared to those whose caregivers described a negative influence of DBS treatment on caregiver burden. There was no significant difference between the two groups for age, gender, UPDRS, BDI, and LARS scores of the patients (_P_> 0.05). Half of the patients whose caregivers described a negative influence of DBS treatment on caregiver burden had ICBs [[Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#aian_210_23-t002)]. The caregivers defined that the worsening of psychiatric symptoms, such as impulsivity and mood changes following DBS surgery caused to increase in CB and marital conflicts. The caregivers who described that DBS treatment positively affected CB stated that the improvement in motor symptoms following DBS surgery decreased the dependency level of the patients.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263)D ISCUSSION

In patients with PD, with a reduction in LEDD fluctuations following surgery, combined effects of STN-DBS treatment and dopaminergic drugs provide an improvement in motor symptoms of PD that is greater than either treatment alone.[[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R22)] A 24-month follow-up study has demonstrated that STN-DBS treatment reduced non-motor symptoms, improving QoL and activities of daily life.[[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R23)] In contrast, STN-DBS treatment may worsen some non-motor symptoms, in particular neuropsychiatric symptoms, such as depression, suicidal behavior, impulsivity, mania, apathy, and cognitive dysfunction.[[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R24)] These non-motor symptoms contribute to increased CB in general PD patients. In the literature, there is still inadequate data about long-term caregiver burden and predictors following STN-DBS.[[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R25)] This study evaluated the CB and contributing factors to CB in PD patients under STN-DBS treatment.

In the study, 50% of caregivers reported negative effects on caregiver burden after DBS surgery and 80% of the caregivers described the caregiver burden as moderate to severe. In the literature, previous studies have reported that 50%–58% of caregivers were not satisfied with the outcomes of DBS surgery in terms of caregiver burden, despite improvements in Parkinsonian motor symptoms and QoL after DBS surgery.[[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R11)[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R26)] A study with a large cohort has demonstrated that there was no difference in terms of CB between patients under STN-DBS treatment and the PD patients without STN-DBS treatment.[[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R7)] This study has also shown that STN-DBS treatment could improve QoL of the patients without affecting CB. Also, other studies have reported that STN-DBS treatment did not change caregiver burden.[[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R8)[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R9)[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R10)] A previous study has found that the effects of DBS treatment at the individual level were negative more frequently than positive in terms of caregivers’ mood, QoL, and burden scores.[[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R12)] Another study has also reported that the CB worsened in the second year after STN DBS surgery, for reasons such as frequent visits to the hospital for post-surgery follow-up, despite improvements in motor symptoms.[[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R27)] On the other hand, another study has concluded that disease progression might result in the worsening of CB, since STN-DBS treatment is not disease-modifying therapy.[[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R28)] Although most studies have reported no improvement in CB after DBS surgery, a study has demonstrated that CB improved in both younger and elderly PD patients in a 2-year follow-up term after DBS surgery.[[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R29)] Another study has also found that caregivers’ QoL improved by 68% 2 years after DBS surgery.[[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R30)]

STN-DBS surgery may deteriorate social maladjustment and marital conflicts, which can affect CB. In a study with a cohort of 29 PD patients, marital conflicts occurred in 70% of couples resulting in divorce for three couples and 33% of spouses becoming depressed within the 2 years after DBS surgery.[[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R26)] Marital conflicts may be related to post-operative changes in social roles within the partnership. For example, the caregivers’ attention to the patients’ condition may be lost or diminished and PD patients may complain about restored responsibility in everyday duties.[[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R31)] On the other hand, after DBS surgery, after gaining autonomy through motor improvement, the patients may reject their spouse and the spouse may not adapt to the new situation and may not give up the caregiver role, and may try to maintain the patients’ dependency. DBS surgery may change caregiver responsibilities due to a sudden decrease in disease-related symptoms and disability. A previous study has reported that social maladjustment occurred as part of the “burden of normality” syndrome following DBS surgery.[[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R32)] This syndrome is characterized by psychological, behavioral, and social function disturbances seen in patients with chronic illnesses, who had a dramatic improvement in clinical status after treatment, including intra-couple relationship dynamics.

In this study, the most important finding was the strong association of total CB with non-motor symptoms. In particular, the presence of impulsivity in the patients significantly increased the total caregiver burden. Motor symptoms and fluctuations, higher Hoehn-Yahr stage and lower QoL of the PD patients caused an increase only in CBI Time dependency, but not total CB. Mosley, _et al._,[[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R9)] have also evaluated 64 PD patients and their caregivers and demonstrated that post-operative psychiatric symptoms, such as depressive symptoms, impulsivity and mood changes, were associated with increased CB. They have also concluded that STN-DBS treatment did not significantly change CB or caregiver-rated psychiatric symptoms. Another previous study with a small cohort has found that CB was not improved six months after bilateral STN DBS surgery, despite a significant improvement in motor function. They have also shown that only pre-operative behavioral problems, specifically disinhibition, was associated with pre-operative increased CB.[[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R10)] Another study has found that the patient’s degree of apathy and depression were linked to caregivers’ QoL.[[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R11)] No correlation between depression, apathy score of the patients and total CB score has been observed in this study. However, higher depression and apathy scores, and low MMSE scores had a significant negative influence on the CBI Time Dependency subscore. Consequently, we concluded that non-motor symptoms, in particular psychiatric symptoms, such as impulsivity, mood, and personality changes, had a greater effect on CB compared to motor symptoms, which is consistent with the literature.[[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R4)[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R9)[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R13)]

The factors, related to caregivers such as older age, pre-existing neuropsychiatric and medical conditions, may play a role in the development of post-operative deterioration in CB. Our study found that the age and gender of caregivers did not cause a change in CB. In a prospective study conducted on 25 patients and caregivers, baseline characteristics of caregivers, such as older age, more severe depression, increased anxiety, and lower QoL, were associated with worse post-operative CB.[[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R11)] A systematic review has concluded that the older age of the caregiver is a critical predictor for post-operative CB and caregivers’ satisfaction with the DBS surgery. They have also demonstrated that the pre-operative BDI score of caregivers is the predictor for caregiver depression one year after DBS surgery.[[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R33)]

In the study, higher CB had a negative effect on caregivers’ mental and physical health status. The presence of impulsivity in the patients worsened the caregivers’ mental and health status. The mental health state of the caregivers was associated with the patients’ non-motor symptoms, but not with other factors of both the patients and their caregivers. For this reason, the patients must be monitored by the clinician for non-motor symptoms, especially neuropsychiatric symptoms, and supported by a neurologist and psychiatrist. The treatment of impulsivity in patients may improve both the patients’ and their caregivers’ QoL. The caregivers must be informed about the stimulation-related neuropsychiatric symptoms during the pre-operative and post-operative phases.

This study has weaknesses. Because of the small sample size, the results should be interpreted cautiously when generalizing them to Caregivers for Patients with Parkinson’s Disease Treated with Subthalamic Nucleus Deep Brain Stimulation populations.

Nevertheless, the present study showed that the CB for the patients under STN-DBS treatment was severe, which had a negative effect on their caregivers’ quality of life. Also, this study, in line with the literature, demonstrated that non-motor symptoms especially neuropsychiatric symptoms are the main factors for increased CB and poor QoL of the caregivers. Awareness of PD patients and their caregivers about possible mood changes after DBS, is still limited.[[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10645263#R34)] Also, unrealistic and unmet expectations contribute to post-operative caregiver dissatisfaction and increased CB. Thus, pre-operative education of PD patients and caregivers and discussion of realistic expectations may help in adaptation to new conditions, awareness of stimulation-related neuropsychiatric symptoms, and elimination of postoperative disappointments. Also, good social support and cognitive behavioral therapy for both patients and their caregivers during the post-operative phase, may reduce CB and have a positive effect on QoL.

args.summary:
This study, published in the Annals of Indian Academy of Neurology (2023), investigates caregiver burden (CB) and quality of life (QoL) among caregivers of Parkinson's disease (PD) patients treated with Subthalamic Nucleus Deep Brain Stimulation (STN-DBS). The cross-sectional study involved 24 PD patients (15 female, 9 male; mean age 57.7 years) and their caregivers (15 female, 9 male; mean age 46.7 years). Most caregivers were spouses (66.7%) or adult children (29.1%).

Key findings:
- Mean caregiver burden scores: CBI = 32.53 ± 19.71, BSFC-s = 11.66 ± 8.86. Nineteen caregivers (79%) reported moderate to severe burden.
- 50% of caregivers reported DBS treatment positively affected burden; 41% described negative effects; two reported no change.
- Non-motor symptoms, particularly impulsivity (impulse control behaviors/ICBs), significantly increased caregiver burden (P < 0.01). Seven patients had ICBs before/after surgery.
- Both CBI and BSFC-s scores were significantly correlated with UPDRS-part-1 (non-motor symptoms) scores, but NOT with age, gender, disease duration, or motor symptom severity.
- Motor improvement from DBS did not correlate with reduced caregiver burden.
- Higher caregiver burden significantly decreased all domains of caregivers' QoL (SF-36 scores), especially mental health.
- Presence of impulsivity in patients significantly worsened caregivers' mental and physical health.

The study concludes that non-motor symptoms, especially neuropsychiatric symptoms like impulsivity, are the main factors for increased CB and poor QoL in caregivers of PD patients treated with STN-DBS. The authors recommend pre-operative education, realistic expectation setting, good social support, and cognitive behavioral therapy for both patients and caregivers.

## Highlights

*   •Studies on the impact of DBS on caregivers of Parkinson's patients were reviewed. 
*   •Caregiver burden and functioning is relatively unchanged after DBS. 
*   •Marital satisfaction and caregiver satisfaction with DBS may deteriorate post-DBS. 
*   •Several patient- and caregiver factors may help predict caregiver outcomes post-DBS. 
*   •Early recognition of potential problem situations may improve post-DBS care. 

## Abstract

### Background

Caregivers of patients with Parkinson's Disease (PD) often provide important support in the pre- and postoperative phase of Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS). DBS-associated changes of patient-functioning may affect caregiver wellbeing and impact the support system. Factors influencing caregiver-wellbeing under these circumstances are incompletely known.

### Objective

to systematically review studies of sufficient methodological quality on the impact of DBS on caregivers of PD patients.

### Methods

using PRISMA guidelines, major databases were searched up to May 2020. Five subcategories were identified: Caregiver burden, Caregiver cognitive and psychiatric functioning, Caregiver Quality of Life (QoL), Marital Satisfaction/Conflicts, and Caregiver Satisfaction. Quality was assessed using an in-house checklist.

### Results

293 studies were identified; 12 were ultimately included. Caregiver burden, psychiatric and cognitive functioning and QoL remained relatively unchanged. Results on marital satisfaction/conflicts were contrasting: an increase in marital conflicts despite improved relationship quality scores DBS. Caregiver satisfaction with surgery was low with 50–58% of caregivers being disappointed with DBS outcomes. Concerning caregiver related factors: a higher preoperative caregiver QoL, younger age, lower scores on psychiatric rating scales, and more favourable preoperative relationship quality scores, were associated with better caregiver wellbeing. A favourable patient-profile includes younger age and age-at-onset, shorter disease duration, lower medication requirements, and lower scores on psychiatric rating scales.

### Conclusion

Although most patient- and caregiver-related subdomains remained unchanged after DBS, dissatisfaction among caregivers and marital problems may constitute a large risk for a well-functioning patient-caregiver dyad. Early recognition of potential problem situations may improve post-DBS care for both patients and caregivers.

*   ### [Patient-Related Factors Influencing Caregiver Burden in Parkinson's Disease Patients: Comparison of Effects Before and After Deep Brain Stimulation](https://doi.org/10.3233/JPD-213093)

2022, Journal of Parkinson's Disease  Show abstract Caregivers of Parkinson’s disease (PD) patients provide important support during the pre- and postoperative phase of deep brain stimulation (DBS). High levels of caregiver burden have been reported after DBS. However, a comparison between preoperative and postoperative burden and associated factors has been insufficiently studied. To investigate the influence of DBS on caregiver burden, and to identify the differential impact of patient-related factors on caregiver burden before and after DBS. Consecutive patients referred for DBS eligibility screening or during one-year follow-up assessments were included. Caregiver burden was measured with the short Zarit Burden Interview (ZBI-12). Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW) was used to compare caregiver burden between preoperative and postoperative assessments. We included 47 patients (24 screening, 23 follow-up) (median age 65 years, 29.4% female sex). DBS did not impact caregiver burden (screening: median ZBI-12 9.5 (IQR 3.25, 16.75); follow-up median ZBI-12 6 (IQR 4, 14); IPW-coefficient 0.57 (95% CI –2.75, 3.89)). Worse caregiver burden during DBS screening was associated with worse patient-related scores on depressive symptoms, anxiety, QoL, and impulsiveness. Worse scores on depressive symptoms, anxiety, apathy, postural-instability-gait-disorder, and QoL were associated with worse caregiver burden at one-year follow-up. DBS appears not associated with changes in caregiver burden. Various symptoms are valued differently between screening and follow-up assessments in terms of caregiver burden. This is a peer-reviewed systematic review article published in Parkinsonism & Related Disorders (Volume 81, December 2020, Pages 20-27) titled "Effect of deep brain stimulation on caregivers of patients with Parkinson's disease: A systematic review" by van Hienen et al.

**Objective:** To systematically review studies on the impact of Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) on caregivers of Parkinson's Disease (PD) patients.

**Methods:** Using PRISMA guidelines, major databases were searched up to May 2020. Of 293 studies identified, 12 were ultimately included. Five subcategories were examined: Caregiver burden, Caregiver cognitive and psychiatric functioning, Caregiver Quality of Life (QoL), Marital Satisfaction/Conflicts, and Caregiver Satisfaction.

**Key Findings:**
- Caregiver burden, psychiatric and cognitive functioning, and QoL remained relatively unchanged after DBS.
- Marital satisfaction/conflicts showed contrasting results: increased marital conflicts despite improved relationship quality scores post-DBS.
- Caregiver satisfaction with surgery was low—50–58% of caregivers were disappointed with DBS outcomes.
- **Favorable caregiver factors** for better post-DBS wellbeing: higher preoperative caregiver QoL, younger age, lower scores on psychiatric rating scales, and more favorable preoperative relationship quality.
- **Favorable patient profile:** younger age and age-at-onset, shorter disease duration, lower medication requirements, and lower scores on psychiatric rating scales.

**Conclusion:** Although most patient- and caregiver-related subdomains remained unchanged after DBS, dissatisfaction among caregivers and marital problems may pose a significant risk to a well-functioning patient-caregiver dyad. Early recognition of potential problem situations may improve post-DBS care for both patients and caregivers.

The article has been cited by 20 subsequent publications (as of the page capture date).

The Depression and Bipolar Support Alliance (DBSA) is the leading national organization focused on depression and bipolar disorder, providing peer-led support, trusted resources, and wellness tools for individuals living with mood disorders, as well as their family members, friends, parents, and caregivers.

**Key offerings include:**
- **Support Groups:** Both in-person and online support groups providing a safe, welcoming space for sharing experiences and coping skills.
- **Education:** Resources on depression, bipolar disorder, anxiety, trauma, identity and culture, and more.
- **Wellness Tools:** Free tools including the DBSA Wellness Wheel (for reflecting on key areas of wellness), the DBSA Wellness Tracker (for tracking moods and daily habits), and the DBSA Mood Crew (designed for kids and families).
- **Peer Specialist Training:** Training that turns lived experience into meaningful support for others.
- **Advocacy:** Efforts focused on mental health parity, access to medication, peer specialist workforce development, and mental health research participation.
- **Peer Stories:** Personal narratives from individuals like Caroline M., Aidan M., and Brionna H. sharing their experiences with mood disorders.

**Recent updates include:** 2025 Impact Report titled "The Power of Peer Support," DBSA joining a coalition supporting bipartisan peer support expansion, and information about 2026 tax law changes affecting charitable giving.

The organization also provides crisis resources, resources for clinicians, and a variety of educational materials including podcasts, videos, webinars, and brochures.

# Caregiver Burnout

Caregiver burnout is a state of physical, emotional and mental exhaustion that happens while you’re taking care of someone else. Stressed caregivers may experience fatigue, anxiety and depression. You can reduce your risk of burnout by participating in respite care, joining a support group or talking with a mental health professional.

### Who is a caregiver?

The main responsibility of a caregiver is to make sure the person within their care is safe and healthy.

### What is caregiver burnout?

Caregiver burnout is a state of physical, emotional and mental exhaustion that can happen when you dedicate time and energy to manage the health and safety of someone else. Caregivers who experience burnout may feel tired, stressed, withdrawn, anxious and depressed. Caregiver burnout can impact a person in various ways, including physically, psychologically, financially and socially.

Burnout feels like a candle that ran out of a wick — it doesn’t have what it needs to continue to provide light. It can occur when you don't get the help you need personally, as you devote all of your time and energy to helping someone else. It can also happen when you try to do more than you’re able to, emotionally, physically or financially.

Your health and well-being matter just as much as the person you’re caring for. It’s important to know the signs and symptoms of caregiver burnout so you can get the help you need when you need it most.

#### How common is caregiver burnout?

Caregiver burnout is very common. Studies show that more than 60% of caregivers experience symptoms of burnout.

## Symptoms and Causes

### What are the signs and symptoms of caregiver burnout?

The signs and symptoms of caregiver burnout are similar to those of [stress](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/11874-stress) and [depression](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/9290-depression). They include:

If at any time you feel overwhelmed, you need someone to talk to or you’re thinking about hurting yourself or [suicide](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/11352-recognizing-suicidal-behavior), call or text [988](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/suicide-hotline/) to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline (U.S.). Someone is available to help you 24/7.

If your burnout causes resentment toward the person you’re caring for or you feel like you may be hurting that person, reach out for help immediately. You could contact a friend or family member, a healthcare provider, a social worker or a mental health professional.
